children.title: Noisy Black-Box Optimization Problem
children.top_down_role: Optimization when simulator responses are observable but internal analytical structure is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simulation Optimization Through Noisy Output Observations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the simulation-based objective-access model; decision variables may be discrete, continuous, or mixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simulation-optimization problem has the form \(\min_{x\in\Theta} f(x)\), where \(\Theta\) is the feasible region and \(x\) may be discrete, continuous, or mixed. The value \(f(x)\) is not computed exactly; instead, simulation-replication outputs are observed and may be represented by a random variable \(Y(x,\xi)\), where \(\xi\) denotes simulation randomness, and these observations are used to estimate objective performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulation optimization minimizes an objective over a feasible region when objective values are not directly available. Performance is instead estimated from random simulation outputs, with discrete, continuous, or mixed decisions allowed.
assumptions_latex: x\in\Theta
f(x)\text{ cannot be computed exactly}
Y(x,\xi)\text{ is observed through stochastic or Monte Carlo simulation}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in\Theta}f(x)\text{ is accessed through random simulation outputs }Y(x,\xi).

source_evidence.locator: Overview of the Handbook / 1. Overview of the Handbook / Definition 1-extra-1

source_refs.locator: Overview of the Handbook / 1. Overview of the Handbook / Definition 1-extra-1

knowledge_statements.title: Simulation Optimization Through Noisy Output Observations

source_witnesses.locator: Overview of the Handbook / 1. Overview of the Handbook / Definition 1-extra-1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimization via Simulation Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-value optimization when the objective response distribution is unknown but realizations are observable through stochastic simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimization-via-simulation problem has the form \(\min_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta} g(\mathbf{x})\), where \(g(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}[Y(\mathbf{x},\xi)]\), \(\xi\) represents simulation randomness, the distribution of \(Y(\mathbf{x},\xi)\) as a function of \(\mathbf{x}\) is unknown, and realizations of \(Y(\mathbf{x},\xi)\) can be observed through simulation. A maximization problem can be converted to an equivalent minimization problem by negating the objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An optimization-via-simulation problem minimizes an expected simulation response over a feasible set. Its response distribution is unknown as a function of the decision, but response realizations can be observed through simulation. Maximization can be converted to minimization by negating the objective.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf{x}\in\Theta
g(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{E}[Y(\mathbf{x},\xi)]
\text{The distribution of }Y(\mathbf{x},\xi)\text{ is unknown as a function of }\mathbf{x}.
\text{Realizations of }Y(\mathbf{x},\xi)\text{ are observable through simulation.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{\mathbf{x}\in\Theta}g(\mathbf{x}),\quad\text{with maximization reducible to minimization by objective negation.}

children.title: Continuous Noisy Black-Box Problems
children.top_down_role: Continuous decision spaces supporting local or global stochastic search.

assumptions_latex: The feasible region satisfies \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\).
For every \(x\in X\), the simulator returns an integrable random response \(Y(x,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimization problem is \(\inf_{x\in X} f(x)\).

notation.meaning: simulation response under decision x and random input xi

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-response minimization over a continuous feasible set with simulation-only evaluations.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.5 The black-box and the white-box approach p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous noisy black-box problem is an optimization problem \[\inf_{x\in X} f(x),\qquad f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)],\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) contains continuously variable decisions and the analytic form or derivatives of \(f\) are unavailable. Querying \(x\) produces a realization of \(Y(x,\xi)\), or an estimator formed from finitely many such realizations, rather than an exact value of \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize an unknown expected response over continuous decisions when each simulator query supplies only a noisy response or finite-sample estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Noisy Black-Box Problems

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.5 The black-box and the white-box approach p. 18

children.title: Discrete-Combinatorial Search-Space Family
children.top_down_role: Large discrete decision spaces that cannot be exhaustively simulated.

children.title: Discrete Noisy Black-Box Problems
children.top_down_role: Noisy optimization over large decision spaces composed of individually represented choices.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(D\) is a finite or countably infinite subset of \(\mathbb{Z}^d\).
Each \(x\in D\) has an integrable simulated response \(Y(x,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is \(\inf_{x\in D}\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)]\) with noisy pointwise observations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise noisy optimization on a finite or countable integer-valued domain.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Discrete Optimization p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A discrete noisy black-box problem has the form \[\inf_{x\in D} f(x),\qquad f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)],\] where \(D\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^d\) is finite or countably infinite. The simulator can be queried at an individual \(x\in D\), but it reveals only random responses \(Y(x,\xi)\) or finite-sample estimates of \(f(x)\); an exact objective formula and exact point values are unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize expected simulated performance over a finite or countable integer domain using noisy evaluations at individual feasible points.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete Noisy Black-Box Problems

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Discrete Optimization p. 46

children.title: Combinatorial Noisy Black-Box Problems
children.top_down_role: Noisy optimization over structured configurations, subsets, sequences, or graph-based decisions.

assumptions_latex: The feasible objects form a family \(\mathcal{C}\subseteq 2^E\) or an equivalent finite combinatorial class.
Each \(C\in\mathcal{C}\) has an integrable simulated response \(Y(C,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is \(\inf_{C\in\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{E}[Y(C,\xi)]\), with feasibility and neighborhood structure determined by combinatorial constraints.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noisy optimization whose feasible decisions are structured combinatorial objects.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Discrete Optimization p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A combinatorial noisy black-box problem is \[\inf_{C\in\mathcal{C}} f(C),\qquad f(C)=\mathbb{E}[Y(C,\xi)],\] where \(\mathcal{C}\) is a family of subsets, permutations, graphs, schedules, paths, or other finitely encoded objects subject to combinatorial feasibility constraints. Simulation at \(C\in\mathcal{C}\) returns a noisy response, while the objective is analytically unavailable. The encoding-induced adjacency or exchange operations provide structure beyond mere enumeration of isolated alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize noisy expected performance over structured objects such as subsets, paths, permutations, schedules, or graphs subject to combinatorial feasibility constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Noisy Black-Box Problems

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Discrete Optimization p. 46

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited general discrete-optimization section does not establish the proposed defining distinction based on encoding-induced adjacency or exchange operations. A source specifically supporting this combinatorial noisy-black-box formulation is required.

children.title: Discrete-to-Combinatorial Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions determining whether decisions are treated as isolated points or composed objects.

assumptions_latex: A feasible family \(D\) has a finite encoding \(e:D\to\{0,1\}^m\) or \(e:D\to\mathbb{Z}^m\).
A neighborhood relation \(N(x)\subseteq D\) is available to the optimization method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem is combinatorial relative to \((e,N)\) when feasibility and admissible moves exploit relations among encoded components; otherwise it is only pointwise discrete.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The boundary depends on whether an algorithm uses relational structure in the decision encoding.

source_refs.locator: 1.5 Discrete Optimization p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be discrete. Relative to an encoding \(e\) and neighborhood map \(N\), the problem crosses from pointwise discrete to combinatorial when feasible decisions are composed of finitely encoded components and feasibility or admissible moves are expressed through relations among those components. Formally, membership in \(D\) or membership of \(y\) in \(N(x)\) must depend on joint restrictions on coordinates of \(e(x)\), rather than solely on the identity of \(x\). This boundary is representation-relative: the same finite set can be treated as unstructured alternatives or as structured objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discrete problem is combinatorial when its encoding exposes component relations that determine feasibility or admissible moves; the distinction depends on representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-to-Combinatorial Boundary

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5 Discrete Optimization p. 46

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed necessary boundary—joint coordinate restrictions in a selected encoding—is representation-dependent and is not a generally established criterion separating discrete from combinatorial optimization. The cited locator is insufficient to validate this exact condition.

children.title: Mixed-Variable Noisy Black-Box Problems
children.top_down_role: Coupled continuous, integer, categorical, or conditional decisions.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set satisfies \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_c}\times\mathbb{Z}^{d_i}\times\mathcal{K}\).
For each feasible decision, the simulator returns an integrable response \(Y(x,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is \(\inf_{x\in X}\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)]\) over coupled variable types.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled continuous, integer, and categorical decisions with simulation-only objective evaluations.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Stochastic optimization problems p. 3
1.2.5 The black-box and the white-box approach p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-variable noisy black-box problem is \[\inf_{x\in X} f(x),\qquad f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x,\xi)],\] where \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d_c}\times\mathbb{Z}^{d_i}\times\mathcal{K}\) couples continuous coordinates, integer coordinates, and categorical or conditional choices from \(\mathcal{K}\). Feasibility may make some coordinates active only under particular categorical choices. The simulator supplies noisy evaluations of \(f\), while an exact objective formula is unavailable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize an unknown expected simulation response over coupled continuous, integer, categorical, and possibly conditionally active decisions.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Variable Noisy Black-Box Problems

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Stochastic optimization problems p. 3
1.2.5 The black-box and the white-box approach p. 18

children.title: Structured Simulator Optimization
children.top_down_role: Optimization using simulator-exposed paths, events, states, likelihoods, derivatives, or random-input transformations.

children.title: Sample-Path-Exposing Simulators
children.top_down_role: Simulators exposing realized trajectories for reuse, differentiation, or pathwise optimization.

assumptions_latex: Randomness is represented by \(\xi\) on a probability space, and \(x\in X\) is the simulator input.
The exposed trajectory \(Z_{0:T}(x,\xi)\) determines the performance \(Y(x,\xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A query returns \((Z_{0:T}(x,\xi),Y(x,\xi))\), not merely the scalar response.

notation.meaning: exposed simulated trajectory through horizon T

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simulator interface exposing the realized state path underlying each performance observation.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.5 The black-box and the white-box approach p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A sample-path-exposing simulator is a mapping \[S(x,\xi)=\bigl(Z_{0:T}(x,\xi),Y(x,\xi)\bigr),\qquad Y(x,\xi)=H\bigl(x,Z_{0:T}(x,\xi)\bigr),\] that returns the realized trajectory \(Z_{0:T}\) together with, or instead of, its aggregate performance. Consequently, evaluations sharing the same \(\xi\) can reuse a realized path when well-defined, and pathwise derivatives may be computed whenever \(x\mapsto H(x,Z_{0:T}(x,\xi))\) is differentiable almost surely and interchange with expectation is justified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simulator reveals the realized trajectory generating each response, enabling path reuse or pathwise differentiation when the required regularity holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Path-Exposing Simulators

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2.5 The black-box and the white-box approach p. 18

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The black-box/white-box locator does not clearly support the asserted trajectory-returning interface or the consequences concerning path reuse and pathwise differentiation. Reusing a realized path across decisions also requires additional coupling assumptions because the trajectory depends on the decision.

children.title: Likelihood-Exposing Simulators
children.top_down_role: Simulators whose path or transition laws support likelihood-based estimation.

assumptions_latex: For each \(x\in X\), the simulator law \(P_x\) is dominated by a common measure \(\mu\).
The density \(p_x=dP_x/d\mu\) is differentiable and its score is integrable where used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The simulator exposes \(p_x(Z)\) or \(\nabla_x\log p_x(Z)\), permitting likelihood-ratio identities under valid differentiation-expectation interchange.

notation.meaning: law of the simulated path or output under x
density of P_x with respect to mu

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dominated simulator laws with evaluable likelihoods or scores for realized outputs or paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A likelihood-exposing simulator generates \(Z\sim P_x\) and additionally makes evaluable the density \(p_x(Z)\), a likelihood ratio \(p_{x'}(Z)/p_x(Z)\), or the score \(s_x(Z)=\nabla_x\log p_x(Z)\). If \(h(Z)\) is integrable and differentiation under the integral is valid, then the exposed score supports \[\nabla_x\mathbb{E}_{P_x}[h(Z)]=\mathbb{E}_{P_x}\bigl[h(Z)s_x(Z)\bigr].\] Exposure of sampled outputs alone does not satisfy this definition; the relevant likelihood quantity must also be computable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simulator reveals an evaluable likelihood, likelihood ratio, or score for each realized path, supporting likelihood-ratio estimation under regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Likelihood-Exposing Simulators

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation is supplied for the exact likelihood-exposing interface or its score identity. The mathematical version therefore cannot be promoted at candidate-review level without an authoritative source and locator.

children.title: Event-Exposing Simulators
children.top_down_role: Event-driven simulators exposing clocks, event order, and state transitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Exposing Simulators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-event simulator interface revealing clocks, event identities, ordering, innovations, and state updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a decision \(x\in X\), an event-exposing simulator represents a path by an ordered marked-event sequence \[\bigl(T_n,K_n,Z_{n-1},Z_n\bigr)_{n\geq 1},\qquad Z_n=\Phi(Z_{n-1},K_n,U_n;x),\] where \(T_n\) is the time of event \(n\), \(K_n\) is its event type, \(U_n\) is the random innovation used at that event, and \(\Phi\) is the state-transition map. The interface reveals event times, event order, event types, and pre- and post-event states, so performance may be reconstructed from the event sequence rather than supplied only as an aggregate output.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a chosen decision, the simulator exposes the ordered event times, event types, random event inputs, and associated state transitions from which performance can be reconstructed.
assumptions_latex: The decision belongs to a specified set \(x\in X\).
The simulation state changes at ordered event times \(0=T_0<T_1<T_2<\cdots\).
Each event has a type \(K_n\), a random innovation \(U_n\), and a state update determined by \(\Phi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exposed event record contains \(\bigl(T_n,K_n,Z_{n-1},Z_n\bigr)\) for each simulated event \(n\geq1\).

notation.meaning: random innovation used at the nth event
state immediately after the nth event

source_refs.locator: 2 Discrete-Event processes p. 55
2.5.2 The Markovian structure of a Discrete-Event process p. 121

source_witnesses.locator: 2 Discrete-Event processes p. 55
2.5.2 The Markovian structure of a Discrete-Event process p. 121

children.title: Performance-Horizon Regimes
children.top_down_role: Simulation objectives distinguished by run termination and temporal aggregation.

children.title: Terminating-Simulation Performance
children.top_down_role: Performance derived from naturally terminating replications.

assumptions_latex: For each \(x\in X\), a replication has an almost surely finite stopping time \(\tau(x)\).
The terminal replication performance \(Y(x)\) is integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Performance is \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x)]\) and independent replications yield an unbiased sample-mean estimator.

notation.meaning: natural termination time of a replication

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected performance from complete, naturally terminating, independent simulation replications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Terminating-simulation performance is defined from a replication ending at an almost surely finite, model-determined stopping time \(\tau(x)\). For a measurable integrable functional \(H\), let \[Y(x)=H\bigl(x,Z_{0:\tau(x)}\bigr),\qquad f(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y(x)].\] Given independent complete replications \(Y_1(x),\ldots,Y_n(x)\), the standard estimator is \(\widehat f_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i(x)\), which satisfies \(\mathbb{E}[\widehat f_n(x)]=f(x)\). No steady-state limit is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Performance is the expected output of a complete replication that ends naturally in finite time; independent replication averages estimate it unbiasedly.
knowledge_statements.title: Terminating-Simulation Performance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation is mathematically plausible, but no source is supplied for the model-determined stopping-time definition or its placement in the terminating-simulation regime.

children.title: Steady-State Simulation Performance
children.top_down_role: Long-run performance in persistent stochastic systems.

assumptions_latex: For fixed \(x\), the persistent process \((Z_t^x)_{t\geq0}\) is positive recurrent and ergodic with invariant law \(\pi_x\).
The reward \(g(x,\cdot)\) is integrable under \(\pi_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The long-run average converges almost surely to \(f(x)=\int g(x,z)\,\pi_x(dz)\).

notation.meaning: persistent simulated state process under x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ergodic long-run average performance for a nonterminating stochastic system.

source_refs.locator: 3.3 Infinite Horizon Problems p. 66

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Steady-state simulation performance for decision \(x\) is the invariant-law expectation \[f(x)=\int g(x,z)\,\pi_x(dz).\] If \((Z_t^x)_{t\geq0}\) is positive recurrent and ergodic with invariant distribution \(\pi_x\), and \(g(x,\cdot)\) is \(\pi_x\)-integrable, then \[\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T g(x,Z_t^x)\,dt\longrightarrow f(x)\] almost surely as \(T\to\infty\). The discrete-time analogue replaces the integral by \(T^{-1}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}g(x,Z_t^x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Steady-state performance is the invariant-distribution mean, estimated by a long-run time average when the persistent simulated process is ergodic.
knowledge_statements.title: Steady-State Simulation Performance

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Infinite Horizon Problems p. 66

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record embeds an almost-sure continuous-time ergodic theorem inside a definition. The generic infinite-horizon locator does not verify that its stated positive-recurrence and ergodicity hypotheses suffice for the asserted convergence from the intended initial conditions.

children.title: Transient Finite-Horizon Performance Regime
children.top_down_role: Time-dependent performance before or without stationarity.

children.title: Transient Performance
children.top_down_role: Time-varying performance during pre-stationary system evolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Transient Performance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-specific performance retaining dependence on initialization and nonstationary evolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Transient performance is the expectation of an integrable time-specific or path-specific response under a specified initial distribution, without assuming stationarity or convergence to steady state.
assumptions_latex: The decision satisfies \(x\in X\), the initial law \(\nu_x\) is specified, and the observation time satisfies \(t<\infty\).
The observable \(g(x,Z_t^x)\), or the generalized trajectory functional \(H_t(x,Z_{0:t}^x)\), is measurable and integrable.

notation.meaning: state at time t under decision x
measurable integrable functional of the trajectory through time t

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Finite Horizon Problems p. 65

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Finite Horizon Problems p. 65

children.title: Finite-Horizon Performance
children.top_down_role: Performance evaluated over a prescribed bounded simulation window.

assumptions_latex: A deterministic finite horizon \(T\in\mathbb{N}\) and initial law are fixed.
Stage rewards \(g_t(x,Z_t^x)\) and terminal reward \(h(x,Z_T^x)\) are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite-horizon performance is the expected cumulative reward through \(T\), including any terminal reward.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected cumulative performance over a fixed, deterministic evaluation horizon.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Finite Horizon Problems p. 65

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a fixed deterministic horizon \(T<\infty\), finite-horizon performance under decision or policy \(x\) is \[J_T(x)=\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}g_t(x,Z_t^x)+h(x,Z_T^x)\right],\] provided the displayed random sum is integrable. The initial law and the horizon are part of the performance specification. The criterion requires neither natural termination at \(T\) nor a stationary distribution, and it may therefore retain transient effects throughout the evaluation window.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-horizon performance is expected cumulative stage and terminal reward over a fixed evaluation horizon, with initialization included in the specification.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Horizon Performance

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2 Finite Horizon Problems p. 65

children.title: Stationarity-Free Evaluation Windows
children.top_down_role: Evaluation settings where stationarity is unavailable or irrelevant to the optimization objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity-Free Evaluation Windows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon simulation performance defined without steady-state or stationarity assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in\mathcal X\) be a decision and let \(Y_{1:H}(x,\xi)=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_H)\) denote one simulated trajectory over a fixed finite horizon \(H\in\mathbb N\). Given a measurable path-loss functional \(L_H\), define the window performance by \[J_H(x)=\mathbb E[L_H(Y_{1:H}(x,\xi))].\] This is a stationarity-free evaluation window when the definition requires neither an invariant distribution nor convergence of \(Y_t\) as \(t\to\infty\). The optimization problem is \(\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}J_H(x)\), with all initialization and transient effects included in the trajectory law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-window objective averages a measurable loss over finite simulated trajectories, retaining initialization and transient effects without assuming steady state.
assumptions_latex: \(H<\infty\) is fixed.
\(L_H(Y_{1:H}(x,\xi))\) is integrable for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_H(x)=\mathbb E[L_H(Y_{1:H}(x,\xi))]\) is defined without a stationarity assumption.

notation.meaning: simulated trajectory under decision x and randomness xi

review_flags: Exact source for the stationarity-free finite-horizon formulation is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the terminal container and is mathematically coherent, but no inspectable source supports this particular stationarity-free finite-window formulation.

children.top_down_role: Optimization in which objective or feasibility information is obtained from stochastic simulation.

children.title: Explicit Constraints with Simulated Objectives
children.top_down_role: Known feasible regions paired with simulation-estimated objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Constraints with Simulated Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Known deterministic feasibility conditions with an objective accessible through stochastic simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) and let explicitly evaluable functions \(g_j:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\), define \(F=\{x\in\mathcal X:g_j(x)\le 0\text{ for all }j\}\). If a simulator returns an integrable random response \(Y(x,\xi)\) whose mean \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)]\) is not directly available, then simulation optimization with explicit constraints is \[\min_{x\in F} f(x)=\min_{x\in F}\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)].\] Feasibility can be checked without simulation; simulation is required only to estimate or compare objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The feasible region is known and directly testable, while each objective value is an expectation estimated from stochastic simulator outputs.
assumptions_latex: \(Y(x,\xi)\) is integrable for every \(x\in F\).
Each \(g_j(x)\) is directly evaluable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{x\in F}\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)]\) has explicit feasibility and a simulated objective.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Stochastic optimization problems p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Stochastic optimization problems p. 3

children.title: Noisy Response Constraints
children.top_down_role: Constraint performance observed through stochastic simulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Noisy Response Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-response constraints whose values must be inferred from stochastic simulator observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y_0(x,\xi)\) be an objective response and let \(Y_j(x,\xi)\), \(j=1,\ldots,m\), be integrable constraint responses. Define \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y_0(x,\xi)]\) and \(c_j(x)=\mathbb E[Y_j(x,\xi)]\). A simulation problem with noisy response constraints is \[\min_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad c_j(x)\le b_j,\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.\] The simulator supplies noisy realizations rather than exact values of \(c_j(x)\), so feasibility itself must be statistically estimated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both objective performance and constraint feasibility depend on unknown mean responses estimated from noisy simulation output.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_j(x,\xi)\) is integrable for every \(x\in\mathcal X\) and \(j=0,\ldots,m\).
The thresholds \(b_1,\ldots,b_m\) are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible exactly when \(\mathbb E[Y_j(x,\xi)]\le b_j\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,m\).

children.title: Latent Simulator Feasibility Boundary
children.top_down_role: Feasibility revealed only through simulator completion, failure, or categorical output.

children.title: Hidden Simulator Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Feasibility information exposed only through simulator behavior rather than explicit constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Simulator Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility defined by an unobserved simulator-validity region rather than explicit analytic constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a declared input domain and let \(F_{\mathrm{sim}}\subseteq\mathcal X\) be an unknown set on which the simulator produces a valid performance response. Hidden simulator feasibility means that no evaluable analytic description of \(F_{\mathrm{sim}}\) is supplied. A query at \(x\) returns either a valid response \(Y(x,\xi)\) or feasibility information generated by the simulator. Thus the optimization domain is \(F_{\mathrm{sim}}\), but membership must be learned from queries rather than checked before simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simulator is valid only on an unknown subset of inputs, and membership in that subset must be learned through simulator queries.
assumptions_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{sim}}\subseteq\mathcal X\) is fixed during the optimization run.
A valid objective response exists only for \(x\in F_{\mathrm{sim}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_{\mathrm{sim}}\) is the feasible set, but no explicit membership predicate is initially available.
review_flags: A source distinguishing hidden feasibility from noisy constraints is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits hidden simulator feasibility, but a source is required to establish the intended distinction between an unknown validity region, hidden constraints, and noisy response constraints.

children.title: Binary Simulator Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Feasibility evidence returned solely as a categorical success or failure outcome.

knowledge_statements.title: Binary Simulator Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simulator feasibility observed through a binary random response and an acceptance threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in\mathcal X\), let the simulator return \(B(x,\xi)\in\{0,1\}\), where \(B=1\) denotes a feasible or valid run. Define the feasibility probability \(p(x)=\mathbb P(B(x,\xi)=1)\). Given a tolerance \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), binary simulator feasibility declares \(x\) feasible when \[p(x)\ge 1-\alpha.\] For deterministic simulator validity, this specializes to \(\alpha=0\) and an almost-sure binary membership response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary simulator output records success or feasibility; a decision is accepted when its success probability meets a prescribed threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(B(x,\xi)\) is measurable and binary for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
\(\alpha\in[0,1]\) is fixed before evaluation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_\alpha=\{x\in\mathcal X:\mathbb P(B(x,\xi)=1)\ge1-\alpha\}\) is the binary-response feasible set.

notation.meaning: probability of a feasible simulator response

review_flags: A source is needed to confirm the intended probabilistic threshold convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The probabilistic binary-response formulation is coherent, but the terminal title does not itself determine the chance-threshold convention or the claimed deterministic specialization.

children.title: Simulator Failure as Feasibility Evidence
children.top_down_role: Use of crashes, noncompletion, or invalid outputs as indirect feasibility signals.

knowledge_statements.title: Simulator Failure as Feasibility Evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which run failure may legitimately be interpreted as evidence of infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(x,\xi)\in\{0,1\}\) indicate successful simulator completion. A failed run \(R=0\) is evidence about feasibility only if the failure mechanism is coupled to feasibility, for example when \(\mathbb P(R=0\mid x\in F)=0\). Under that condition, observing \(R(x,\xi)=0\) certifies \(x\notin F\). If feasible inputs can fail because of numerical errors, timeouts, or unrelated randomness, then a single failure does not certify infeasibility; it identifies only a failed evaluation unless the failure probabilities are separately modeled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulator failure certifies infeasibility only when feasible inputs cannot fail; otherwise failures may reflect numerical or operational errors.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq\mathcal X\) is the intended feasible set.
\(R=0\) records failure to produce a valid simulator response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(x,\xi)=0\Rightarrow x\notin F\) is valid only under a no-false-failure condition such as \(\mathbb P(R=0\mid x\in F)=0\).
review_flags: The calibration condition is mathematically necessary but lacks a supplied supporting source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container, but the displayed condition conditions on the proposition `x in F` while x is presented as fixed. Certification requires a sourced pointwise no-false-failure condition for every feasible input, together with a clear probability model.

children.title: Search-Objective Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Distinctions among terminal recommendation, cumulative performance, and tracking.

children.title: Offline Terminal Recommendation
children.top_down_role: Simulation effort evaluated by the quality of a final recommended decision.

knowledge_statements.title: Offline Terminal Recommendation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-budget search assessed solely by the final decision recommended after simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let an adaptive policy use \(N\) simulator calls and then return a terminal recommendation \(\widehat x_N\in\mathcal X\). For a minimization objective \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)]\) with optimum \(f^*=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), offline terminal performance is measured by the simple regret \[r_N=\mathbb E[f(\widehat x_N)-f^*].\] Simulator inputs used during search incur no performance charge in this criterion; only the quality of \(\widehat x_N\) after the budget is exhausted is evaluated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An offline policy spends a simulation budget, returns one final decision, and is judged by that recommendation’s expected optimality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb N\) is a fixed simulation budget.
\(f(\widehat x_N)\) is integrable and \(f^*>-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r_N=\mathbb E[f(\widehat x_N)-f^*]\) evaluates terminal recommendation quality.

children.title: Online Cumulative Performance
children.top_down_role: Performance accumulated while information is acquired.

knowledge_statements.title: Online Cumulative Performance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential simulation decisions assessed by losses accumulated during information acquisition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At rounds \(t=1,\ldots,T\), an online policy selects \(X_t\in\mathcal X\), observes a stochastic response with mean \(f(X_t)\), and then updates its information. For stationary minimization with \(f^*=\inf_{x\in\mathcal X}f(x)\), its expected cumulative regret is \[R_T=\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\bigl(f(X_t)-f^*\bigr)\right].\] Unlike an offline terminal criterion, every exploratory decision contributes to performance, so information acquisition and immediate objective quality are jointly assessed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An online policy is judged by the objective gaps accumulated at every decision while it learns, not merely by a final recommendation.
assumptions_latex: \(T\in\mathbb N\) is the evaluation horizon.
\(f(X_t)\) is integrable for every round \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T=\mathbb E[\sum_{t=1}^T(f(X_t)-f^*)]\) measures cumulative online performance.
review_flags: The supplied sources do not specifically locate the online cumulative-regret formulation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stationary cumulative-regret definition fits online cumulative performance and is internally coherent, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-horizon online-learning cumulative reward objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance is accumulated while measurements are selected and information is acquired, rather than evaluated only through a terminal recommendation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a measurement policy \(\pi\), horizon \(N\), stage weights \(\gamma^n\), and decisions \(x^n\) generated by \(\pi\), the online-learning objective is
\[
\operatorname*{maximize}_{\pi}\;\mathbb E^{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{n=1}^{N}\gamma^n\mu_{x^n}\right].
\]
The expectation is over the uncertain alternative values and the observations made during learning. Such online-learning problems are called bandit problems; with a finite discrete alternative set, they are multi-armed bandit problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Online learning values rewards earned while information is being acquired. A measurement policy maximizes expected weighted cumulative reward over the finite horizon. The finite-discrete specialization is the multi-armed bandit problem.
assumptions_latex: N\in\mathbb N\text{ is the measurement horizon}
x^n\text{ is the stage-}n\text{ decision generated by policy }\pi
\gamma^n\text{ is the stated stage-}n\text{ reward weight}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{maximize}_{\pi}\;\mathbb E^{\pi}\!\left[\sum_{n=1}^{N}\gamma^n\mu_{x^n}\right].

children.title: Nonstationary Tracking Regime Family
children.top_down_role: Adaptation to changing simulation responses or drifting optima.

children.title: Nonstationary Simulation Optimization
children.top_down_role: Optimization when simulator responses change over calendar time or decision epochs.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonstationary Simulation Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simulation optimization with objective or response laws that vary over decision time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For rounds \(t=1,\ldots,T\), let \(f_t:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be a time-indexed objective and let the simulator return \(Y_t(x,\xi_t)\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[Y_t(x,\xi_t)]=f_t(x)\). A nonstationary simulation-optimization policy selects \(X_t\) using information available before round \(t\). Relative to instantaneous minimizers \(x_t^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f_t(x)\), a standard tracking criterion is dynamic regret \[R_T^{\mathrm{dyn}}=\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T\bigl(f_t(X_t)-f_t(x_t^*)\bigr)\right].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The simulated response law changes over time, so decisions are compared with the optimum applicable at each round.
assumptions_latex: \(f_t\) attains a minimum on \(\mathcal X\) for every \(t\).
\(Y_t(x,\xi_t)\) is integrable with mean \(f_t(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_T^{\mathrm{dyn}}\) measures performance against the time-varying sequence of instantaneous optima.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports nonstationary dynamic-regret simulation optimization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The time-indexed simulation model and dynamic-regret criterion fit nonstationary simulation optimization, but no source supports the selected formulation and benchmark.

children.title: Optimum Tracking
children.top_down_role: Maintenance of recommendations near a moving optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimum Tracking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance comparison between sequential decisions and instantaneous time-varying minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_t:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) attain its minimum at some \(x_t^*\) for each \(t=1,\ldots,T\). For a decision sequence \((X_t)_{t=1}^T\), define the pointwise tracking gap \(e_t=f_t(X_t)-f_t(x_t^*)\ge0\). Its cumulative tracking error is \[E_T=\sum_{t=1}^T e_t.\] Consequently, \(E_T=0\) if and only if \(X_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f_t(x)\) for every \(t\); small \(E_T\) quantifies approximate optimum tracking.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tracking error sums each decision’s gap from the current optimum and vanishes exactly when every decision is currently optimal.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_t\) attains a finite minimum on \(\mathcal X\).
\(X_t\in\mathcal X\) for every \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_T=0\iff X_t\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f_t(x)\) for all \(t=1,ldots,T\).
review_flags: A source for this optimum-tracking criterion is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tracking-gap property is mathematically valid and fits the container, but no source is supplied and the conclusion contains `ldots` instead of `\ldots`.

children.title: Abrupt-Regime Response
children.top_down_role: Adaptation following sudden changes in the simulated system.

knowledge_statements.title: Abrupt-Regime Response
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tracking under piecewise-stationary objectives separated by discrete change points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(1=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_K<\tau_{K+1}=T+1\) be change points and let \(f^{(0)},\ldots,f^{(K)}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\). An abrupt-regime model has \[f_t=f^{(k)}\quad\text{whenever}\quad \tau_k\le t<\tau_{k+1}.\] If \(x_k^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}f^{(k)}(x)\), response after change \(\tau_k\) may be quantified by the first delay \(d_k\ge0\) for which the selected decision satisfies \(f^{(k)}(X_{\tau_k+d_k})-f^{(k)}(x_k^*)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective changes at discrete times and remains fixed between changes; response delay records how quickly decisions become near-optimal afterward.
assumptions_latex: Every regime objective \(f^{(k)}\) attains a minimum on \(\mathcal X\).
The accuracy tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_k=\inf\{d\ge0:f^{(k)}(X_{\tau_k+d})-f^{(k)}(x_k^*)\le\varepsilon\}\) measures post-change response.
review_flags: The precise abrupt-change and response-delay convention requires a supporting source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The piecewise-stationary model fits abrupt-regime response, but the response-delay convention lacks a source and does not specify integer delays, the finite admissible time range, or the value when the tolerance is never reached.

children.title: Gradual-Drift Response
children.top_down_role: Adaptation under progressive movement of responses or optimal decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradual-Drift Response
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A bounded-variation condition for objectives that evolve incrementally over time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_t:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), \(t=1,\ldots,T\), be time-indexed objectives. Their cumulative uniform drift is \[V_T=\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|f_{t+1}(x)-f_t(x)|.\] The sequence satisfies a gradual-drift condition with per-round bound \(\delta\ge0\) when \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|f_{t+1}(x)-f_t(x)|\le\delta\) for every \(t<T\). This implies \(V_T\le(T-1)\delta\), providing a quantitative environment-change scale for evaluating tracking response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive objective functions differ uniformly by at most a prescribed amount, bounding total environmental variation over the horizon.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_t\) is real-valued on the common domain \(\mathcal X\).
The displayed suprema are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|f_{t+1}(x)-f_t(x)|\le\delta\) for all \(t<T\) implies \(V_T\le(T-1)\delta\).
review_flags: A source for the selected uniform-drift convention is missing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded uniform-drift condition and its variation bound are correct and the condition kind fits the container, but the selected drift convention has no cited source.

children.title: Simulator Access Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Access patterns governing how optimization procedures submit decisions, receive outputs, or control replications.

assumptions_latex: The feasible decision set is \(X\neq\varnothing\).
For each \(x\in X\), the simulator can generate an output from a distribution \(P_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The access interface determines which simulator operations an optimization method may invoke.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-level taxonomy for stochastic simulators used by optimization procedures.

source_refs.locator: 3. Simulation-Based Optimization: An Overview p. 29
source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simulator access interface is an oracle \(\mathcal O\) whose permitted queries are specified from the following operations: sampling, \(\mathcal O(x)\sim P_x\); coupled sampling, \((\mathcal O(x_1,u),\ldots,\mathcal O(x_k,u))\) under a shared random input \(u\); and, when exposed, structural queries returning pathwise derivatives, likelihood ratios, constraints, or state trajectories. An optimization method is compatible with the interface only if every observation it uses is obtainable through the declared operations. A sampling-only interface reveals neither an analytic expression for \(P_x\) nor exact values of expectations under \(P_x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An access interface specifies whether an optimizer may request independent samples, coupled samples, trajectories, constraints, or derivative information from the simulator.
knowledge_statements.title: Simulator Access Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: 3. Simulation-Based Optimization: An Overview p. 29
source_witnesses.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the leaf, but the proposed oracle taxonomy and the claims about coupled, derivative, constraint, and trajectory queries are more specific than the cited overview locator can presently support. The plain statement also calls samples independent although the LaTeX statement does not impose independence. A source directly defining simulator-access models is required.

children.title: Simulator Evaluation Contracts
children.top_down_role: Evaluation protocols governing returned responses, execution status, metadata, or resource limits.

assumptions_latex: Each evaluation uses a declared decision \(x\in X\), fidelity or horizon \(h\), and randomization identifier \(s\).
All returned quantities are measurable functions of the simulator inputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The contract fixes the conditional law and metadata required to interpret, reproduce, and compare simulator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal contract for interpreting individual evaluations and their dependence structure.

source_refs.locator: 4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A simulator evaluation contract is satisfied when every call with inputs \((x,h,s)\) returns a tuple \((Y,C,M)\), where \(Y\) is the objective observation, \(C\) contains declared constraint observations, and \(M\) records cost, horizon, fidelity, termination status, and randomization metadata. The contract must specify the conditional law \(\mathcal L((Y,C)\mid x,h,s)\), whether distinct calls are independent, and whether equal identifiers induce common random numbers. It must also declare integrability requirements, failure handling, and which component estimates the target performance \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An evaluation contract specifies returned outputs, their conditional distribution, dependence across calls, computational metadata, failure handling, and the target performance being estimated.
knowledge_statements.title: Simulator Evaluation Contracts

source_witnesses.locator: 4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role is plausible, but this detailed evaluation contract, including seeds, fidelity, metadata, failure handling, and common-random-number semantics, is a synthesized interface specification not reliably supported by the cited general simulation section. A direct source or explicit standard-field rationale is required.

children.title: Objective Estimation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Simulation estimators organized by run structure and temporal dependence.

children.title: Independent-Replication Estimation
children.top_down_role: Replication-based estimation for terminating simulations.

assumptions_latex: For a fixed decision \(x\), the terminating-run outputs \(Y_1(x),Y_2(x),\ldots\) are independent and identically distributed.
The mean \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y_1(x)]\) exists and the variance satisfies \(0<\sigma^2(x)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1(x))<\infty\).
The finite-sample estimators are formed with an integer \(n\ge 2\), and the confidence level uses \(0<\alpha<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sample mean is unbiased with variance \(\sigma^2(x)/n\), and its Studentized error is asymptotically standard normal.

notation.meaning: standard-normal quantile of cumulative probability p

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminating simulations with independent, identically distributed replications.

source_refs.locator: 4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\bar Y_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i(x)\) and \(S_n^2(x)=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i(x)-\bar Y_n(x))^2\). Then \(\mathbb E[\bar Y_n(x)]=f(x)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n(x))=\sigma^2(x)/n\). As \(n\to\infty\), \(\sqrt n(\bar Y_n(x)-f(x))/S_n(x)\Rightarrow N(0,1)\). Consequently, \(\bar Y_n(x)\pm z_{1-\alpha/2}S_n(x)/\sqrt n\) is an asymptotic two-sided confidence interval with coverage \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent and identically distributed terminating runs with positive finite variance, the sample mean is unbiased, its variance decreases inversely with the replication count, and Studentization gives an asymptotic normal confidence interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Independent-Replication Estimation

source_witnesses.locator: 4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

children.title: Dependent-Output Estimation Family
children.top_down_role: Output analysis for serially dependent simulation runs.

children.title: Batch-Means Estimation
children.top_down_role: Aggregation-based output analysis for serially dependent simulation observations.

assumptions_latex: The stationary output sequence \((Y_t)_{t\ge1}\) has mean \(\mu\) and satisfies a central limit theorem with long-run variance \(\tau^2\).
The run length is \(n=ab\), with batch size \(b\to\infty\) and number of batches \(a\to\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Batch averages estimate the sampling variance of the overall mean while retaining within-batch dependence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonoverlapping batch means for a stationary dependent simulation output sequence.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) into \(a\) consecutive nonoverlapping batches of length \(b\). Compute \(\bar Y_j^{(b)}=b^{-1}\sum_{t=(j-1)b+1}^{jb}Y_t\), \(\bar Y_n=a^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^a\bar Y_j^{(b)}\), and \(\widehat{\tau}^2=b(a-1)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^a(\bar Y_j^{(b)}-\bar Y_n)^2\). Report \(\bar Y_n\) with estimated variance \(\widehat{\tau}^2/n\), stopping when a prespecified run budget or confidence-interval half-width criterion is met. Under the stated limits and standard mixing conditions, \(\widehat{\tau}^2\) is consistent for \(\tau^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide one dependent run into long consecutive batches, treat batch averages as asymptotically independent, and use their sample variance to estimate the mean's long-run variance.
knowledge_statements.title: Batch-Means Estimation

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm fits the leaf and its formulas use the conventional long-run-variance scaling. However, a central limit theorem alone does not imply consistency of the batch-means variance estimator, and the phrase 'standard mixing conditions' does not state sufficient hypotheses. The cited Markov-chain locator is indirect and cannot establish the required batch-means consistency theorem.

children.title: Time-Series Output Estimation
children.top_down_role: Dependence-aware estimation based on temporal models or spectral structure.

assumptions_latex: The process \((Y_t)_{t\in\mathbb Z}\) is covariance-stationary with mean \(\mu\).
Its autocovariances \(\gamma_k=\operatorname{Cov}(Y_0,Y_k)\) are absolutely summable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The variance of the sample mean is governed by the spectral density at frequency zero, not merely by the marginal variance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary time-series representation of uncertainty in a dependent simulation average.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\bar Y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^nY_t\), 
\[n\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_n)=\gamma_0+2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{n}\right)\gamma_k\longrightarrow \tau^2:=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\gamma_k=2\pi g(0).\]
Thus consistent uncertainty quantification for \(\mu\) requires an estimator of \(\tau^2\), such as a consistent spectral-variance or batch-means estimator. If a central limit theorem also holds, then \(\sqrt n(\bar Y_n-\mu)\Rightarrow N(0,\tau^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For dependent stationary output, the sample mean's uncertainty is determined by all autocovariances, equivalently the spectrum at zero frequency.
knowledge_statements.title: Time-Series Output Estimation

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

children.title: Serial-Dependence Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Assessment of dependence patterns that affect output-estimation choices.

assumptions_latex: After removal of any prescribed transient, \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\) are observations from a covariance-stationary process.
The sample autocovariances are computed using a common declared normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Autocorrelation and effective-sample-size diagnostics quantify observed serial dependence but do not by themselves establish stationarity or independence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample diagnostics for dependence in a single simulation-output series.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For chosen lag limit \(K<n\), compute \(\widehat\rho_k=\widehat\gamma_k/\widehat\gamma_0\) for \(1\le k\le K\), inspect the autocorrelation sequence, and estimate \(\widehat n_{\mathrm{eff}}=n/(1+2\sum_{k=1}^{K}w_k\widehat\rho_k)\) using declared nonnegative truncation weights \(w_k\). Large persistent values of \(\lvert\widehat\rho_k\rvert\), or \(\widehat n_{\mathrm{eff}}\ll n\), diagnose material serial dependence. A portmanteau statistic may test selected zero-autocorrelation restrictions, but failure to reject them is not a certificate of independence or adequate warm-up.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample autocorrelations, effective sample size, and portmanteau tests can flag serial dependence, but cannot certify stationarity or independence.
knowledge_statements.title: Serial-Dependence Diagnostics

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a diagnostic procedure rather than a mathematical condition, so algorithm is the better terminal kind. Moreover, the finite-lag effective-sample-size denominator can be nonpositive or unstable, and its interpretation depends on a specified truncation or initial-sequence rule. The indirect Markov-chain locator does not support these diagnostic conventions or the portmanteau claim.

children.title: Regenerative Estimation
children.top_down_role: Cycle-based estimation using recurring stochastic states.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Atom and regenerative return cycles for an ergodic Markov chain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition together with the regenerative-block consequence stated in the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf P\) be an ergodic Markov transition kernel with unique stationary probability measure \(\pi\). A Borel set \(A\) is an atom for \(\mathbf P\) if, for every measurable \(B\), \(\mathbf P(w,B)\) is independent of \(w\in A\), and \(\pi(A)>0\). If \(M(0)\in A\), define \[T_1^{(A)}=\min\{n:M(n)\in A\},\qquad T_{i+1}^{(A)}=\min\{n>T_i^{(A)}:M(n)\in A\}.\] Then \(M(1),M(T_1^{(A)}+1),M(T_2^{(A)}+1),\ldots\) have the same distribution, and the path segments delimited by successive return times are independent regenerative pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An atom is a positive-stationary-probability Borel set on which the transition law is constant. When the chain starts in the atom, successive returns delimit independent regenerative path pieces.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf P\text{ is an ergodic Markov transition kernel with unique stationary law }\pi
A\text{ is a Borel set}
M(0)\in A\text{ for the regenerative-cycle conclusion}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall B,\ \mathbf P(w,B)\text{ is constant for }w\in A\bigr]\land \pi(A)>0,\quad\text{and successive returns to }A\text{ delimit independent regenerative pieces.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regenerative cycle formula for stationary expectations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded cycle-reward representation using the regeneration time defined in the surrounding text.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbf P\) be an ergodic Markov process with atom \(A\) and stationary distribution \(\pi\). For every measurable \(H\) integrable with respect to \(\pi\), \[\int H(w)\,d\pi(w)=\frac{\mathbb E\!\left[\sum_{n=1}^{T^{(A)}}H(M(n))\right]}{\mathbb E[T^{(A)}]}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an ergodic Markov process with an atom, a stationary expectation equals the expected reward accumulated during one regenerative cycle divided by the expected cycle length.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf P\text{ is an ergodic Markov process with atom }A
\pi\text{ is the stationary distribution of }\mathbf P
H\text{ is measurable and integrable with respect to }\pi
T^{(A)}\text{ is the regenerative cycle time defined in the surrounding text}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \int H\,d\pi=\frac{\mathbb E\left[\sum_{n=1}^{T^{(A)}}H(M(n))\right]}{\mathbb E[T^{(A)}]}.

children.title: Natural Regeneration
children.top_down_role: Regeneration arising directly from simulated system dynamics.

assumptions_latex: The simulated process \((X_t)_{t\ge0}\) has stopping times \(0=T_0<T_1<T_2<\cdots\) at which its physical state naturally resets.
Post-regeneration evolution is independent of the past and has the same law after every \(T_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The complete cycles between successive regeneration times are independent and identically distributed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regeneration induced by an actual recurrent reset state or event of the simulated system.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Natural regeneration occurs when stopping times \((T_k)_{k\ge0}\) are generated by events in the original simulated dynamics and, for every \(k\), the shifted future \((X_{T_k+t})_{t\ge0}\) is independent of the history through \(T_k\) and has a common law. For a reward \(r\), define \(L_k=T_k-T_{k-1}\) and \(R_k=\sum_{t=T_{k-1}}^{T_k-1}r(X_t)\). Then the complete cycle pairs \((R_k,L_k)\) are independent and identically distributed, permitting estimation of the steady-state mean by ratios of accumulated cycle rewards and lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A natural reset event makes successive simulation cycles independent and identically distributed, so steady-state performance can be estimated from cycle rewards and lengths.
knowledge_statements.title: Natural Regeneration

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regenerative system and regeneration cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines probabilistic regeneration and states the cycle structure available under additional regularity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A system is regenerative at deterministic or random times \(\tau_0<\tau_1<\tau_2<\cdots\) when, at each \(\tau_i\), it probabilistically restarts: its future behavior has the applicable restart law and is independent of its past behavior. Under suitable additional conditions, successive regenerative cycles are independent and identically distributed stochastic processes. If the regeneration points are random, their successive cycle lengths \(\tau_{i+1}-\tau_i\) are i.i.d. random variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regenerative system probabilistically starts anew at each regeneration time, making its future independent of its past. Under suitable additional conditions, successive cycles are i.i.d.; when regeneration times are random, the cycle lengths are also i.i.d.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_0<\tau_1<\tau_2<\cdots\) are deterministic or random regeneration times.
At every \(\tau_i\), the system has the applicable restart law and its future behavior is independent of its past behavior.
Suitable additional conditions hold for the asserted i.i.d. cycle conclusions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successive regenerative cycles are i.i.d.; if the regeneration points are random, then \(\{\tau_{i+1}-\tau_i\}_{i\ge 0}\) are i.i.d. random lengths.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: State-dependent minorization condition for artificial regeneration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded kernel domination condition used to construct regenerative structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist a measurable function \(\lambda\) satisfying \(0\leq\lambda(z)<1\) and a probability measure \(\nu\) such that, for every applicable state \(z\) and measurable set \(B\), \[\mathbf P(z,B)\geq \lambda(z)\nu(B).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transition kernel dominates a fixed probability measure at each state, with a measurable state-dependent coefficient between zero and one.
assumptions_latex: \mathbf P\text{ is a Markov transition kernel}
\nu\text{ is a probability measure}
\lambda\text{ is measurable and }0\leq\lambda(z)<1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf P(z,B)\geq\lambda(z)\nu(B)\quad\text{for every applicable }z\text{ and measurable }B.

children.title: Constructed Regeneration
children.top_down_role: Artificial regenerative structure introduced through model-specific state or event design.

assumptions_latex: A Markov kernel \(P\) admits an exactly implementable decomposition on a measurable set \(C\).
The auxiliary randomization used to declare regenerations is independent conditional on the simulated transition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented simulation has regeneration times while preserving the original \(X\)-marginal transition kernel.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Artificial cycle construction that preserves the simulator's marginal dynamics.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a valid mixture \(P(x,\cdot)=\varepsilon\nu(\cdot)+(1-\varepsilon)R(x,\cdot)\) for \(x\in C\), augment the simulation with \(\Delta_n\in\{0,1\}\). Whenever \(X_n\in C\), draw \(\Delta_n\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\varepsilon)\); if \(\Delta_n=1\), draw \(X_{n+1}\sim\nu\), and otherwise draw \(X_{n+1}\sim R(X_n,\cdot)\). Outside \(C\), draw from \(P(X_n,\cdot)\). Declare \(n+1\) a regeneration time when \(\Delta_n=1\). Output complete augmented cycles, discarding any initial incomplete cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Construct regeneration by expressing selected transitions as an exact mixture, sampling a latent mixture indicator, and declaring regeneration whenever its state-independent component is selected.
knowledge_statements.title: Constructed Regeneration

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed mixture construction is recognizable, and algorithm is the correct role, but the assumption that auxiliary randomization is independent conditional on the simulated transition is ambiguous and does not directly describe the generative split used in the statement. The cited general Markov-chain section does not provide inspectable support for this exact construction.

children.title: Split-Chain Regeneration
children.top_down_role: Regenerative structure obtained through an augmented chain representation.

assumptions_latex: For a Markov kernel \(P\), a measurable set \(C\), constant \(\varepsilon>0\), and probability measure \(\nu\), \(P(x,A)\ge\varepsilon\nu(A)\) for every \(x\in C\) and measurable \(A\).
The chain returns to \(C\) with probability one from the relevant initial laws.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nummelin splitting yields an augmented chain with an atom whose returns are regeneration times and whose \(X\)-marginal kernel remains \(P\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete-time Nummelin splitting under a one-step small-set minorization.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in C\), define the residual kernel \(R(x,A)=(P(x,A)-\varepsilon
u(A))/(1-\varepsilon)\) when \(\varepsilon<1\). The split transition selects \(
u\) with probability \(\varepsilon\) and \(R(x,\cdot)\) otherwise; outside \(C\), it uses \(P\). Its marginal transition satisfies \(\varepsilon
u(A)+(1-\varepsilon)R(x,A)=P(x,A)\). In the augmented state space, the selected \(
u\)-component is an atom, and successive returns to that atom define regenerative cycles under the recurrence assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small-set minorization decomposes a Markov transition into state-independent and residual parts; an auxiliary indicator turns the state-independent part into a regenerative atom.
knowledge_statements.title: Split-Chain Regeneration

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minorization and residual-kernel identity are standard, but merely saying that the chain returns to the small set with probability one does not explicitly guarantee the repeated returns needed for successive regenerative cycles. The atom construction also depends on the precise split-chain convention. A direct theorem locator with the recurrence hypotheses is required.

children.title: Artificial-Regeneration Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural limitations affecting whether introduced regeneration supports reliable output analysis.

assumptions_latex: Artificial regeneration is proposed for a simulated process with transition kernel \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Regenerative inference is invalid unless the augmentation preserves \(P\) and produces genuinely regenerative, integrable cycles.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions whose failure invalidates artificial-regeneration estimators or their uncertainty statements.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Artificial-regeneration inference fails if the alleged minorization is false, if the residual kernel is not nonnegative, or if the auxiliary splitting rule changes the \(X\)-marginal kernel \(P\). Even with a valid split, ordinary regenerative variance estimation is unavailable when regeneration times are not almost surely recurrent, \(\mathbb E[L_1]=\infty\), or the moment conditions required for the cycle central limit theorem fail, such as \(\mathbb E[(R_1-\mu L_1)^2]=\infty\). Approximate resets or merely frequent visits to a set do not create independent and identically distributed cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Artificial regeneration is invalid if splitting changes the original chain, lacks a true minorization, fails to recur, or produces cycles without the moments required for inference.
knowledge_statements.title: Artificial-Regeneration Validity Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 2.1 Markov chains with discrete time p. 58

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct content kind, and the listed failure modes are plausible. The exact recurrence and moment requirements for regenerative laws of large numbers, central limit theorems, and variance estimation must nevertheless be tied to a direct regenerative-process source; the cited general Markov-chain section is insufficient.

children.title: Monte Carlo Sampling Error
children.top_down_role: Finite-simulation uncertainty in estimated performance.

assumptions_latex: For a fixed decision \(x\), the simulator outputs \(Y_1(x),Y_2(x),\ldots\) are independent and identically distributed with mean \(f(x)\) and finite variance \(\sigma^2(x)\).
The replication count \(n\) is a positive integer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite replication produces zero-mean estimation error with standard deviation \(\sigma(x)/\sqrt n\).

notation.meaning: standard deviation of one simulator output

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pure finite-sampling error at a fixed decision, excluding model and discretization bias.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat f_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i(x)\) and \(E_n(x)=\widehat f_n(x)-f(x)\). Then \(\mathbb E[E_n(x)]=0\), \(\operatorname{Var}(E_n(x))=\sigma^2(x)/n\), and \(E_n(x)=O_{\mathbb P}(n^{-1/2})\). If the classical central limit theorem applies, then \(\sqrt nE_n(x)\Rightarrow N(0,\sigma^2(x))\). This error is conditional on the chosen simulator model, horizon, initialization, discretization, and decision; it excludes bias and input-model uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Monte Carlo sampling error is the random difference between an average of independent and identically distributed simulator outputs and their simulator expectation; its standard deviation decreases at the square-root rate.
knowledge_statements.title: Monte Carlo Sampling Error

knowledge_statements.statement_title: IID Monte Carlo Average: Unbiasedness, Variance, and Asymptotics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic finite-sample and asymptotic properties of an IID Monte Carlo average.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let s=\mathbb{E}_p[f(X)] and let X_1,\ldots,X_n\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}p. Define \widehat{s}_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i). Then \mathbb{E}[\widehat{s}_n]=s. If \sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}_p(f(X))<\infty, then \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{s}_n)=\sigma^2/n, \widehat{s}_n\to s almost surely, and \sqrt n(\widehat{s}_n-s)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2). Estimating \sigma^2 from the sampled values and dividing by n yields an estimated variance for \widehat{s}_n and supports asymptotic normal confidence intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent samples from the target distribution, the sample average is unbiased. If the integrand has finite variance, the estimator variance is that variance divided by the sample size, the average converges almost surely to the target expectation, and its normalized error is asymptotically normal.
assumptions_latex: s=\mathbb{E}_p[f(X)]
X_1,\ldots,X_n\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}p
\operatorname{Var}_p(f(X))=\sigma^2<\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb{E}[\widehat{s}_n]=s,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{s}_n)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},\quad \widehat{s}_n\xrightarrow{a.s.}s,\quad \sqrt n(\widehat{s}_n-s)\Rightarrow\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monte Carlo sample-mean estimator and its variance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation estimation and finite-sample uncertainty for independent sampling from a probability density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(n)} be independent draws from a probability density p, with \operatorname{Var}_{X\sim p}(f(X))<\infty. The Monte Carlo sample mean \widehat{\mu}_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(X^{(i)}) estimates \mathbb{E}_{X\sim p}[f(X)]=\int f(x)p(x)\,\mathrm{d}x, and \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\mu}_n)=\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim p}(f(X))/n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent draws from the density p, the sample mean estimates the expectation of f(X). When f(X) has finite variance, the variance of this estimator equals the variance of f(X) divided by the sample size.
assumptions_latex: X^{(1)},\ldots,X^{(n)}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}p
\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim p}(f(X))<\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat{\mu}_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}f(X^{(i)})\ \text{estimates}\ \mathbb{E}_{X\sim p}[f(X)]=\int f(x)p(x)\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\mu}_n)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}_{X\sim p}(f(X))}{n}.

children.title: Warm-Up Deletion Regimes
children.top_down_role: Output-analysis regimes distinguished by how early observations are excluded.

knowledge_statements.title: Warm-Up Deletion Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion schedules for estimating a steady-state mean from one finite simulation run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given outputs \(Y_1(x),\ldots,Y_n(x)\), choose an integer deletion schedule \(w_n\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\) and return
\[\widehat\mu_n(x)=\frac{1}{n-w_n}\sum_{t=w_n+1}^{n}Y_t(x).\]
Three deletion regimes are fixed deletion \(w_n=w\), fractional deletion \(w_n=\lfloor\rho n\rfloor\) with \(0<\rho<1\), and increasing sublinear deletion with \(w_n\to\infty\) and \(w_n/n\to0\). Stop at a prescribed horizon \(n\), and report both \(w_n\) and the retained sample size \(n-w_n\) with the estimate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delete a fixed, fractional, or increasing sublinear prefix, then average retained observations and report the deletion and retained sample sizes.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1(x),\ldots,Y_n(x)\) are sequential outputs from one simulation run.
\(0\leq w_n<n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\mu_n(x)=(n-w_n)^{-1}\sum_{t=w_n+1}^{n}Y_t(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bias Rates of Markov Sensitivity Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic initialization- and finite-horizon bias rates for three Markov sensitivity estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H\) be bounded and Lipschitz, and let the process start with distribution \(\gamma\). As \(n,m\), respectively \(N\), tend to infinity,
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{weak})})=O(r(\gamma,\pi_x))O(\rho^m)+O(\rho^n),
\]
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{single})})=O(r(\gamma,\pi_x))O(N\rho^N)+O(\rho^N),
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{average})})=O(N^{-1}).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bounded Lipschitz H, the weak and single-run estimators have geometrically decreasing bias terms involving initialization and horizon length, while the averaged estimator has bias of order 1/N.
assumptions_latex: H\text{ is bounded and Lipschitz}
\gamma\text{ is the starting distribution}
n,m\to\infty\text{ for }Y_x^{(\mathrm{weak})}
N\to\infty\text{ for }Y_x^{(\mathrm{single})}\text{ and }Y_x^{(\mathrm{average})}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{weak})})=O(r(\gamma,\pi_x))O(\rho^m)+O(\rho^n),\quad\operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{single})})=O(r(\gamma,\pi_x))O(N\rho^N)+O(\rho^N),\quad\operatorname{Bias}(Y_x^{(\mathrm{average})})=O(N^{-1}).

children.title: Finite-Horizon Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion caused by evaluating a system over a bounded simulation horizon.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Horizon Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias caused by replacing an infinite-horizon or steady-state objective with finite simulation time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J_\infty(x)\) be the target infinite-horizon performance and let \(J_T(x)\) be the expected performance computed over horizon \(T<\infty\) under the same decision and model. The finite-horizon bias is
\[b_T^{\mathrm{FH}}(x)=J_T(x)-J_\infty(x).\]
For a time-average criterion, \(J_T(x)=T^{-1}\mathbb E[\sum_{t=1}^{T}Y_t(x)]\). Finite-horizon consistency means \(b_T^{\mathrm{FH}}(x)\to0\) as \(T\to\infty\); its sign is not determined without additional monotonicity or transient assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-horizon bias is the expected truncated-horizon performance minus its infinite-horizon target; its sign need not be fixed.
assumptions_latex: \(J_T(x)\) and \(J_\infty(x)\) are finite and use the same decision \(x\).
\(T<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_T^{\mathrm{FH}}(x)=J_T(x)-J_\infty(x)\).
