children.title: Numerical-Discretization Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion caused by approximate temporal, spatial, or state discretization.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical-Discretization Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak bias induced by numerically discretizing a continuous-state or continuous-time simulator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) denote an exact simulated object, \(X^{(h)}\) its numerical approximation at resolution \(h>0\), and \(F\) an integrable performance functional. The numerical-discretization bias is
\[b_h^{\mathrm{disc}}=\mathbb E[F(X^{(h)})]-\mathbb E[F(X)].\]
The approximation has weak order \(p>0\) for \(F\) if constants \(C,h_0>0\) exist such that \(\lvert b_h^{\mathrm{disc}}\rvert\leq Ch^p\) for every \(0<h\leq h_0\). This bias is distinct from Monte Carlo sampling error at fixed \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discretization bias is the difference between expected performance under a numerical simulator and under the exact model; weak order describes its decay.
assumptions_latex: \(F(X)\) and \(F(X^{(h)})\) are integrable.
\(h>0\) indexes numerical resolution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b_h^{\mathrm{disc}}=\mathbb E[F(X^{(h)})]-\mathbb E[F(X)]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak-error definition is standard and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied for either the bias formula or weak-order condition.

children.title: Approximation-Scale Bias Interaction
children.top_down_role: Joint bias behavior when horizon length and numerical resolution vary together.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Scale Bias Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact decomposition separating horizon, discretization, and nonadditive interaction biases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J_{T,h}(x)\) be expected simulated performance at horizon \(T\) and discretization scale \(h\), with limits \(J_{T,0}(x)\), \(J_{\infty,h}(x)\), and \(J_{\infty,0}(x)\) well defined. Then
\[J_{T,h}-J_{\infty,0}=(J_{T,0}-J_{\infty,0})+(J_{\infty,h}-J_{\infty,0})+\Delta_{T,h},\]
where
\[\Delta_{T,h}=J_{T,h}-J_{T,0}-J_{\infty,h}+J_{\infty,0}.\]
Thus \(\Delta_{T,h}\) is the approximation-scale interaction: it vanishes exactly when the joint horizon-discretization bias is additive at \((T,h)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total approximation bias equals pure horizon bias plus pure discretization bias plus a cross-difference measuring their nonadditive interaction.
assumptions_latex: \(J_{T,h}(x)\), \(J_{T,0}(x)\), \(J_{\infty,h}(x)\), and \(J_{\infty,0}(x)\) are finite.
All four quantities use the same decision \(x\) and performance convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_{T,h}-J_{\infty,0}=(J_{T,0}-J_{\infty,0})+(J_{\infty,h}-J_{\infty,0})+\Delta_{T,h}\).

notation.meaning: performance at horizon T and scale h

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cross-difference is an exact and appropriate representation of nonadditive interaction, but the record has no cited source supporting this interpretation in the simulation-bias setting.

children.title: Input-Model Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty inherited from estimated input laws and dependence models.

children.title: Parametric Input Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty in fitted input parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Parametric Input Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncertainty propagated from finite-data estimation of parameters within a fixed input family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the simulator input law belong to a fixed family \(\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\), let \(D\) be input data generated under \(P_{\theta_0}\), and let \(\widehat\theta(D)\) estimate \(\theta_0\). For decision \(x\), write \(\mu(x;\theta)=\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[Y(x)]\). Parametric input uncertainty is the sampling-induced uncertainty in
\[U_D(x)=\mu(x;\widehat\theta(D))-\mu(x;\theta_0),\]
with randomness taken over repeated input datasets \(D\). It conditions on the chosen parametric family and therefore excludes uncertainty about whether that family is correctly specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parametric input uncertainty is variation in simulated performance caused by estimating a fixed input model's parameters from finite data.
assumptions_latex: \(P_{\theta_0}\) belongs to the specified family \(\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\).
\(\mu(x;\theta)\) is finite for relevant \(x\) and \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(U_D(x)=\mu(x;\widehat\theta(D))-\mu(x;\theta_0)\).

notation.meaning: mean simulation response under parameter theta

children.title: Distribution-Dependence Uncertainty Family
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty in distribution families, tails, and dependence structure.

children.title: Distributional-Family Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty about the family or shape of simulator input distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional-Family Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input uncertainty arising from ambiguity over the parametric or nonparametric distribution family itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal M\) index candidate input-distribution families \(\mathcal P_m\), and let \(\mathcal A(D)\subseteq\bigcup_{m\in\mathcal M}\mathcal P_m\) contain distributions compatible with input data \(D\). For decision \(x\), define \(\mu(x;P)=\mathbb E_P[Y(x)]\). Distributional-family uncertainty is present when there exist \(m\neq m'\), \(P\in\mathcal A(D)\cap\mathcal P_m\), and \(Q\in\mathcal A(D)\cap\mathcal P_{m'}\) such that
\[\mu(x;P)\neq\mu(x;Q).\]
It concerns variation across families, rather than parameter estimation within one fixed family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributional-family uncertainty occurs when data-compatible input laws from different model families produce different expected simulation responses.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A(D)\) contains input laws judged compatible with the observed data.
\(\mu(x;P)\) is finite for every considered law \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists P,Q\in\mathcal A(D)\) from distinct families with \(\mu(x;P)\neq\mu(x;Q)\).

notation.meaning: candidate distribution family indexed by m

children.title: Tail-Behavior Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty concentrated in extreme input behavior or rare outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Behavior Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input uncertainty caused by poorly identified probabilities or magnitudes of extreme events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A(D)\) be a set of data-compatible input laws and let \(T_\tau(P)\) be a tail functional, such as an exceedance probability or an upper-tail quantile at level \(\tau\). Tail-behavior uncertainty relevant to decision \(x\) is present if there exist \(P,Q\in\mathcal A(D)\) satisfying the imposed central-distribution constraints but
\[T_\tau(P)\neq T_\tau(Q)\quad\text{and}\quad \mu(x;P)\neq\mu(x;Q),\]
where \(\mu(x;P)=\mathbb E_P[Y(x)]\). The definition isolates performance variation attributable to unresolved tail behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tail-behavior uncertainty exists when data-compatible laws agree on central features but differ in tails and consequently in simulated performance.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) satisfy the same specified central-distribution constraints.
\(T_\tau(P)\), \(T_\tau(Q)\), \(\mu(x;P)\), and \(\mu(x;Q)\) are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_\tau(P)\neq T_\tau(Q)\) and \(\mu(x;P)\neq\mu(x;Q)\).

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Stochastic optimization problems p. 3

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Stochastic optimization problems p. 3

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed notion is plausible, but 'central-distribution constraints' is not formally specified and the cited introductory section does not support this specialized tail-uncertainty criterion.

children.title: Dependence-Structure Uncertainty
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty about temporal, cross-sectional, or multivariate input dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence-Structure Uncertainty
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Input uncertainty induced by unknown joint dependence when marginal distributions are fixed or separately estimated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_1,\ldots,P_d\) be prescribed input marginals and let \(\mathcal C(D)\) be a data-compatible set of copulas. Each \(C\in\mathcal C(D)\) induces a joint law \(P_C\) with those marginals. For decision \(x\), dependence-structure uncertainty is present if there exist \(C,C'\in\mathcal C(D)\) such that
\[\mu(x;P_C)=\mathbb E_{P_C}[Y(x)]\neq\mathbb E_{P_{C'}}[Y(x)]=\mu(x;P_{C'}).\]
Thus the response changes solely through admissible dependence structures, not through marginal input laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dependence-structure uncertainty occurs when different data-compatible copulas with identical marginals yield different expected simulation responses.
assumptions_latex: \(P_C\) and \(P_{C'}\) have the same prescribed marginals.
The corresponding simulation responses are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists C,C'\in\mathcal C(D)\) with \(\mu(x;P_C)\neq\mu(x;P_{C'})\).

notation.meaning: joint input law induced by copula C and fixed marginals

children.title: Search-Selection Bias Coupling
children.top_down_role: Bias produced when noisy data are reused for search and evaluation.

children.title: Optimization Bias
children.top_down_role: Optimistic distortion arising from optimizing over noisy performance estimates.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Downward bias from minimizing unbiased noisy objective estimates over a finite candidate set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be finite, let \(\mu(x)\) be the true objective for minimization, and suppose \(\widehat\mu(x)\) is integrable with \(\mathbb E[\widehat\mu(x)]=\mu(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\). Define
\[B_{\mathrm{opt}}=\mathbb E\!\left[\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\widehat\mu(x)\right]-\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x).\]
Then
\[B_{\mathrm{opt}}\leq0.\]
The inequality requires no independence among the estimators. For maximization, replacing both minima by maxima reverses the inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum of unbiased noisy estimates is optimistically biased downward; the maximum is biased upward.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is finite and nonempty.
\(\widehat\mu(x)\) is integrable and pointwise unbiased for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\widehat\mu(x)]\leq\min_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu(x)\).

children.title: Selection Bias
children.top_down_role: Distortion arising from evaluating alternatives after data-dependent selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias in an in-sample estimate caused by selecting the reported candidate using the same estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\) be finite and nonempty, let \(\widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathcal X}\widehat\mu(x)\) under a fixed measurable tie rule, and let \(\mu(x)\) be true expected performance. The selection bias of the reported in-sample value is
\[B_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathbb E[\widehat\mu(\widehat x)-\mu(\widehat x)].\]
Pointwise unbiasedness of \(\widehat\mu(x)\) does not imply \(B_{\mathrm{sel}}=0\), because \(\widehat x\) depends on the estimation errors. If, additionally, \(\mathbb E[\widehat\mu(x)]=\mu(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\) and all candidates have the same true mean, then
\[B_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathbb E\!\left[\min_{x\in\mathcal X}(\widehat\mu(x)-\mu(x))\right]\leq0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selection bias is the expected in-sample estimation error at a candidate chosen using those same estimates. Pointwise unbiasedness does not generally remove it; with equal true means and pointwise-unbiased estimates, it is nonpositive for minimization.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is finite and nonempty.
\(\widehat\mu(x)\) is integrable for every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
The tie-breaking rule defining \(\widehat x\) is measurable and fixed in advance.
For the nonpositivity conclusion, \(\mathbb E[\widehat\mu(x)]=\mu(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), and \(\mu(x)\) is constant over \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{sel}}=\mathbb E[\widehat\mu(\widehat x)-\mu(\widehat x)]\); under equal true means and pointwise unbiasedness, \(B_{\mathrm{sel}}\leq0\).

notation.meaning: candidate selected by minimizing noisy estimates

children.title: Search-Generated Evaluation Bias
children.top_down_role: Evaluation distortion caused by reusing exploratory simulation evidence for final assessment.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Generated Evaluation Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of fixed-design unbiasedness when search and evaluation reuse the same random data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z\) be simulation data, let \(g(x,Z)\) satisfy \(\mathbb E[g(x,Z)]=\mu(x)\) for every fixed \(x\), and let search return the data-dependent decision \(\widehat x=s(Z)\). Reusing \(Z\) gives adaptive evaluation bias
\[B_{\mathrm{SG}}=\mathbb E[g(s(Z),Z)-\mu(s(Z))],\]
which need not vanish because fixed-\(x\) unbiasedness does not extend to \(s(Z)\). If \(Z'\) is independent of \(Z\) and \(g(x,Z')\) is unbiased for every fixed \(x\), then
\[\mathbb E[g(\widehat x,Z')-\mu(\widehat x)\mid\widehat x]=0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reusing search data for evaluation can create bias at the adaptive decision; independent unbiased validation removes this reuse bias conditionally.
assumptions_latex: \(g(x,Z)\) is integrable and unbiased for every fixed decision \(x\).
\(\widehat x=s(Z)\) is measurable.
Validation data \(Z'\), when used, are independent of \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{SG}}\) may be nonzero, whereas \(\mathbb E[g(\widehat x,Z')-\mu(\widehat x)\mid\widehat x]=0\).

notation.meaning: data reused by the search and evaluation

children.title: Paired Simulation Coupling
children.top_down_role: Cross-alternative dependence designed to sharpen performance differences.

children.title: Common Random Numbers
children.top_down_role: Shared random inputs across alternatives or perturbations.

knowledge_statements.title: Common Random Numbers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired comparison of two simulated alternatives using identical random inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let simulator outputs be \(Y_a=g(a,U)\) and \(Y_b=g(b,U)\), where both alternatives use the same random input \(U\). For independent replications \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\), estimate \(\Delta=\mathbb E[Y_a]-\mathbb E[Y_b]\) by \(\widehat\Delta_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(g(a,U_i)-g(b,U_i)\bigr)\). Then \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\Delta_n)=n^{-1}\bigl(\operatorname{Var}(Y_a)+\operatorname{Var}(Y_b)-2\operatorname{Cov}(Y_a,Y_b)\bigr)\). Thus common random numbers reduce variance relative to independent streams exactly when the induced covariance is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared random inputs yield an unbiased paired difference estimator and reduce its variance when the two simulated outputs are positively correlated.
assumptions_latex: \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) are independent copies of \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_a,Y_b)>0\) implies lower variance than using independent input streams.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The paired-estimator variance identity, hypotheses, plain statement, and principle content kind fit the Common Random Numbers container. However, the record has no inspectable citation, so the positive-covariance variance-reduction claim requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-random-numbers coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired Monte Carlo comparison of two parameter choices or alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To compare \(\mu(\theta)=\mathbb E[f(\theta,Z)]\) and \(\mu(\theta')=\mathbb E[f(\theta',Z)]\), evaluate both alternatives using the same draws \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_S\sim p\): \[\widehat\Delta_{\mathrm{CRN}}=\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S\bigl(f(\theta,Z_s)-f(\theta',Z_s)\bigr).\] Its variance is \[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\Delta_{\mathrm{CRN}})=\frac1S\left(\operatorname{Var}(f(\theta,Z))+\operatorname{Var}(f(\theta',Z))-2\operatorname{Cov}(f(\theta,Z),f(\theta',Z))\right).\] Thus common random numbers reduce variance relative to independent evaluations when the induced covariance is positive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common random numbers evaluate competing parameter values with the same random inputs. This reduces the variance of their paired comparison when the resulting outputs are positively correlated. Holding the samples fixed can also produce a deterministic sampled objective as a function of the parameters.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_S\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}p\).
\(f(\theta,Z)\) and \(f(\theta',Z)\) have finite second moments.
Variance reduction relative to independent sampling requires \(\operatorname{Cov}(f(\theta,Z),f(\theta',Z))>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive covariance induced by shared random inputs reduces the variance of the paired Monte Carlo comparison.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variance-minimizing common random numbers under componentwise monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes full componentwise common-random-number coupling as variance minimizing for each coordinate of the paired gradient estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\mathbf V_k^{(+)}\) and \(\mathbf V_k^{(-)}\) have the same number of components, the components within each vector are independent, and cross-vector dependence is permitted only between matching components. Suppose they are generated componentwise by inverse transforms of \(\mathbf U_k^{(+)}\) and \(\mathbf U_k^{(-)}\). For almost every \(\boldsymbol\Delta_k\), assume that \(Q(\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k+c_k\boldsymbol\Delta_k,\mathbf V_k^{(+)})\) and \(Q(\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k-c_k\boldsymbol\Delta_k,\mathbf V_k^{(-)})\) are monotone in the same direction in each matching component over its allowable range, although that direction may vary between components. Then, for every \(i\), \(\operatorname{var}[\widehat g_{ki}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k)\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k]\) is minimized by setting \(\mathbf U_k^{(+)}=\mathbf U_k^{(-)}=\mathbf U_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When paired simulation outputs are generated componentwise by inverse transforms and are monotone in the same direction in every matching input component, using identical uniforms for the plus and minus evaluations minimizes each coordinate's conditional gradient-estimator variance.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbf V_k^{(+)}\) and \(\mathbf V_k^{(-)}\) have the same number of components, with independent components within each vector.
Dependence between the two vectors is allowed only for matching components: \(V_{ki}^{(+)}\) and \(V_{ki}^{(-)}\) may be dependent, while \(V_{ki}^{(+)}\perp V_{kj}^{(-)}\) for \(i\ne j\).
Both vectors are generated componentwise by inverse transforms of \(\mathbf U_k^{(+)}\) and \(\mathbf U_k^{(-)}\).
For almost every \(\boldsymbol\Delta_k\), the paired outputs are monotone in the same direction in each matching component throughout its allowable range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbf U_k^{(+)}=\mathbf U_k^{(-)}=\mathbf U_k\quad\text{minimizes}\quad \operatorname{var}\!\left[\widehat g_{ki}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k)\mid\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}_k\right]\quad\text{for every }i.

children.title: Partial Common Random Numbers
children.top_down_role: Partial coupling when complete stream alignment is unavailable.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Common Random Numbers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupling only a selected component of each alternative's random input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the input for alternative \(d\) is decomposed as \((U,V_d)\). A partial-common-random-numbers coupling uses the same realization of \(U\) for all compared alternatives while generating the residual inputs \(V_d\) according to a joint law whose marginal for each \(d\) equals its required simulation law. For alternatives \(a,b\), the paired estimator remains unbiased, and its variance is determined by the covariance induced through the shared component \(U\) and any permitted dependence between \(V_a\) and \(V_b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial common random numbers share only selected input components while preserving every alternative's correct marginal simulation law.
assumptions_latex: \(g(d,U,V_d)\in L^1\) for every compared alternative \(d\).
Each coupled pair \((U,V_d)\) has the prescribed marginal input law for alternative \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting paired difference estimator is unbiased for the difference of expected performances.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the intended partial-coupling container and correctly emphasizes preservation of each alternative's marginal input law. Because Partial Common Random Numbers is less standardized terminology and no citation is supplied, the precise definition and unbiasedness claim need authoritative support.

children.title: Antithetic Variates
children.top_down_role: Negatively associated random-input constructions.

knowledge_statements.title: Antithetic Variates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variance reduction by averaging negatively correlated, identically distributed outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,1]^s)\), let \(Y=g(U)\in L^2\), and form the antithetic output \(Y^{\mathrm a}=g(\mathbf 1-U)\). Since \(\mathbf 1-U\) is also uniform, \(\overline Y^{\mathrm a}=(Y+Y^{\mathrm a})/2\) is unbiased for \(\mathbb E[Y]\), with \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y^{\mathrm a})=\tfrac12\operatorname{Var}(Y)+\tfrac12\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Y^{\mathrm a})\). It improves upon the mean of two independent outputs exactly when \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Y^{\mathrm a})<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging an output with its reflected-input counterpart is unbiased and beats two independent runs precisely when their covariance is negative.
assumptions_latex: \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,1]^s)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y,Y^{\mathrm a})<0\) gives variance below that of two independent replications.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reflected-uniform construction and variance comparison are mathematically precise, and principle is an appropriate content kind for this variance-reduction mechanism. No source reference or inspectable locator is provided.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Antithetic-variates estimator and variance-reduction condition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Paired antithetic estimation for independent random-vector components using componentwise complementary uniforms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(N\) be even. For \(j=1,\ldots,N/2\), generate independent \(U^j\sim\operatorname{Unif}([0,1]^{d_\xi})\) and construct \((\underline\xi^j,\bar\xi^j)\) from \((U^j,1-U^j)\), with each member having the distribution of \(\xi\). Then
\[
f_{N,\mathrm{AV}}(x)=\frac{2}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N/2}\frac{Y(x,\underline\xi^j)+Y(x,\bar\xi^j)}{2}
\]
is unbiased and satisfies
\[
\operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{AV}}(x))=\frac{\sigma^2(x)}{N}+\frac{1}{N}\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(Y(x,\underline\xi^j),Y(x,\bar\xi^j)\right),
\quad \sigma^2(x)=\operatorname{Var}(Y(x,\xi)).
\]
Thus it has strictly smaller variance than crude Monte Carlo when the within-pair output covariance is negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Antithetic variates pair inputs generated from complementary uniform vectors. The paired-average estimator is unbiased, and its variance equals the crude Monte Carlo variance plus one over N times the within-pair output covariance. Negative output covariance therefore gives strict variance reduction.
assumptions_latex: N\in2\mathbb N
\xi\text{ has independent components}
U^1,\ldots,U^{N/2}\stackrel{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\operatorname{Unif}([0,1]^{d_\xi})
\underline\xi^j\stackrel{d}{=}\bar\xi^j\stackrel{d}{=}\xi
\operatorname{Var}(Y(x,\xi))<\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E[f_{N,\mathrm{AV}}(x)]=\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)],\quad \operatorname{Cov}(Y(x,\underline\xi^j),Y(x,\bar\xi^j))<0\Rightarrow\operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{AV}}(x))<\sigma^2(x)/N

children.title: Control Variates
children.top_down_role: Variance reduction using correlated reference statistics.

knowledge_statements.title: Control Variates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear control-variate estimator with known auxiliary mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\in L^2\) have unknown mean \(\mu\), and let \(C\in L^2\) have known mean \(m_C\) and positive variance. For independent copies \((Y_i,C_i)\), define \(\widehat\mu_\beta=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(Y_i-\beta(C_i-m_C)\bigr)\). This estimator is unbiased for every fixed \(\beta\). Its variance is minimized by \(\beta^*=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)/\operatorname{Var}(C)\), yielding \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\beta^*})=\operatorname{Var}(Y)(1-\rho_{YC}^2)/n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting an optimally weighted, centered reference statistic preserves the target mean and reduces variance by the squared correlation fraction.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(C)>0\) and \(m_C=\mathbb E[C]\) is known.
\((Y_i,C_i)\) are independent copies of \((Y,C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta^*=\operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)/\operatorname{Var}(C)\) minimizes variance over fixed scalar coefficients.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scalar control-variate estimator, optimal fixed coefficient, and variance formula are correctly scoped. Representation is suitable because the record presents the canonical estimator form, but the claims lack an authoritative citation and locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Optimal scalar control-variate coefficient and plug-in bias boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sample unbiasedness and variance minimization for a fixed coefficient, together with the limitation of estimating the coefficient from data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathbb E[C]=0\), \(0<\operatorname{Var}(C)<\infty\), and \(\sigma^2(x)=\operatorname{Var}(Y(x,\xi))<\infty\). For i.i.d. paired observations \((Y(x,\xi^j),C^j)\) and fixed \(\lambda\), \[f_{N,\mathrm{CV}}(x;\lambda)=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(Y(x,\xi^j)+\lambda C^j\bigr)\] is unbiased and has variance \[\frac1N\left(\sigma^2(x)+\lambda^2\operatorname{Var}(C)+2\lambda\operatorname{Cov}(Y(x,\xi),C)\right).\] Its variance is minimized at \[\lambda^*=-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y(x,\xi),C)}{\operatorname{Var}(C)},\] giving \[\operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{CV}}(x;\lambda^*))=\frac1N\left(\sigma^2(x)-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y(x,\xi),C)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(C)}\right).\] This is strictly smaller than crude Monte Carlo variance exactly when \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y(x,\xi),C)\ne0\). A coefficient estimated from the data generally need not preserve exact finite-sample unbiasedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed coefficient multiplying a zero-mean control variable preserves unbiasedness. The variance-minimizing coefficient is minus the response-control covariance divided by the control variance, and it gives strict variance reduction exactly when the covariance is nonzero. A coefficient estimated from data generally need not preserve exact finite-sample unbiasedness.
assumptions_latex: N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}
\mathbb E[C]=0
0<\operatorname{Var}(C)<\infty
\operatorname{Var}(Y(x,\xi))=\sigma^2(x)<\infty
(Y(x,\xi^j),C^j)_{j=1}^N\text{ are i.i.d. paired observations}
\lambda\text{ is fixed for the unbiasedness statement}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda^*=-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)}{\operatorname{Var}(C)},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{CV}}(x;\lambda^*))=\frac1N\left(\sigma^2(x)-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(C)}\right),\qquad \operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{CV}})<\frac{\sigma^2(x)}N\iff\operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)\ne0.

children.title: Conditional Monte Carlo
children.top_down_role: Variance reduction through conditional averaging.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Monte Carlo
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rao–Blackwell variance reduction by conditioning simulation output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\in L^2\) be a simulation output and \(\mathcal G\) a sub-sigma-algebra for which \(Z=\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G]\) can be evaluated. Then \(\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E[Y]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)-\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid\mathcal G)]\leq\operatorname{Var}(Y)\). Consequently, the sample mean of independent copies of \(Z\) is unbiased and has no greater variance than the sample mean of the same number of independent copies of \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing an output by an evaluable conditional expectation preserves its mean and removes the expected conditional variance.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal G\) is a sub-sigma-algebra and \(\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal G]\) is evaluable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Z]=\mathbb E[Y]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\leq\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional-expectation and total-variance identities accurately express the defining variance-reduction property of Conditional Monte Carlo, and property is an appropriate content kind. The record nevertheless has no inspectable source.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rao–Blackwellized Monte Carlo estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional averaging as a Monte Carlo variance-reduction method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U=f(X,Y)\) have finite variance and suppose \(g(X)=\mathbb E[U\mid X]\) is tractable. For iid \(X_1,\ldots,X_S\sim p_X\), define \[\widehat f_{\mathrm{RB}}=\frac1S\sum_{s=1}^S g(X_s).\] Then \(\widehat f_{\mathrm{RB}}\) is unbiased for \(\bar f=\mathbb E[U]\), and \[\operatorname{Var}(g(X))=\operatorname{Var}(U)-\mathbb E[\operatorname{Var}(U\mid X)]\leq\operatorname{Var}(U).\] Consequently, its variance is no greater than that of the naive iid estimator \(S^{-1}\sum_s f(X_s,Y_s)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When one component of a joint Monte Carlo sample can be integrated out conditionally, replace each raw value by its conditional expectation. The Rao–Blackwellized estimator remains unbiased and has variance no greater than the naive joint-sampling estimator.
assumptions_latex: \((X,Y)\sim p\) and \(\mathbb E[f(X,Y)^2]<\infty\).
\(g(x)=\mathbb E[f(X,Y)\mid X=x]\) is tractable.
\(X_1,\ldots,X_S\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}p_X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat f_{\mathrm{RB}}]=\mathbb E[f(X,Y)]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_{\mathrm{RB}})\leq\operatorname{Var}(S^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^S f(X_s,Y_s))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Stratified Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased estimation using a finite measurable partition and within-stratum samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_H\) be a measurable partition with \(p_h=\mathbb P(X\in A_h)>0\). Draw \(n_h\geq1\) independent samples from the conditional law of \(X\) given \(X\in A_h\), independently across strata, and set \(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{str}}=\sum_{h=1}^H p_h n_h^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_h}f(X_{hj})\). Then \(\mathbb E[\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{str}}]=\mathbb E[f(X)]\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{str}})=\sum_{h=1}^H p_h^2\operatorname{Var}(f(X)\mid X\in A_h)/n_h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted averages of within-stratum sample means unbiasedly estimate the population mean, with variance determined by conditional variances and allocations.
assumptions_latex: \(A_1,\ldots,A_H\) form a measurable partition with positive probabilities.
Samples are conditionally independent within and across strata.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed estimator is unbiased with variance \(\sum_h p_h^2\sigma_h^2/n_h\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stratified-estimator mean and variance decomposition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The estimator and its variance formula correctly describe finite stratified sampling with independent within-stratum samples. Representation fits the displayed estimator architecture, but no authoritative source or locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stratified modification of a grid-based sampling plan
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines stratified sampling for a grid-based design whose sampled cells would otherwise be represented by their centers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a grid-based sampling plan, stratified sampling replaces the center point of each sampled cell \(C\) with a point \(X_C\) chosen uniformly at random within that cell: \(X_C\sim\operatorname{Unif}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stratified sampling modifies a grid-based sampling plan by choosing a uniformly random point within each sampled cell instead of using the cell's center.
assumptions_latex: \text{The underlying sampling plan is grid-based and partitions its domain into cells }C.
\text{Each cell sampled by the underlying plan would otherwise be represented by its center.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall C\text{ sampled by the plan},\quad X_C\sim\operatorname{Unif}(C)\text{ instead of }X_C=\operatorname{center}(C).

children.title: Latin Hypercube Simulation

knowledge_statements.title: Latin Hypercube Simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized design stratifying every uniform input coordinate into equal-probability intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An \(n\)-point Latin hypercube design in \([0,1]^s\) is generated by independently choosing, for each coordinate \(k\), a uniform random permutation \(\pi_k\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and independent jitters \(V_{ik}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), then setting \(U_{ik}=(\pi_k(i)-V_{ik})/n\). For every coordinate, exactly one point lies in each interval \(((j-1)/n,j/n)\), while each \(U_i\) is marginally uniform on \([0,1]^s\). Hence \(n^{-1}\sum_i f(U_i)\) is unbiased for the uniform integral of integrable \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Latin hypercube places one randomized point in every marginal stratum of every coordinate while retaining uniform point marginals and unbiased integration.
assumptions_latex: The permutations, jitters, and coordinate constructions are mutually independent.
\(f\) is integrable on \([0,1]^s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each marginal stratum is occupied once, and \(n^{-1}\sum_i f(U_i)\) is unbiased for \(\int_{[0,1]^s}f(u)\,du\).

children.title: Randomized Quasi-Monte Carlo
children.top_down_role: Randomized low-discrepancy simulation designs.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Quasi-Monte Carlo
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized low-discrepancy integration retaining uniform marginals and replication-based error assessment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_n=\{u_1,\ldots,u_n\}\subset[0,1]^s\) be a low-discrepancy point set. A randomized quasi-Monte Carlo design is a random transformation producing \(\widetilde P_n=\{\widetilde U_1,\ldots,\widetilde U_n\}\) such that each \(\widetilde U_i\) is uniform on \([0,1]^s\) and the transformed set retains the designated low-discrepancy structure almost surely. For integrable \(f\), \(\widehat I_n=n^{-1}\sum_i f(\widetilde U_i)\) is unbiased for \(I=\int_{[0,1]^s}f(u)\,du\); independent randomizations provide independent estimator replications.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomization makes every low-discrepancy point uniform, preserving unbiased integration while independent randomizations permit statistical error estimation.
assumptions_latex: Each randomized point is marginally uniform on \([0,1]^s\).
\(f\) is integrable on \([0,1]^s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat I_n]=I\), and independent randomizations yield independent copies of \(\widehat I_n\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record states a reasonable general definition through uniform marginals and preservation of designated low-discrepancy structure, but the latter condition depends on the randomization class and is not independently verifiable from any cited source. An authoritative RQMC source must establish the stated generality and replication claim.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(Q\) are probability measures on a common measurable space, with \(P\ll Q\).
\(h\) is measurable and \(hL\in L^1(Q)\); finite-variance claims require \(hL\in L^2(Q)\).
\(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are independent random elements with law \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E_Q[\widehat\mu_n]=\mu\), with \(\operatorname{Var}_Q(\widehat\mu_n)=\operatorname{Var}_Q(hL)/n\) when \(hL\in L^2(Q)\).

notation.meaning: Radon-Nikodym likelihood ratio from the target measure to the simulation measure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Change-of-measure identity and finite-variance condition for rare-event estimation.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.5 Importance sampling p. 227

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a target probability measure and \(Q\) a simulation probability measure on the same measurable space, with \(P\ll Q\), and define the likelihood ratio \(L=dP/dQ\). For a measurable integrand \(h\) satisfying \(hL\in L^1(Q)\), \(\mu=\mathbb E_P[h(X)]=\mathbb E_Q[h(X)L(X)]\). Thus independent draws \(X_i\sim Q\) give the unbiased estimator \(\widehat\mu_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n h(X_i)L(X_i)\). If \(hL\in L^2(Q)\), then \(\operatorname{Var}_Q(\widehat\mu_n)=\operatorname{Var}_Q(hL)/n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the target measure is dominated by the simulation measure, likelihood-ratio weighting preserves the target expectation; square integrability of the weighted integrand gives finite variance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Importance-sampling estimator, unbiasedness, and variance boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Change-of-measure estimator for a fixed simulation response, including its support requirement and the failure of admissibility alone to guarantee variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\in\Theta\). Let \(\xi\) have density \(p\) on \(\Xi\), let \(q\) be another density with \(p\ll q\), and define \(\mathcal L=p/q\), taking \(\mathcal L=0\) where both densities vanish. For i.i.d. \(\widetilde\xi^1,\ldots,\widetilde\xi^N\sim q\), \[f_{N,\mathrm{IS}}(x)=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N Y(x,\widetilde\xi^j)\mathcal L(\widetilde\xi^j).\] If the weighted response is integrable, then \(\mathbb E_q[f_{N,\mathrm{IS}}(x)]=\mathbb E_p[Y(x,\xi)]\). Thus the estimator is unbiased, but an admissible choice of \(q\) can increase rather than reduce variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Importance sampling draws independently from a proposal density q and weights each response by p/q. Absolute continuity and integrability give an unbiased estimator of the original expectation, but they do not guarantee variance reduction; a poor proposal can increase variance.
assumptions_latex: x\in\Theta
N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}
p\ll q
\widetilde\xi^1,\ldots,\widetilde\xi^N\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}q
\mathbb E_q\!\left[\left|Y(x,\widetilde\xi)\mathcal L(\widetilde\xi)\right|\right]<\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E_q[f_{N,\mathrm{IS}}(x)]=\mathbb E_p[Y(x,\xi)],\qquad \operatorname{Var}(f_{N,\mathrm{IS}}(x))\text{ need not be below the crude Monte Carlo variance.}

children.title: Level-Based Rare-Event Simulation Family
children.top_down_role: Level-based and population-based rare-event simulation.

children.title: Rare-Event Splitting
children.top_down_role: Population replication or pruning organized around intermediate rare-event levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Rare-Event Splitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multilevel particle replication for estimating a rare hitting probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose nested sets \(B_0\supset B_1\supset\cdots\supset B_m=B\), an initial particle count \(N\), and offspring counts \(r_1,\ldots,r_{m-1}\). Simulate each particle until it reaches \(B_1\) or fails; every success at level \(k<m\) is replaced by \(r_k\) conditionally independent continuations from its entrance state. Assign each child its parent's weight divided by \(r_k\). Stop particles upon failure or arrival at \(B\), and output the sum of the terminal weights of particles reaching \(B\), divided by \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Particles reaching successive rare-event levels are replicated with divided weights; summed terminal weights estimate the final hitting probability.
assumptions_latex: Continuation simulations have the correct conditional law from each entrance state.
Splitting decisions use only information available at the corresponding entrance time.
Initial particles are independent and correctly distributed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an unbiased estimator of the probability of reaching \(B\) under weight-conserving splitting.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind for this terminal container, but the particular fixed-offspring, entrance-state continuation scheme and its unbiasedness conclusion depend on filtration, stopping, and weight-conservation details that require an authoritative source. No citation is supplied.

children.title: Subset Simulation
children.top_down_role: Rare-event estimation through nested conditional-event populations.

knowledge_statements.title: Subset Simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rare-event probability factorization estimated through sequential conditional sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose nested events \(F_0\supset F_1\supset\cdots\supset F_m=F\) with \(F_0=\Omega\). Using samples from the law conditional on \(F_{k-1}\), estimate \(p_k=\mathbb P(F_k\mid F_{k-1})\) by the observed fraction in \(F_k\); use selected samples in \(F_k\) as seeds for a Markov transition kernel invariant for the law conditional on \(F_k\). Continue until \(F\) is reached and output \(\widehat p_F=\prod_{k=1}^m\widehat p_k\), corresponding to \(\mathbb P(F)=\prod_{k=1}^m p_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subset simulation factors a rare probability into moderate conditional probabilities estimated through sequential conditional sampling over nested events.
assumptions_latex: \(F_0\supset F_1\supset\cdots\supset F_m=F\) are measurable.
Each transition kernel has the required conditional distribution as an invariant law.
The stopping level and probability estimator follow the stated nested-event factorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The target probability satisfies \(\mathbb P(F)=\prod_{k=1}^m\mathbb P(F_k\mid F_{k-1})\), estimated by the displayed product.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the Subset Simulation leaf, and the exact nested-event probability factorization is correct. However, the sequential MCMC sampling procedure and product estimator are method-specific; invariance alone does not resolve initialization, dependence, or finite-sample behavior. An authoritative source with a precise locator is required.

children.title: Intermediate-Level Design
children.top_down_role: Structural choices governing level placement and population progression.

knowledge_statements.title: Intermediate-Level Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Design criterion for stable multilevel rare-event probability estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nested events \(F_0\supset F_1\supset\cdots\supset F_m=F\), define \(p_k=\mathbb P(F_k\mid F_{k-1})\). An admissible intermediate-level design requires \(0<p_k<1\) for every level, supports simulation from or continuation under the conditional law given \(F_{k-1}\), and satisfies \(\mathbb P(F)=\prod_{k=1}^m p_k\). A balanced design additionally selects levels so that the \(p_k\) are approximately equal and bounded away from zero, preventing any single conditional stage from remaining a rare event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intermediate levels must preserve the nested probability factorization and make every conditional transition simulable; balanced levels avoid extremely small stage probabilities.
assumptions_latex: \(F_0\supset F_1\supset\cdots\supset F_m=F\) are measurable events.
The conditional probabilities \(p_k\) are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid design has simulable stages with \(0<p_k<1\) and \(\mathbb P(F)=\prod_{k=1}^m p_k\).

notation.meaning: conditional probability of advancing one level

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Condition is an appropriate content kind for an intermediate-level design criterion. The nested-event factorization is standard, but requiring every conditional probability to be strictly below one and characterizing approximately equal probabilities bounded away from zero as balanced are method-dependent design choices that need a cited authoritative formulation.

children.title: Change-of-Measure Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instability from poorly targeted measures or degenerate simulation weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Change-of-Measure Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure conditions for importance-sampling estimators under an inadequately chosen proposal measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the target be \(\mu=\mathbb E_P[H(X)]\), and suppose samples are drawn from \(Q\). A likelihood-weighted estimator requires \(P\ll Q\) on \(\{x:H(x)\ne0\}\), with weight \(W=dP/dQ\). It is invalid if domination fails, and it has infinite variance whenever \(\mathbb E_Q[H(X)^2W(X)^2]=\infty\). Even with finite variance, concentration of \(W\) on vanishingly few samples causes effective-sample-size degeneration and unstable finite-sample estimates. Thus unbiasedness alone does not ensure a usable change of measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Change of measure fails through missing support, infinite weighted second moments, or extreme weight concentration that leaves effectively few useful simulations.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is measurable and \(\mathbb E_P[|H(X)|]<\infty\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sample-Path Recycling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common-input reuse across several parameter evaluations of a simulator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given design points \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_K\), a simulator \(h(\theta,U)\), and replication count \(n\), generate independent base inputs \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) once. For every \(k\), compute \(Y_{ik}=h(\theta_k,U_i)\) and return \(\widehat F_n(\theta_k)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nY_{ik}\). Stop after all requested designs are evaluated or a prescribed simulation budget is exhausted. Each marginal estimate remains unbiased for \(F(\theta_k)=\mathbb E[h(\theta_k,U)]\); recycling induces covariance across designs, which can reduce the variance of paired comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generate each exogenous path once, evaluate every requested design on it, and use the induced coupling to estimate objectives or differences.
assumptions_latex: \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) are independent with a distribution not depending on \(\theta\).
\(\mathbb E[|h(\theta_k,U)|]<\infty\) for every evaluated design.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat F_n(\theta_k)]=F(\theta_k)\), while paired differences retain the covariance created by common paths.

notation.meaning: Recycled exogenous simulation path or random input.

knowledge_statements.title: Likelihood Reweighting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Off-policy representation of parameterized expectations using samples from a reference distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_\theta\) and \(P_{\theta_0}\) be probability measures on a common measurable space \((\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\), let \(P_\theta\ll P_{\theta_0}\), and let \(H_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be measurable. With \(w_{\theta,\theta_0}=dP_\theta/dP_{\theta_0}\), if \(H_\theta w_{\theta,\theta_0}\) is integrable under \(P_{\theta_0}\), then \[F(\theta)=\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[H_\theta(X)]=\mathbb E_{P_{\theta_0}}[H_\theta(X)w_{\theta,\theta_0}(X)].\] Hence independent reference samples \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P_{\theta_0}\) give the unbiased estimator \[\widehat F_n(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nH_\theta(X_i)w_{\theta,\theta_0}(X_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the parameterized simulation law is absolutely continuous with respect to a reference law, its expectation can be represented and estimated from reference samples using likelihood-ratio weights.
assumptions_latex: \(P_\theta\) and \(P_{\theta_0}\) are probability measures on \((\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\), with \(P_\theta\ll P_{\theta_0}\).
\(H_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) is measurable.
\(\mathbb E_{P_{\theta_0}}[|H_\theta(X)w_{\theta,\theta_0}(X)|]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E_{P_{\theta_0}}[H_\theta(X)w_{\theta,\theta_0}(X)]\), and \(\mathbb E[\widehat F_n(\theta)]=F(\theta)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-sided and central finite-difference simulation-gradient estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise finite differences for stochastic simulator output, including evaluation cost, perturbation trade-offs, and common-random-number coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For stochastic simulator output $Y(\theta,\xi)$, coordinate vector $e_i$, and $c_i\ne0$, the forward and central estimators are
\[
\widehat g_i^{\mathrm F}(\theta)=\frac{Y(\theta+c_i e_i,\xi_{2,i})-Y(\theta,\xi_{1,i})}{c_i},\qquad
\widehat g_i^{\mathrm C}(\theta)=\frac{Y(\theta+c_i e_i,\xi_{2,i})-Y(\theta-c_i e_i,\xi_{1,i})}{2c_i}.
\]
The central estimator is more accurate but uses $2d$ simulator evaluations for a full gradient, whereas the forward estimator uses $d+1$. Setting $\xi_{1,i}=\xi_{2,i}$ gives common-random-number coupling, which can substantially reduce variance when the paired simulations are properly synchronized. Excessively small perturbations amplify simulation noise, producing a bias--variance trade-off that may require componentwise scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forward estimator compares the nominal output with one positive coordinate perturbation, while the central estimator compares positive and negative perturbations. Central differences are more accurate but require 2d evaluations per gradient rather than d+1. Common random numbers can substantially reduce variance when paired simulations remain synchronized. Very small perturbations amplify stochastic noise and create a componentwise bias–variance trade-off.
assumptions_latex: \theta\in\mathbb R^d
c_i\ne0\quad(i=1,\ldots,d)
Y(\theta,\xi)\text{ is stochastic simulator output}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat g_i^{\mathrm F}(\theta)=\frac{Y(\theta+c_i e_i,\xi_{2,i})-Y(\theta,\xi_{1,i})}{c_i},\qquad \widehat g_i^{\mathrm C}(\theta)=\frac{Y(\theta+c_i e_i,\xi_{2,i})-Y(\theta-c_i e_i,\xi_{1,i})}{2c_i}.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Finite Differences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central coordinatewise gradient estimation from perturbed simulator evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\) for \(\theta\) in an evaluation domain \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). Given \(\theta\in D\), \(c>0\), and \(m\in\mathbb N\), for each coordinate \(j\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\) generate \(m\) pairs \((U_{ij}^+,U_{ij}^-)\) whose two marginals equal the law of \(U\), independently across \(i\). Compute \[\widehat g_j(\theta)=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\frac{Y(\theta+ce_j,U_{ij}^+)-Y(\theta-ce_j,U_{ij}^-)}{2c}.\] Common random numbers use \(U_{ij}^+=U_{ij}^-\); independent sampling may instead be used. Return \(\widehat g=(\widehat g_1,\ldots,\widehat g_d)\) after evaluating the requested coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate each gradient component by averaging central simulator differences along that coordinate, using inputs with the correct marginal law and optionally common random numbers.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), \(\theta\in D\), and \(\theta\pm ce_j\in D\) for every evaluated coordinate \(j\).
Each \(U_{ij}^+\) and \(U_{ij}^-\) has the same marginal distribution as \(U\), and pairs are independent across replications.
\(\mathbb E[|Y(\theta\pm ce_j,U)|]<\infty\) for every evaluated coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_j(\theta)]=(F(\theta+ce_j)-F(\theta-ce_j))/(2c)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate Finite-Difference Policy-Gradient Estimator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise policy-parameter perturbations evaluated through Monte Carlo trajectory returns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each coordinate \(i=1,\ldots,n\), form \(\theta_i^+=\theta+\delta\mathbf e_i\). Estimate both \(U(\theta_i^+)\) and \(U(\theta)\) using \(m\) rollouts of depth \(d\), with initial states sampled from \(b\) and return \(R(\tau)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\gamma^{k-1}r_k\). If these estimates are denoted by \(\widehat U_{m,i}^+\) and \(\widehat U_{m,i}^0\), return \[\widehat g_i=\frac{\widehat U_{m,i}^+-\widehat U_{m,i}^0}{\delta},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every policy-parameter coordinate, estimate the rollout utility at a positive coordinate perturbation and at the current parameters, then divide their difference by the step size. Each utility estimate averages discounted returns from m trajectories of depth d. The algorithm does not itself specify coupling the random samples across evaluations.
assumptions_latex: \theta\in\mathbb{R}^n
\delta>0
m,d\in\mathbb{N}
s_{j,1}\sim b
\pi(\theta,\cdot)\text{ can be simulated in }P
R(\tau)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\gamma^{k-1}r_k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat{\nabla U}(\theta)=\left(\frac{\widehat U_{m,i}^+-\widehat U_{m,i}^0}{\delta}\right)_{i=1}^{n}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise central finite differences with simulation noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central finite-difference gradient estimation from separate noisy simulator evaluations in each coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x^n\in\mathbb R^K\), coordinate vector \(e_k\), and perturbation magnitude \(h_n>0\), define
\[
g_k^n=\frac{F(x^n+h_ne_k,W_k^{n+1,+})-F(x^n-h_ne_k,W_k^{n+1,-})}{2h_n},\qquad k=1,\ldots,K.
\]
Using separate simulations for the two perturbations, a full \(K\)-coordinate estimate requires \(2K\) simulator evaluations. The extract identifies a qualitative tradeoff: small perturbations amplify simulation noise, whereas large perturbations increase finite-difference bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate every gradient coordinate from simulator responses at equal positive and negative coordinate perturbations. The full estimate costs two simulations per coordinate and has a perturbation-size tradeoff between simulation noise and finite-difference bias.

h_n>0
e_k\text{ is the }k\text{-th coordinate vector}
F(x,W)\text{ is observable through simulator runs}
W_k^{n+1,+}\text{ and }W_k^{n+1,-}\text{ drive separate simulations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_k^n=\frac{F(x^n+h_ne_k,W_k^{n+1,+})-F(x^n-h_ne_k,W_k^{n+1,-})}{2h_n},\qquad N_{\mathrm{eval}}=2K

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate Forward Finite-Difference Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise forward differences, including their specialization to policy-utility gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable at \(\mathbf{x}\), then for each coordinate \(i\), \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{x})=\lim_{\delta\to0}\frac{f(\mathbf{x}+\delta\mathbf e^{(i)})-f(\mathbf{x})}{\delta}.\] Thus, for a small nonzero step \(\delta\), the quotient gives a forward finite-difference approximation. Applied to policy utility, \(\partial U/\partial\theta_i\) is approximated by \([U(\theta+\delta\mathbf e^{(i)})-U(\theta)]/\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each gradient component is the limit of a coordinatewise forward difference quotient. A small finite step gives an approximation, and the same construction applies to expected policy utility as a function of its policy parameters.

f\text{ is differentiable at }\mathbf{x}
\delta\ne0
\mathbf e^{(i)}\text{ is the }i\text{th standard basis vector}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \frac{f(\mathbf{x}+\delta\mathbf e^{(i)})-f(\mathbf{x})}{\delta}\to\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(\mathbf{x})\quad\text{as }\delta\to0.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Direction Differences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided gradient estimation using randomized simultaneous perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\) for \(\theta\in D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). Given \(c>0\) and \(m\in\mathbb N\), independently draw directions \(\Delta_i\in\{-1,1\}^d\) with independent Rademacher coordinates. For each \(i\), generate inputs \(U_i^+\) and \(U_i^-\) having the law of \(U\), independently of \(\Delta_i\), and compute \[G_i=\frac{Y(\theta+c\Delta_i,U_i^+)-Y(\theta-c\Delta_i,U_i^-)}{2c}\,\Delta_i.\] The two inputs may be coupled by common random numbers. Return \(\widehat g_m=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mG_i\). If the third derivatives of \(F\) are bounded on a neighborhood containing all perturbed points, then \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_m]=\nabla F(\theta)+O(c^2)\) as \(c\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Average two-sided simulator differences along random sign directions; with correctly distributed simulation inputs and bounded third derivatives, the result has quadratic finite-perturbation bias.
assumptions_latex: \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\) is finite near the evaluated point.
The third partial derivatives of \(F\) are bounded on a neighborhood containing \(\theta\pm c\Delta\).
Each \(U_i^+\) and \(U_i^-\) has the law of \(U\) and is independent of \(\Delta_i\).
\(\theta\pm c\Delta_i\in D\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_m]=\nabla F(\theta)+O(c^2)\) as \(c\downarrow0\).

notation.meaning: Random vector with independent Rademacher coordinates.

children.title: Perturbation Bias-Variance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Estimator behavior across perturbation scale, simulation noise, and coupling regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation Bias-Variance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling laws for central finite differences under independent or coupled simulation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\) for a scalar parameter \(\theta\), and define \(Y_i^+=Y(\theta+c,U_i^+)\), \(Y_i^-=Y(\theta-c,U_i^-)\), and \[\widehat g_c=\frac{1}{2mc}\sum_{i=1}^m(Y_i^+-Y_i^-).\] If the pairs are identically distributed and independent across \(i\), then \[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat g_c)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y_1^+-Y_1^-)}{4mc^2}.\] If \(F\) has bounded third derivative near \(\theta\), then \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_c]-F'(\theta)=O(c^2)\). Independent perturbation noise with nonvanishing difference variance gives \(O((mc^2)^{-1})\) variance, whereas a common-random-number coupling satisfying \(\mathbb E[(Y(\theta+c,U)-Y(\theta-c,U))^2]=O(c^2)\) gives \(O(m^{-1})\) variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Central differences have quadratic truncation bias. Their variance scales inversely with the squared step under uncoupled noise but stays bounded in the step size under a sufficiently smooth common-random-number coupling.
assumptions_latex: \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\) and \(F\) has bounded third derivative near \(\theta\).
Each \(U_i^+\) and \(U_i^-\) has the law of \(U\), and the pairs are independent across \(i\).
\(Y_i^+-Y_i^-\) has a finite second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat g_c)=O(c^2)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat g_c)=\operatorname{Var}(Y_1^+-Y_1^-)/(4mc^2)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Pathwise Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interchange of differentiation and expectation for regular simulator paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d\) be open, let \(	heta_0\in\Theta\), and define \(F(	heta)=\mathbb E[Y(	heta,U)]\). Suppose \(\mathbb E[|Y(	heta_0,U)|]<\infty\), \(Y(\cdot,U)\) is almost surely differentiable on a neighborhood \(N\) of \(	heta_0\), and there is an integrable random variable \(M\) such that \(\sup_{	heta\in N}\|
abla_	heta Y(	heta,U)\|\le M\) almost surely. Then \[
abla F(	heta_0)=\mathbb E[
abla_	heta Y(	heta_0,U)].\] Consequently, the sample-path derivative is an unbiased estimator of \(
abla F(	heta_0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the output is integrable at the base point and simulator paths have locally dominated derivatives, differentiation and expectation can be interchanged.

\(\mathbb E[|Y(\theta_0,U)|]<\infty\).
\(Y(\cdot,U)\) is almost surely differentiable on a neighborhood \(N\) of \(\theta_0\).
\(\sup_{\theta\in N}\|\nabla_\theta Y(\theta,U)\|\le M\) almost surely for an integrable \(M\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differentiation of an expected finite maximum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiates the expectation of a finite maximum when the active component is almost surely unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let H_1(x,\cdot),\ldots,H_n(x,\cdot) be continuous in w and L^{1+\delta}-differentiable in x, with derivatives h_1,\ldots,h_n. Define
\[
H(x,w)=\max_{1\le k\le n}H_k(x,w)
\]
and assume
\[
\mu\{w:H_k(x,w)=H_\ell(x,w)\}=0\qquad(k\ne\ell).
\]
For C_k(x)=\{w:H_k(x,w)=\max_jH_j(x,w)\},
\[
H(x,w)=\sum_k H_k(x,w)\mathbf 1_{C_k(x)}(w)\quad\text{a.s.}
\]
and
\[
\nabla_x\int H(x,w)\,d\mu(w)=\sum_k\int h_k(x,w)\mathbf 1_{C_k(x)}(w)\,d\mu(w).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If pairwise ties between finitely many differentiable random functions have measure zero, the expected maximum is differentiated by integrating the derivative of the almost surely unique active component.
assumptions_latex: H_k(x,\cdot)\text{ is continuous in }w\quad(k=1,\ldots,n)
H_k\text{ is }L^{1+\delta}\text{-differentiable in }x\text{ with derivative }h_k
H(x,w)=\max_{1\le k\le n}H_k(x,w)
\mu\{w:H_k(x,w)=H_\ell(x,w)\}=0\quad\forall k\ne\ell
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H(x,w)=\sum_kH_k(x,w)\mathbf 1_{C_k(x)}(w)\ \text{a.s.},\qquad \nabla_x\int H(x,w)\,d\mu(w)=\sum_k\int h_k(x,w)\mathbf 1_{C_k(x)}(w)\,d\mu(w)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Process p-differentiability and process derivative pairs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines differentiability of a parametric probability-law family through an Lp-differentiable process representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A family (\mu_x)_x is process p-differentiable at x_0 if it admits, in a neighborhood of x_0, a process representation (Z_x)_x and a random variable Y_{x_0} such that
\[
\|s\|^{-1}\bigl\|Z_{x_0+s}-Z_{x_0}-sY_{x_0}\bigr\|_p\longrightarrow0\qquad(s\to0).
\]
The variable Y_{x_0} is a process derivative, and (Z_{x_0},Y_{x_0}) is a process derivative pair. Process derivative pairs are identified by their joint distributions, and need not be unique for a given family (\mu_x)_x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family of probability measures is process p-differentiable when it has a common process representation that is differentiable in Lp. Its value and derivative form a generally nonunique process derivative pair, considered up to joint distribution.
assumptions_latex: (\mu_x)_x\text{ admits a process representation }(Z_x)_x\text{ near }x_0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mu_x)_x\text{ is process }p\text{-differentiable at }x_0;\ Y_{x_0}\text{ is a process derivative and }(Z_{x_0},Y_{x_0})\text{ is a process derivative pair}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pathwise mean-square sensitivity process for a parameterized SDE
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct parameter differentiation of a diffusion trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta\in[a,b]\) and let \(x(t,\theta)\in\mathbb R^k\) solve \(dx(t,\theta)=b(x(t,\theta),\theta)\,dt+\sigma(x(t,\theta))\,dw(t)\). Define \(y(t,\theta)\) by \(dy=[b_x(x,\theta)y+b_\theta(x,\theta)]\,dt+D\sigma(x)[y] \,dw\), where its \(i\)-th diffusion component is \(\sum_{j,p}(\partial\sigma_{ij}/\partial x_p)y_p\,dw_j\). Then \(y(t,\theta)\) is the pathwise mean-square derivative of \(x(t,\theta)\) with respect to \(\theta\). Under the bounded-derivative assumptions, the state and sensitivity equations have unique strong and weak solutions for each initial condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smoothly parameterized diffusion with bounded first derivatives, differentiating the drift and diffusion coefficients yields a linearized SDE whose solution is the pathwise mean-square parameter derivative of the state trajectory. Both SDEs have unique strong and weak solutions for each initial condition.
assumptions_latex: \(\theta\in[a,b]\), \(x(t,\theta)\in\mathbb R^k\), and \(w\) is a standard vector-valued Wiener process.
\(b(x,\theta)\) is continuously differentiable with bounded first partial derivatives in \(x\) and \(\theta\).
\(\sigma(x)\) is continuously differentiable with bounded first partial derivatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: y(t,\theta)=\frac{\partial x(t,\theta)}{\partial\theta}\text{ in the pathwise mean-square sense, and both displayed SDEs have unique strong and weak solutions for each initial condition.}

children.title: Smoothed Perturbation Analysis
children.top_down_role: Smoothing-based sensitivity estimation for irregular simulation responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothed Perturbation Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian smoothing converts an irregular objective into a differentiable surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]\), let \(\sigma>0\), and define \(F_\sigma(\theta)=\mathbb E[F(\theta+\sigma Z)]\) for \(Z\sim N(0,I_d)\). Draw independent perturbations \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\sim N(0,I_d)\) and simulator inputs such that \(\mathbb E[Y(\theta+\sigma Z_i,U_i)\mid Z_i]=F(\theta+\sigma Z_i)\). Choose integrable baselines \(b_i\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[b_iZ_i]=0\), and compute \[\widehat g_\sigma=\frac{1}{m\sigma}\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(Y(\theta+\sigma Z_i,U_i)-b_i\bigr)Z_i.\] Under the stated integrability conditions, return \(\widehat g_\sigma\), which is unbiased for \(\nabla F_\sigma(\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gaussian smoothing produces a differentiable surrogate whose gradient can be estimated with random perturbations and any integrable baseline orthogonal to the perturbation direction.
assumptions_latex: \(F(\theta+\sigma Z)\) and \(F(\theta+\sigma Z)Z\) are integrable.
\(\mathbb E[Y(\theta+\sigma Z_i,U_i)\mid Z_i]=F(\theta+\sigma Z_i)\).
Each \(b_i\) is integrable and satisfies \(\mathbb E[b_iZ_i]=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g_\sigma]=\nabla F_\sigma(\theta)=\sigma^{-1}\mathbb E[F(\theta+\sigma Z)Z]\).

notation.meaning: Integrable baseline orthogonal in expectation to its perturbation direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular Sample-Path Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient local regularity conditions for valid pathwise sensitivity estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A jointly measurable simulator \(Y:\Theta\times\mathcal U\to\mathbb R\) is in the regular sample-path regime at \(\theta_0\in\operatorname{int}\Theta\) if \(\mathbb E[|Y(\theta_0,U)|]<\infty\) and there is a neighborhood \(N\) of \(\theta_0\) such that almost every map \(\theta\mapsto Y(\theta,U)\) is differentiable on \(N\), the simulated event identities and path dimension remain locally constant except on a null set, and an integrable random variable \(M\) satisfies \(\sup_{\theta\in N}\|\nabla_\theta Y(\theta,U)\|\le M\) almost surely. These conditions permit differentiation under expectation at \(\theta_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular regime requires an integrable base output, almost-sure local differentiability, stable path structure, and an integrable uniform bound on path derivatives.
assumptions_latex: \(Y:\Theta\times\mathcal U\to\mathbb R\) is jointly measurable.
\(\theta_0\in\operatorname{int}\Theta\).
\(\mathbb E[|Y(\theta_0,U)|]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla_\theta\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]|_{\theta=\theta_0}=\mathbb E[\nabla_\theta Y(\theta_0,U)]\).

notation.meaning: Neighborhood of the parameter under consideration.

knowledge_statements.title: Path Discontinuity Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Indicator simulation demonstrating failure of naive pathwise differentiation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(Y(\theta,U)=\mathbf 1\{U\le\theta\}\) for \(0<\theta<1\). For every fixed \(\theta\), the sample path is locally constant for all \(U\ne\theta\), so \(\partial_\theta Y(\theta,U)=0\) almost surely. Nevertheless, \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,U)]=\theta\), and hence \(F'(\theta)=1\). The expectation changes through paths crossing the moving discontinuity, a contribution invisible to the almost-sure path derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an indicator with a moving threshold, almost every path derivative is zero although the expected output has derivative one.
assumptions_latex: \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\partial_\theta Y(\theta,U)]=0\ne1=F'(\theta)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Reordering Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Competing-event simulation where a parameter perturbation changes which event occurs first.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) be the time of one event, let a competing event occur at time \(\theta\in(0,1)\), and define \(Y(\theta,U)=\mathbf 1\{\theta<U\}\). Away from the crossing \(U=\theta\), the event order and output are locally constant, giving \(\partial_\theta Y(	heta,U)=0\) almost surely. However, \(F(\theta)=\mathbb P(U>\theta)=1-\theta\), so \(F'(\theta)=-1\). Pathwise differentiation therefore omits the first-order mass of trajectories whose event order changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When perturbing a scheduled event changes which competing event occurs first, locally constant paths can conceal a nonzero expectation derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\partial_\theta Y(\theta,U)]=0\ne-1=F'(\theta)\).

notation.meaning: Random time of the competing event.
Parameterized time of the scheduled event.
Indicator that the scheduled event occurs first.

children.title: Event-Topology Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary where perturbations alter the active event structure of a simulated path.

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Topology Failure Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mechanism by which topology-switching paths contribute missing first-order sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y(\theta,U)\) be pathwise differentiable within each fixed-topology region, and let a topology switch be represented locally by \(s(\theta,U)=0\). For \(h>0\), define \(A_h=\{U:s(\theta,U)s(\theta+h,U)\le0\}\), and let \(J_h(U)\) denote the signed output jump attributable to the topology switch. Suppose \(\mathbb P(A_h)=\lambda h+o(h)\) for some \(\lambda>0\) and \(\mathbb E[J_h\mid A_h]\to j\ne0\). Then \[\mathbb E[J_h\mathbf 1_{A_h}]=\lambda jh+o(h).\] Thus switching paths produce a nonzero one-sided derivative contribution \(\lambda j\) that derivatives computed solely within fixed-topology regions omit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pathwise differentiation crosses its validity boundary when an order-step set of switching paths has a nonvanishing average signed jump, producing a first-order contribution absent from fixed-topology derivatives.
assumptions_latex: \(Y(\theta,U)\) is differentiable within each fixed-topology region.
The topology switch is represented locally by a measurable function \(s\).
\(\mathbb P(A_h)=\lambda h+o(h)\) as \(h\downarrow0\), with \(\lambda>0\).
The signed switch jump satisfies \(\mathbb E[J_h\mid A_h]\to j\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h^{-1}\mathbb E[J_h\mathbf 1_{A_h}]\to\lambda j\ne0\), so fixed-topology path derivatives omit this switching contribution.

notation.meaning: Local switching function for event topology.
Set of paths crossing the switching surface under a positive perturbation h.
Signed output jump attributable to the topology switch.

knowledge_statements.title: Path Likelihood-Ratio Estimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-path score representation for a differentiable finite-horizon simulation law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_\theta\) have density \(p_\theta\) relative to a fixed measure, and let \(J(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[Y(X)]\), where \(Y\) has no direct dependence on \(\theta\). If differentiation may pass under the integral and \(S_\theta(X)=\partial_\theta\log p_\theta(X)\) is integrable with \(Y\), then \[J'(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[Y(X)S_\theta(X)].\] For a path \(X_{0:T}\) with density \(p_{\theta,0}(x_0)\prod_{t=1}^T p_{\theta,t}(x_t\mid x_{0:t-1})\), \[S_\theta(X_{0:T})=\partial_\theta\log p_{\theta,0}(X_0)+\sum_{t=1}^T\partial_\theta\log p_{\theta,t}(X_t\mid X_{0:t-1}).\] Thus \(Y S_\theta\) is an unbiased path likelihood-ratio estimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The derivative of an expected path payoff equals the expected payoff times the sum of the initial and transition log-likelihood scores.
assumptions_latex: \(p_\theta\) has parameter-independent support and is differentiable in \(\theta\).
Differentiation and integration may be interchanged.
\(\mathbb E_\theta[|Y S_\theta|]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J'(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[Y S_\theta]\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reward-to-go localization of transition scores for additive path performance when the initial law is parameter independent.

source_refs.locator: 4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\) be the path filtration, let \(Y=\sum_{u=0}^T R_u\), where each \(R_u\) is \(\mathcal F_u\)-measurable, and let \(s_t=\partial_\theta\log p_{\theta,t}(X_t\mid X_{0:t-1})\). Assume the initial path law is independent of \(\theta\). Since \(\mathbb E_\theta[s_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0\), \(\mathbb E_\theta[R_u s_t]=0\) whenever \(u<t\). Consequently, when the likelihood-ratio identity and the required integrability conditions hold, \[J'(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[Y\sum_{t=1}^T s_t\right]=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T s_t\sum_{u=t}^T R_u\right].\] The right-hand expression is a transition-local score representation using each transition's reward-to-go.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the initial law is parameter independent, past rewards can be removed from each transition-score product, yielding an unbiased representation based on transition scores and their rewards-to-go.

children.title: Score-Estimator Variance Growth
children.top_down_role: Long-horizon or rare-event deterioration of likelihood-based estimators.

knowledge_statements.title: Score-Estimator Variance Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear long-horizon variance growth caused solely by accumulated transition scores.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((s_t,\mathcal F_t)_{t=1}^T\) be square-integrable score increments satisfying \(\mathbb E[s_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[s_t^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]\ge c>0\). Then the cumulative score \(S_T=\sum_{t=1}^T s_t\) obeys \[\operatorname{Var}(S_T)=\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb E[s_t^2]\ge cT.\] In particular, for the constant payoff \(Y\equiv1\), the likelihood-ratio estimator \(G_T=Y S_T=S_T\) is unbiased for the zero derivative of \(\mathbb E_\theta[Y]\), yet \(\operatorname{Var}(G_T)\ge cT\). Thus unbiasedness does not prevent horizon-induced deterioration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for a constant payoff, an unbiased cumulative-score estimator can have variance growing at least linearly with the simulation horizon.
assumptions_latex: \(s_t\in L^2\) and \(\mathbb E[s_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=0\).
\(\mathbb E[s_t^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]\ge c>0\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(G_T)\ge cT\) for \(G_T=\sum_{t=1}^T s_t\).

notation.meaning: Cumulative path score through horizon T.
Uniform lower bound on conditional score variance.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Derivative Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed-measure representation of a derivative through two probability laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_\theta\) be a differentiable family of probability measures whose weak derivative at \(\theta\) admits the decomposition \[P_\theta'=c_\theta(P_\theta^+-P_\theta^-),\] where \(c_\theta\ge0\) and \(P_\theta^+,P_\theta^-\) are probability measures. For every measurable performance \(h\) integrable under both component laws, \[\frac{d}{d\theta}\int h(x)P_\theta(dx)=c_\theta\left(\mathbb E_{P_\theta^+}[h(X^+)]-\mathbb E_{P_\theta^-}[h(X^-)]\right).\] Hence paired or independent simulations from the two component laws produce the unbiased estimator \(c_\theta(h(X^+)-h(X^-))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak derivative decomposed into two probability laws yields sensitivity as a scaled difference of their expected performances.
assumptions_latex: \(P_\theta'=c_\theta(P_\theta^+-P_\theta^-)\) as a finite signed measure.
\(h\) is integrable under \(P_\theta^+\) and \(P_\theta^-\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac{d}{d\theta}P_\theta h=c_\theta(P_\theta^+h-P_\theta^-h)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Process-Derivative Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupled simulation of positive and negative derivative-process laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a horizon \(T\), scale \(c_\theta\), component process laws \(P_{\theta,T}^+\) and \(P_{\theta,T}^-\), a performance \(H\), and replication count \(m\). For each replication \(r\), simulate a coupling \((X_{0:T}^{+,r},X_{0:T}^{-,r})\) having the prescribed marginal laws and compute \[G_r=c_\theta\left(H(X_{0:T}^{+,r})-H(X_{0:T}^{-,r})\right).\] Output \(\widehat J_m'=m^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^mG_r\). If the path-law derivative is \(P_{\theta,T}'=c_\theta(P_{\theta,T}^+-P_{\theta,T}^-)\), then \(\mathbb E[\widehat J_m']=J_T'(\theta)\). The coupling may be chosen to reduce variance without changing this expectation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulate coupled positive and negative derivative processes, difference their path performances, scale, and average to estimate sensitivity without bias.
assumptions_latex: \(P_{\theta,T}'=c_\theta(P_{\theta,T}^+-P_{\theta,T}^-)\).
Each simulated pair has marginals \(P_{\theta,T}^+\) and \(P_{\theta,T}^-\).
Both path performances are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat J_m']=J_T'(\theta)\).
