knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Couple paths \(X^{\theta+h}\) and \(X^\theta\), define \(A_h=\{X^{\theta+h}\ne X^\theta\}\), and set \(\Delta_h=H(X^{\theta+h})-H(X^\theta)\). Suppose, as \(h\downarrow0\), that \(\mathbb P(A_h)=\lambda h+o(h)\) for some \(0<\lambda<\infty\), that \(\Delta_h=0\) off \(A_h\), and that \(\mathbb E[\Delta_h\mid A_h]\to d\). Then \[\lim_{h\downarrow0}\frac{\mathbb E[H(X^{\theta+h})]-\mathbb E[H(X^\theta)]}{h}=\lambda d.\] Thus the one-sided sensitivity separates into a perturbation-event intensity and its limiting conditional effect. If additionally \(\mathbb E[\Delta_h^2\mid A_h]\to v\) for some \(0<v<\infty\), then \[\operatorname{Var}(\Delta_h/h)\sim\frac{\lambda v}{h}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If coupled paths differ with positive probability proportional to the perturbation size, the one-sided sensitivity equals the event intensity times the limiting conditional payoff change; the raw difference quotient has inverse-perturbation variance under a positive limiting conditional second moment.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) have a parameter-independent law \(P_U\), let the conditional law of \(Z\) given \(U=u\) have density \(q_\theta(z\mid u)\), and define \(J(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta[H(\theta,U,Z)]\). Suppose \(H\) is differentiable in its explicit \(\theta\)-argument for fixed \((U,Z)\), while the parameter dependence of the irregular component is represented by the conditional score \(s_\theta(z\mid u)=\partial_\theta\log q_\theta(z\mid u)\). Under valid interchange and integrability conditions, \[J'(\theta)=\mathbb E_\theta\!\left[\partial_\theta H(\theta,U,Z)+H(\theta,U,Z)s_\theta(Z\mid U)\right].\] The first term is the pathwise contribution and the second is the likelihood-ratio contribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Analytic-Simulation Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Analytic differentiation of a tractable term plus simulated residual sensitivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the objective admits the decomposition \[J(\theta)=A(\theta)+\mathbb E[R(\theta,\xi)],\] where \(A\) is analytically differentiable. Let \(G(\theta,\xi)\) be an integrable simulation estimator satisfying \(\mathbb E[G(\theta,\xi)]=\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E[R(\theta,\xi)]\). Then \[J'(\theta)=A'(\theta)+\mathbb E[G(\theta,\xi)],\] and, for independent replications \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\), \[\widehat J_m'(\theta)=A'(\theta)+\frac1m\sum_{r=1}^mG(\theta,\xi_r)\] is unbiased. Only the residual derivative requires simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiate the tractable objective component exactly and add an unbiased simulation estimate of the residual derivative.

\(G(\theta,\xi)\) is integrable and unbiased for the residual derivative.
\(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\) are independent replications.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat J_m'(\theta)]=J'(\theta)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Stage Indifference-Zone Procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A conservative Gaussian two-stage procedure using pilot variance bounds and fresh final samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(k\ge2\) independent normal systems with unknown means and variances, choose \(n_0\ge2\), indifference gap \(\delta>0\), and error \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). Stage one takes \(n_0\) observations per system and computes \(S_i^2\). With \(
u=n_0-1\) and lower \(\alpha/(2k)\) quantile \(q\) of \(\chi_
u^2\), set \(U_i=
u S_i^2/q\). Stage two takes \[N_i=\left\lceil4U_i\delta^{-2}\log\!\left( rac{2(k-1)}{\alpha}ight)ightceil\] fresh observations from system \(i\), then selects the largest stage-two sample mean. If the best mean exceeds every other mean by at least \(\delta\), the probability of correct selection is at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pilot samples produce simultaneous variance bounds; a separately sampled final stage allocates enough observations to select a δ-separated best system with prescribed confidence.
assumptions_latex: Each system produces independent \(N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)\) observations.
Systems, pilot samples, and fresh second-stage samples are mutually independent.
There is a unique best system with \(\mu_* - \max_{j\ne *}\mu_j\ge\delta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected algorithm content kind fits the leaf, but the candidate gives a newly specified Gaussian allocation rule and a finite-sample probability guarantee without any citation. children.title: Fully Sequential Indifference-Zone Procedures
children.top_down_role: Procedures using repeated sampling and screening.

knowledge_statements.title: Fully Sequential Indifference-Zone Procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated sampling and elimination using simultaneous anytime-valid confidence sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each system \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), construct intervals \(C_i(n)=[L_i(n),U_i(n)]\) satisfying \[\mathbb P\!\left(\mu_i\in C_i(n)\text{ for every }i,n\right)\ge1-\alpha.\] Initialize all systems as active. At each round, sample every active system, update its interval, and eliminate active \(i\) whenever \(U_i(n_i)<\max_{j\ne i}L_j(n_j)\). Stop when one system remains and return it. If interval widths converge almost surely to zero and the unique best mean is separated from every competitor by at least \(\delta>0\), the procedure stops almost surely and returns the best system with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly sample active systems and eliminate any whose upper confidence bound falls below a competitor's lower bound; simultaneous confidence sequences protect the best.
assumptions_latex: The confidence sequences have simultaneous coverage at least \(1-\alpha\).
Their widths converge almost surely to zero under continued sampling.
The unique best mean has gap at least \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\widehat i=*)\ge1-\alpha\), and the stopping time is almost surely finite.

notation.meaning: Anytime-valid confidence interval for system-i mean.
Current sample count for active system i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role matches the fully sequential leaf, and the confidence-sequence construction is plausible, but no source supports this particular elimination rule, simultaneous coverage requirement, or stopping guarantee. A specific authoritative procedure locator is required.

children.title: Subset Selection
children.top_down_role: Retention of a statistically defensible subset of strong alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Subset Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-confidence retention of a random subset containing a best alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\ge2\) alternatives have unknown performance means \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k\), with larger values preferred, and define the best-index set \(B(\mu)=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{1\le i\le k}\mu_i\). A level-\((1-\alpha)\) subset-selection procedure is a data-dependent, nonempty random set \(S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}\) satisfying \[\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal M}\mathbb P_\mu\bigl(S\cap B(\mu)\ne\varnothing\bigr)\ge1-\alpha,\] where \(\mathcal M\) is the declared model class. The procedure may retain several alternatives; its validity requires that at least one truly best alternative be retained with the stated uniform probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subset selection returns one or more alternatives while uniformly retaining at least one truly best alternative with the prescribed confidence.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is measurable with respect to the simulation data and is almost surely nonempty.
\(\mathcal M\) specifies the admissible joint sampling distributions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal M}\mathbb P_\mu(S\cap B(\mu)\ne\varnothing)\ge1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Set of alternatives attaining the largest mean.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is the correct content kind and the formulation is mathematically coherent, including ties through the best-index set. However, the record has no citation or explicit standard-field rationale, so it does not satisfy the evidence contract.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quantile-calibrated subset-selection rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a small subset intended to contain the best finite alternative with prescribed probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be finite, let \(x^*\in\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu_x\), and choose \(\alpha\) such that \(1/|\mathcal X|<1-\alpha<1\). With a common known sampling scale \(\sigma>0\), include \(x\) in \(S\) when \[\bar\mu_x^n\geq\max_{x'\neq x}\bar\mu_{x'}^n-h\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2}{n}},\] where \(h\) is the \((1-\alpha)\)-quantile of the stated random variable \(\max_i Z_i^n\), with \[Z_i^n=\frac{(\bar\mu_i^n-\bar\mu_x^n)-(\mu_i-\mu_x)}{\sigma\sqrt{2/n}}.\] The design objective is \[\mathbb P(x^*\in S)\geq1-\alpha,\] with \(|S|\) preferably as small as possible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternative is retained when its estimated mean is within a quantile-calibrated margin of the best competing estimate. The objective is to obtain a small subset containing a true best alternative with probability at least one minus alpha.
assumptions_latex: |\mathcal X|<\infty
x^*\in\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu_x
\frac{1}{|\mathcal X|}<1-\alpha<1
\sigma>0\text{ is the common known sampling scale used in the normalization}
n\geq1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S=\left\{x\in\mathcal X:\bar\mu_x^n\geq\max_{x'\neq x}\bar\mu_{x'}^n-h\sigma\sqrt{2/n}\right\},\qquad \mathbb P(x^*\in S)\geq1-\alpha\text{ is the stated objective}

children.title: Multiple Comparisons with the Best
children.top_down_role: Simultaneous comparison against an unknown leading alternative.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Comparisons with the Best
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous confidence bounds certify which alternatives can still be best.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For means \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k\), define \(\Delta_i=\mu_i-\max_{j\ne i}\mu_j\). Suppose random intervals \([L_i,U_i]\) satisfy \[\mathbb P\bigl(\Delta_i\in[L_i,U_i]\text{ for every }i\bigr)\ge1-\alpha.\] Then \(U_i<0\) certifies, on the simultaneous-coverage event, that alternative \(i\) is not best. The retained set \[S_{\mathrm{MCB}}=\{i:U_i\ge0\}\] contains at least one best alternative on that event and therefore satisfies \(\mathbb P(S_{\mathrm{MCB}}\cap\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i\mu_i\ne\varnothing)\ge1-\alpha\). Thus the simultaneous comparison intervals provide a directly checkable selection certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous intervals for each mean minus its strongest competitor certify exclusions; alternatives whose upper difference bound is nonnegative form a confidence subset containing a best.
assumptions_latex: \([L_i,U_i]\) jointly cover every \(\Delta_i=\mu_i-\max_{j\ne i}\mu_j\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).
Larger mean performance is preferred.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(S_{\mathrm{MCB}}\cap\operatorname*{arg\,max}_i\mu_i\ne\varnothing)\ge1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Mean of alternative i minus the largest competing mean.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Comparisons with a Control
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided simultaneous comparison of finitely many simulated systems against a designated control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let system \(0\) be the control and let systems \(1,\ldots,k\) have unknown mean performances \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k\), with larger values preferred. Multiple comparisons with a control constructs simultaneous confidence bounds \(L_i\) for \(\mu_i-\mu_0\) satisfying \(\mathbb P(\mu_i-\mu_0\ge L_i\text{ for every }i)\ge 1-\alpha\). The selected set is \(S=\{i:L_i>0\}\). Consequently, with probability at least \(1-\alpha\), every selected system truly improves upon the control; an indifference threshold \(\delta\ge0\) may instead define \(S_\delta=\{i:L_i>\delta\}\).

The simultaneous bounds have joint coverage at least \(1-\alpha\).

knowledge_statements.title: Normal Outputs with Known Variances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian finite-alternative selection when every sampling variance is known.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each system \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), suppose \(X_{i1},\ldots,X_{in_i}\) are independent \(N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)\) observations and \(\sigma_i^2\) is known. Then \(\bar X_i\sim N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2/n_i)\), and independent systems satisfy \(\bar X_i-\bar X_j\sim N(\mu_i-\mu_j,\sigma_i^2/n_i+\sigma_j^2/n_j)\). knowledge_statements.title: Normal Outputs with Unknown Variances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian selection using sample variances as estimated noise scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For system \(i\), let \(X_{i1},\ldots,X_{in_i}\) be independent \(N(\mu_i,\sigma_i^2)\) observations with unknown \(\sigma_i^2\). Define \(S_i^2=(n_i-1)^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{n_i}(X_{ir}-\bar X_i)^2\). Then \(\bar X_i\) and \(S_i^2\) are independent, \((n_i-1)S_i^2/\sigma_i^2\sim\chi^2_{n_i-1}\), and \(\sqrt{n_i}(\bar X_i-\mu_i)/S_i\sim t_{n_i-1}\). Selection procedures must therefore allocate enough initial observations to estimate scales and use variance-dependent comparison boundaries or sample sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With unknown Gaussian variances, sample means are paired with independent chi-square variance estimates and Studentized comparison statistics.

children.title: Robust Output-Distribution Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Selection beyond classical normal-output assumptions.

children.title: Non-Normal Output Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection settings with skewed, discrete, multimodal, or otherwise non-Gaussian outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Normal Output Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-alternative selection without an exact Gaussian output model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each system produce independent identically distributed outputs with finite mean \(\mu_i\), and let larger means be preferred. A non-normal selection rule is valid only when its comparison bounds are justified by the actual distributional assumptions: finite-variance asymptotics may support Studentized large-sample bounds, bounded or sub-Gaussian outputs support concentration bounds, and resampling requires conditions ensuring simultaneous coverage. Normal-theory constants alone do not generally provide their nominal finite-sample probability of correct selection for arbitrary non-normal outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-normal selection must calibrate comparisons using justified asymptotic, concentration, or resampling bounds rather than unqualified normal-theory constants.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many systems with well-defined finite means.
The sampling and tail assumptions used by the chosen calibration hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selection guarantee is inherited from valid simultaneous bounds under the stated non-normal output class.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits non-normal output selection, but its assertions about asymptotic, concentration, resampling, and normal-theory calibration span distinct assumption classes and require specific sources.

children.title: Distribution-Robust Selection
children.top_down_role: Selection procedures designed to limit reliance on a fully specified output distribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Distribution-Robust Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection guarantees uniform over an ambiguity class of output laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a specified ambiguity class of joint output distributions and let \(b(P)\) denote a best system under distribution \(P\). A recommendation rule \(\widehat b\) is distribution-robust at confidence \(1-\alpha\) over \(\mathcal P\) if \(\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb P_P(\widehat b=b(P))\ge1-\alpha\), whenever the best system is uniquely defined throughout the asserted parameter region. For indifference-zone selection, the requirement may be restricted to distributions satisfying a prescribed minimum mean gap \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distribution-robust rule meets its selection-confidence target uniformly over every output law in a stated ambiguity class.
assumptions_latex: The ambiguity class \(\mathcal P\) and performance functional are specified.
The asserted region has a unique best system, optionally separated by \(\delta>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb P_P(\widehat b=b(P))\ge1-\alpha\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform guarantee is mathematically coherent as a definition and fits the container, but no source establishes this as the intended meaning of distribution-robust selection in ranking and selection.

children.title: Heavy-Tail Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Selection settings where extreme observations materially affect statistical comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tail Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between mean-selection guarantees with and without tail control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume only that each system has a finite mean. Then the empirical mean need not admit exponential deviation bounds, so Gaussian or sub-Gaussian fixed-confidence sample-size formulas do not uniformly control incorrect selection over this class. If outputs instead satisfy a uniform \((1+\varepsilon)\)-moment bound \(\mathbb E|X_i-\mu_i|^{1+\varepsilon}\le M\) for some \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\), robust estimators such as truncation or median-of-means can yield polynomial- or exponential-confidence comparisons with rates depending on \(M\) and \(\varepsilon\). Thus explicit tail control is necessary for uniform finite-sample calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite means alone cannot justify sub-Gaussian selection guarantees; robust estimation requires an explicit moment or tail bound.
assumptions_latex: Systems are compared through their finite expected outputs.
A claimed uniform guarantee ranges over a specified heavy-tail class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without quantitative tail control, sub-Gaussian finite-sample selection calibration is not uniform over the output class.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role is appropriate, but the impossibility claim and the stated robust-estimation confidence behavior under a finite 1+epsilon moment require authoritative lower-bound and estimator references.

children.title: Probability of Correct Selection Guarantee
children.top_down_role: Reliability-certificate families for terminal selection.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Probability of correct selection and 0-1 loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminal reliability criterion for selecting the unique best member of a finite alternative set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be finite and assume that the largest true mean is unique. Define \[x^*=\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu_x,\qquad x^n\in\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\bar\mu_x^n.\] Under experimental policy \(\pi\), the probability of correct selection is \[P^{CS,\pi}=\mathbb E^\pi\!\left[\mathbf 1\{x^n=x^*\}\right].\] With the 0-1 loss \[L^{CS,\pi}=\mathbf 1\{x^n\neq x^*\},\] equivalently \[P^{CS,\pi}=1-\mathbb E^\pi\!\left[L^{CS,\pi}\right].\] The expectation is taken under the Bayesian or frequentist distribution induced by the experimental model and policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite set having a unique best alternative, probability of correct selection is the probability that the alternative recommended from the estimated means is the true best. It equals one minus the expected 0-1 loss for an incorrect recommendation.
assumptions_latex: |\mathcal X|<\infty
x^*=\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\mu_x\text{ is unique}
x^n\in\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\bar\mu_x^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P^{CS,\pi}=\mathbb E^\pi\!\left[\mathbf 1\{x^n=x^*\}\right]=1-\mathbb E^\pi\!\left[\mathbf 1\{x^n\neq x^*\}\right]

children.title: Finite-Sample Selection Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Nonasymptotic reliability guarantees for finite simulation effort.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sample Selection Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonasymptotic error control for empirical best-system selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let system \(i\) have mean \(\mu_i\), and suppose its sample mean based on \(n_i\) independent observations is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy \(v_i/n_i\). If \(i^*\) is the unique best system, \(\Delta_i=\mu_{i^*}-\mu_i>0\), and \(\widehat i\in\arg\max_i\bar X_i\), then a union bound gives \(\mathbb P(\widehat i\ne i^*)\le\sum_{i\ne i^*}\exp[-\Delta_i^2/(2(v_i/n_i+v_{i^*}/n_{i^*}))]\). Hence any allocation making the displayed sum at most \(\alpha\) guarantees correct selection with probability at least \(1-\alpha\) at the stated finite sample sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sub-Gaussian concentration gives an explicit finite-sample upper bound on the probability that the empirical best system is incorrect.
assumptions_latex: Sample means are independent and sub-Gaussian with proxies \(v_i/n_i\).
The best mean is unique and every inferior-system gap is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\widehat i=i^*)\ge1-\sum_{i\ne i^*}\exp[-\Delta_i^2/(2(v_i/n_i+v_{i^*}/n_{i^*}))]\).

notation.meaning: mean gap from the best system

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed union-bound guarantee is consistent with the stated sub-Gaussian proxy convention and fits the finite-sample container, but it lacks a supporting source.

children.title: Asymptotic Selection Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Selection reliability as simulation effort grows.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Selection Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency of empirical best-system selection under increasing replication counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finitely many systems, let outputs from system \(i\) be independent and identically distributed with finite mean \(\mu_i\). Suppose the best system \(i^*\) is unique and every system is sampled infinitely often, so \(n_i(N)\to\infty\) as total effort \(N\to\infty\). If \(\widehat i_N\in\arg\max_i\bar X_{i,n_i(N)}\), then the strong law of large numbers implies \(\widehat i_N=i^*\) eventually almost surely. In particular, \(\mathbb P(\widehat i_N=i^*)\to1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every system receives infinitely many samples and the best mean is unique, empirical-best selection is eventually correct almost surely.
assumptions_latex: There are finitely many systems with independent identically distributed integrable outputs.
The best mean is unique and \(n_i(N)\to\infty\) for every system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat i_N\to i^*\) almost surely in the eventual-equality sense, and \(\mathbb P(\widehat i_N=i^*)\to1\).

notation.meaning: samples allocated to system i by effort N

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The consistency claim is standard for fixed underlying i.i.d. output sequences, but no source is cited and the statement should be checked for the required almost-sure interpretation of adaptive sample counts tending to infinity.

children.title: Probability of Good Selection
children.top_down_role: Reliability guarantees permitting practically negligible recommendation error.

knowledge_statements.title: Probability of Good Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection success allowing a prescribed practical tolerance from optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu^*=\max_{1\le i\le k}\mu_i\), with larger performance preferred, and let \(\widehat i\) be the recommended system. For tolerance \(\delta\ge0\), a good selection is the event \(G_\delta=\{\mu_{\widehat i}\ge\mu^*-\delta\}\). A procedure has probability-of-good-selection guarantee \(1-\alpha\) if \(\mathbb P(G_\delta)\ge1-\alpha\) for every parameter configuration in its asserted model class. When \(\delta=0\), this reduces to correct selection if the best system is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A good selection recommends a system whose true mean is within a chosen tolerance of the optimal mean.
assumptions_latex: The alternative set is finite and every system has a well-defined mean.
The tolerance satisfies \(\delta\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\mu_{\widehat i}\ge\mu^*-\delta)\ge1-\alpha\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tolerance-based good-selection event is precise and fits the container, but the terminology and uniform guarantee are unsupported by a ranking-and-selection citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indifference-zone and probability-of-good-selection criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Practical-equivalence and reliability criteria for finite-alternative selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\in\arg\max_x\mu_x\), and let \(x^{\pi,N}\) be the alternative selected by policy \(\pi\) after \(N\) experiments. For \(\delta>0\), the selection is \(\delta\)-good when \[\mu_{x^*}-\mu_{x^{\pi,N}}\leq\delta.\] An indifference-zone correct-selection requirement is \[\mathbb P^\pi\!\left(x^{\pi,N}=x^*\mid\mu\right)>1-\alpha\quad\text{for all }\mu\text{ such that }\mu_{[1]}-\mu_{[2]}>\delta.\] If \(V^{\pi,n}\) is the selected solution value after \(n\) experiments, then the stated probability of good selection is \[P^{IZ,\pi}=\mathbb P^\pi\!\left(V^{\pi,n}>\mu^*-\delta\right),\] using the applicable Bayesian or frequentist distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A selected alternative is practically acceptable when its mean is within delta of the best. Indifference-zone procedures require high correct-selection probability when the best and second-best means differ by more than delta, while probability of good selection measures the chance that the reported value is strictly above the best value minus delta.

\delta>0
\mu_{[1]}\text{ and }\mu_{[2]}\text{ are the largest and second-largest means}
\mu_{[1]}-\mu_{[2]}>\delta\text{ for the correct-selection requirement}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P^{IZ,\pi}=\mathbb P^\pi\!\left(V^{\pi,n}>\mu^*-\delta\right)

children.title: Selection-Guarantee Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Reliability breakdown under ties, dependence, misspecification, or input uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection-Guarantee Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which nominal correct-selection guarantees cease to apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A probability-of-correct-selection claim calibrated for a unique best system, independent correctly specified outputs, and known simulation-input law need not survive removal of those assumptions. At a tie, a single-index correct-selection event is not uniquely defined; unmodeled cross-system or temporal dependence invalidates product-form or independence-based error calibration; output-tail misspecification invalidates nominal comparison quantiles; and estimating a common input distribution without accounting for its uncertainty can create persistent correlated error across systems. The original guarantee applies only after redefining success or recalibrating the joint uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ties, ignored dependence, tail misspecification, and unmodeled input uncertainty can invalidate nominal correct-selection guarantees.
assumptions_latex: The nominal procedure was calibrated under uniqueness, independence, a specified output model, or a known input law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Removing a calibration assumption removes the associated nominal selection guarantee unless validity is re-established under the enlarged model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The content kind and local scope are appropriate, but the claims about ties, dependence, tail misspecification, and input uncertainty require mechanism-specific sources.

children.title: Progressive Elimination Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Progressive removal of statistically inferior alternatives.

children.title: Racing Procedures
children.top_down_role: Sequential comparison families that progressively concentrate simulation on competitive alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Racing Procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Round-based elimination using simultaneous confidence comparisons among active systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input confidence level \(1-\alpha\), systems \(1,\ldots,k\), and simultaneous confidence radii \(r_i(t)\). Initialize \(A_1=\{1,\ldots,k\}\). At round \(t\), sample every \(i\in A_t\), compute estimates \(\widehat\mu_i(t)\), lower bounds \(L_i(t)=\widehat\mu_i(t)-r_i(t)\), and upper bounds \(U_i(t)=\widehat\mu_i(t)+r_i(t)\). Set \(A_{t+1}=\{i\in A_t:U_i(t)\ge\max_{j\in A_t}L_j(t)\}\). Stop when \(|A_t|=1\) and output its member, or apply a stated precision stopping rule. Time-uniform simultaneous coverage makes elimination of the true best occur with probability at most \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A race repeatedly samples active systems and removes any whose upper confidence bound lies below a competitor's lower bound.
assumptions_latex: The confidence intervals jointly cover all active-system means at all elimination times with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).
There is a unique best system for exact identification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On the simultaneous-coverage event, the best system is never eliminated and the sole survivor, when reached, is optimal.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The round-based confidence-bound elimination rule fits racing procedures, and its conditional coverage argument is coherent, but the algorithm and guarantee have no cited source.

children.title: Sequential Elimination Procedures
children.top_down_role: Procedures centered on removing alternatives as statistical evidence accumulates.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Elimination Procedures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive elimination driven by time-uniform pairwise evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input systems \(1,\ldots,k\), confidence level \(1-\alpha\), and confidence sequences \([L_i(t),U_i(t)]\). Initialize the active set \(A=\{1,\ldots,k\}\). At each time \(t\), choose one or more systems in \(A\) by a stated sampling rule, update their statistics, and eliminate every \(i\in A\) satisfying \(U_i(t)<\max_{j\in A\setminus\{i\}}L_j(t)\). Continue until one system remains, and output it. If the confidence sequences cover all means simultaneously for every time with probability at least \(1-\alpha\), the output is the unique best system with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential elimination adaptively samples surviving systems and discards alternatives statistically dominated by another active system.
assumptions_latex: The confidence sequences have joint time-uniform coverage at least \(1-\alpha\).
The best system is unique, and the sampling rule supplies enough information to separate it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\text{output}=i^*)\ge1-\alpha\), provided the procedure terminates.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role and conditional correctness claim fit sequential elimination, but the sampling, termination, and time-uniform coverage conditions require a specific authoritative source.

\[
O\!\left(\frac{K}{\varepsilon^2}\log\frac{2}{\delta}\right)
\]
time steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Median elimination is (ε,δ)-correct and stops after at most order K divided by ε squared times log(2/δ) time steps.
assumptions_latex: K\ge 1
\varepsilon>0
\delta>0
\text{median elimination is applied to the }K\text{ options}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Median elimination is }(\varepsilon,\delta)\text{-correct and stops in }O\!\left(K\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2/\delta)\right)\text{ time steps.}

children.top_down_role: Failure regimes where early statistical evidence removes a competitive alternative.

knowledge_statements.title: Premature-Elimination Risk
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Risk control for confidence-bound elimination of the uniquely best arm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let arm \(i^*=\arg\max_i\mu_i\) be unique. At round \(t\), eliminate arm \(i\) only if \(U_i(t)<\max_{j\in S_t}L_j(t)\). If the simultaneous coverage event \(\mathcal E=\{\mu_i\in[L_i(t),U_i(t)]\text{ for every }i,t\}\) has probability at least \(1-\delta\), then \(i^*\) is never eliminated on \(\mathcal E\), so premature elimination has probability at most \(\delta\). Fixed-time intervals repeatedly reused without a time-uniform or summable-error correction need not satisfy this guarantee, even when each individual interval has nominal coverage \(1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneous confidence coverage protects the best arm from elimination; repeatedly applying uncorrected fixed-time intervals can invalidate the nominal error guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \(i^*\) is the unique mean-maximizing arm.
Elimination uses the displayed confidence-bound rule.
The intervals have simultaneous coverage probability at least \(1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P(\text{the best arm is prematurely eliminated})\leq\delta\).

notation.meaning: set of active arms at round t
confidence interval for arm i at round t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and simultaneous-coverage argument fit the leaf, but no cited source supports the time-uniform guarantee or the warning about repeated fixed-time intervals.

children.title: Evidence-Tracking Allocation Family
children.top_down_role: Allocation guided by instance-dependent statistical evidence.

children.title: Likelihood-Based Allocation
children.top_down_role: Simulation allocation guided by instance-specific likelihood evidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Likelihood-Based Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-likelihood allocation for fixed-confidence identification in identifiable parametric arm models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For model parameter \(\mu\), define \(\operatorname{Alt}(\mu)\) as the parameters having a different best arm and set \(I(w,\mu)=\inf_{\lambda\in\operatorname{Alt}(\mu)}\sum_{i=1}^K w_i d(\mu_i,\lambda_i)\). After initializing by sampling every arm, at time \(t\) compute an estimate \(\widehat\mu(t)\) and a target \(w^*(t)\in\arg\max_{w\in\Delta_K}I(w,\widehat\mu(t))\). Sample an arm whose count is most below \(t w_i^*(t)\), subject to forced exploration. Stop when the generalized likelihood ratio against every alternative exceeds a calibrated threshold, and output the estimated best arm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Estimate the instance, maximize its worst-case likelihood evidence rate, track that allocation, and stop when all competing best-arm explanations are rejected.
assumptions_latex: Each arm belongs to an identifiable parametric family with divergence \(d\).
Every arm is initialized and forced exploration prevents permanent neglect.
The stopping threshold is calibrated for error probability \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sampling proportions target \(\arg\max_{w\in\Delta_K}I(w,\widehat\mu(t))\), while stopping is determined by likelihood evidence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but this blends target computation, deficit tracking, forced exploration, GLR stopping, and recommendation without identifying a precise sourced algorithm or calibrated threshold.

children.title: Allocation-Target Tracking
children.top_down_role: Control of empirical sampling proportions relative to a desired allocation target.

knowledge_statements.title: Allocation-Target Tracking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deficit tracking of a possibly data-dependent target sampling proportion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with \(N_i(K)=1\) for every arm. At each time \(t\geq K\), compute a target vector \(w(t)\in\Delta_K\). If some arm violates a prescribed forced-exploration floor, sample such an arm; otherwise choose \(I_{t+1}\in\arg\max_i\{t w_i(t)-N_i(t)\}\). Update its count and recompute the target. If \(w(t)\to w^*\) almost surely and the number of forced-exploration selections is \(o(t)\), then this deficit-tracking rule satisfies \(N_i(t)/t\to w_i^*\) for every arm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample the arm with the largest deficit relative to the current target; a convergent target is then tracked asymptotically.
assumptions_latex: \(w(t)\in\Delta_K\) and \(w(t)\to w^*\) almost surely.
Forced-exploration selections occur \(o(t)\) times.
Ties are resolved by a fixed measurable rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \frac{N_i(t)}{t}\longrightarrow w_i^*\quad\text{for every }i\).

notation.meaning: number of samples from arm i by time t
target allocation vector at time t
arm selected at the next sampling time

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the container, but the asserted convergence for a data-dependent target under only the stated forced-exploration condition requires a specific tracking lemma and exact hypotheses.

children.title: Evidence-Tracking Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Regimes where noisy evidence or delayed adaptation prevents reliable allocation tracking.

knowledge_statements.title: Evidence-Tracking Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Efficiency loss when empirical sampling proportions track a suboptimal evidence allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I(w,\mu)=\inf_{\lambda\in\operatorname{Alt}(mu)}\sum_i w_i d(\mu_i,\lambda_i)\) and \(I^*(\mu)=\sup_{w\in\Delta_K}I(w,\mu)\). Suppose an allocation rule satisfies \(N_i(t)/t\to w_i\), while its stopping statistic accumulates evidence at asymptotic rate \(I(w,\mu)>0\). If \(I(w,\mu)<I^*(\mu)\), then reaching a threshold asymptotic to \(\log(1/\delta)\) requires first-order sample size \(\log(1/\delta)/I(w,\mu)\), exceeding the optimal scale by the factor \(I^*(\mu)/I(w,\mu)>1\). If \(I(w,\mu)=0\), logarithmic fixed-confidence efficiency fails entirely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tracking the wrong allocation reduces the evidence exponent, inflates sample complexity, and can destroy logarithmic efficiency when the limiting evidence rate is zero.
assumptions_latex: The limiting sampling proportions \(w\) exist.
The likelihood evidence has asymptotic rate \(I(w,\mu)\).
The stopping threshold is asymptotic to \(\log(1/\delta)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(w,\mu)<I^*(\mu)\) implies an asymptotic inflation factor \(I^*(\mu)/I(w,\mu)\).

notation.meaning: parameters with a different best arm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but convergence of an evidence statistic's normalized rate alone does not automatically establish the claimed stopping-time equivalent. A sourced theorem with hitting-time regularity is required; moreover, \(\operatorname{Alt}(mu)\) is inconsistent with \(\operatorname{Alt}(\mu)\).

children.title: Fixed-Confidence Sample-Complexity Theory
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound and optimal-allocation result families.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Confidence Sample-Complexity Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Change-of-measure lower bound and characteristic time for fixed-confidence best-arm identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a uniquely best instance \(\mu\), define \(T^*(\mu)^{-1}=\sup_{wiinin\Delta_K}\inf_{lambda\in\operatorname{Alt}(mu)}\sum_i w_i d(\mu_i,lambda_i)\). Any \(\delta\)-correct algorithm with stopping time \(\tau\) obeys, for every \(\lambda\in\operatorname{Alt}(mu)\), \(\sum_i \mathbb E_mu[N_i(tau)]d(mu_i,lambda_i)\geq\operatorname{kl}(1-delta,delta)\). Consequently, \(\mathbb E_mu[tau]\geq T^*(mu)\operatorname{kl}(1-delta,delta)\), and hence \(\liminf_{delta\downarrow0}\mathbb E_mu[tau]/\log(1/delta)\geq T^*(mu)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every fixed-confidence procedure must collect enough divergence against each alternative, yielding the characteristic-time lower bound on expected samples.
assumptions_latex: The arm model admits the stated change-of-measure divergence.
The best arm under \(\mu\) is unique.
The algorithm is \(\delta\)-correct and has finite expected stopping time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \liminf_{delta\downarrow0}\frac{\mathbb E_mu[tau]}{\log(1/delta)}\geq T^*(mu)\).

notation.meaning: instances having a different best arm

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits and the intended lower bound is standard, but the displayed formulas contain corrupted notation such as \(wiinin\), \(lambda\), \(mu\), \(tau\), and \(delta\). No authoritative theorem citation is supplied to establish the exact model assumptions and bound.

children.title: Fixed-Budget Best-Arm Identification
children.top_down_role: Identification under predetermined simulation effort.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-budget best-arm identification objective
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines best-arm identification when the sampling horizon is prescribed in advance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a horizon \(n\), the learner chooses a policy \(\pi=(\pi_t)_{t=1}^{n+1}\) whose terminal action is \(A_{n+1}\). The fixed-budget objective is \(\min_{\pi}\mathbb{P}_{\nu,\pi}(A_{n+1}\text{ is suboptimal})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a prescribed horizon n, a fixed-budget best-arm identification policy allocates samples and recommends an arm at time n+1 so as to minimize the probability of recommending a suboptimal arm.
assumptions_latex: n\text{ is the prescribed horizon}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi\text{ is chosen to minimize }\mathbb{P}_{\nu,\pi}(A_{n+1}\text{ is suboptimal}).

children.title: Successive-Rejects Family
children.top_down_role: Stagewise rejection under a fixed sampling budget.

knowledge_statements.title: Successive-Rejects Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stagewise fixed-budget elimination with one rejection after each allocation phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(K\) arms, budget \(T\), and nondecreasing cumulative phase allocations \(0=n_0<n_1<\cdots<n_{K-1}\) satisfying \(\sum_{r=1}^{K-1}|S_r|(n_r-n_{r-1})\leq T\), initialize \(S_1=\{1,\ldots,K\}\). In phase \(r\), sample every arm in \(S_r\) until it has received \(n_r\) phase-scheduled observations, compute its empirical mean, and remove an arm attaining the smallest empirical mean. Set the remaining arms to \(S_{r+1}\). After \(K-1\) phases, output the sole surviving arm; unused budget may be assigned by a fixed convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate samples in stages and reject exactly one empirically worst surviving arm after each stage until one remains.
assumptions_latex: Rewards have well-defined means and independent samples within each arm.
The phase schedule respects the total budget \(T\).
The objective is identification of the largest-mean arm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns the unique member of \(S_K\) after using at most \(T\) samples.

notation.meaning: cumulative allocation level for phase r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits, but the wording does not clearly distinguish total cumulative observations from observations newly assigned under the phase schedule. A canonical Successive Rejects source and exact schedule are required.

children.title: Sequential-Halving Family
children.top_down_role: Geometric candidate reduction with staged allocation.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential-Halving Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-budget elimination retaining approximately half of the candidates per round.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given active set \(S_1=\{1,\ldots,K\}\), budget \(T\), and \(R=\lceil\log_2 K\rceil\), divide the budget among \(R\) rounds. In round \(r\), allocate the round budget as equally as possible among arms in \(S_r\), compute empirical means using the samples prescribed by the chosen variant, and let \(S_{r+1}\) contain the \(\lceil |S_r|/2\rceil\) arms with largest empirical means. Resolve ties by a fixed rule. Continue until a singleton remains and output it, assigning rounding residuals without exceeding \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split the budget across logarithmically many rounds, sample survivors equally, and discard approximately the lower empirical half each round.
assumptions_latex: The budget permits at least one scheduled observation per active arm and round.
Rewards have well-defined means and independent samples within each arm.
Ties and integer budget residuals follow fixed conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After at most \(\lceil\log_2 K\rceil\) rounds, the active set is a singleton selected using at most \(T\) samples.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and broad halving structure fit, but the record deliberately leaves cumulative-versus-round-only empirical means and the allocation schedule to an unspecified variant. A canonical source is needed for an exact algorithm statement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential-halving error-probability bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instance-dependent fixed-budget guarantee for sequential halving on the stated unit-subgaussian bandit class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(\nu\in\mathcal{E}_{SG}^{k}(1)\) has mean vector \(\mu=\mu(\nu)\) with \(\mu_1\geq\cdots\geq\mu_k\), and \(\pi\) is sequential halving, then
\[
\mathbb{P}_{\nu,\pi}\!\left(\Delta_{A_{n+1}}>0\right)\leq 3\log_2(k)\exp\!\left(-\frac{n}{16H_2(\mu)\log_2(k)}\right),
\qquad H_2(\mu)=\max_{i:\Delta_i>0}\frac{i}{\Delta_i^2}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a unit-subgaussian k-armed instance with means ordered from largest to smallest, sequential halving recommends a suboptimal arm with probability at most 3 log base 2 of k times exp(-n divided by 16 H2(mu) log base 2 of k), where H2(mu) is the maximum of i divided by the squared positive gap of arm i.
assumptions_latex: \nu\in\mathcal{E}_{SG}^{k}(1)
\mu=\mu(\nu)
\mu_1\geq\cdots\geq\mu_k
\pi\text{ is sequential halving}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb{P}_{\nu,\pi}(\Delta_{A_{n+1}}>0)\leq 3\log_2(k)\exp\!\left(-\frac{n}{16H_2(\mu)\log_2(k)}\right),\quad H_2(\mu)=\max_{i:\Delta_i>0}\frac{i}{\Delta_i^2}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential-halving algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stagewise fixed-budget best-arm identification that repeatedly retains approximately half of the active arms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(n\) and \(k\), set \(L=\lceil\log_2(k)\rceil\) and \(\mathcal A_1=[k]\). For \(\ell=1,\ldots,L\), set
\[
T_\ell=\left\lfloor\frac{n}{L|\mathcal A_\ell|}\right\rfloor,
\]
choose every arm in \(\mathcal A_\ell\) exactly \(T_\ell\) times, compute \(\widehat\mu_i^\ell\) for each \(i\in\mathcal A_\ell\) from its last \(T_\ell\) samples, and let \(\mathcal A_{\ell+1}\) contain the \(\lceil|\mathcal A_\ell|/2\rceil\) arms in \(\mathcal A_\ell\) having the largest empirical means. Return as \(A_{n+1}\) the arm in \(\mathcal A_{L+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential halving starts with all k arms and uses ceiling(log base 2 of k) stages. At each stage it samples every active arm equally, computes empirical means from the latest stage samples, and retains the top half rounded upward. It returns the arm in the final active set.
assumptions_latex: n\text{ and }k\text{ are inputs}
L=\lceil\log_2(k)\rceil
\mathcal A_1=[k]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A_{n+1}\text{ is the arm in }\mathcal A_{L+1}\text{ after the prescribed sequential-halving stages}.

children.title: Fixed-Budget Complexity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Error-exponent, lower-bound, and instance-optimality boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Budget Complexity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-theoretic error-exponent boundary for allocation-limited fixed-budget identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For instance \(\mu\), allocation \(w\in\Delta_K\), and alternatives \(\operatorname{Alt}(mu)\) having a different best arm, define \(C(w,mu)=\inf_{lambda\in\operatorname{Alt}(mu)}\sum_i w_i d(mu_i,lambda_i)\) and \(C^*(mu)=\sup_{wiinin\Delta_K}C(w,mu)\). Under the standard change-of-measure regularity conditions, no consistent fixed-budget procedure whose sampling proportions converge to \(w\) can have error exponent exceeding \(C(w,mu)\). Thus the allocation-optimized information boundary is \(C^*(mu)\); attaining it requires both optimal allocation and a terminal decision rule with matching large-deviation behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smallest divergence to a wrong-best instance bounds the error exponent; optimizing this quantity over allocations gives the fixed-budget information boundary.
assumptions_latex: The statistical model satisfies change-of-measure and large-deviation regularity.
Sampling proportions converge to \(w\).
The procedure is consistent on identifiable instances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \limsup_{T\to\infty}-\frac{1}{T}\log\mathbb P_mu(\widehat i_T\neq i^*)\leq C(w,mu)\leq C^*(mu)\).

notation.meaning: worst-alternative information rate under allocation w

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits, but the claimed exponent boundary depends on the statistical model, sampling adaptivity, consistency notion, and large-deviation conditions. These are not made precise or sourced, and formulas contain corrupted notation such as \(wiinin\), \(mu\), and \(lambda\).

children.title: Generalized Identification Objectives
children.top_down_role: Pure-exploration objectives extending beyond one best alternative.

children.title: Top-Set Identification
children.top_down_role: Identification of a prescribed number of leading alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Top-Set Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-confidence identification of the prescribed number of largest-mean alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\geq2\), choose \(m\in\{1,\ldots,K-1\}\), and order the means as \(\mu_{(1)}\geq\cdots\geq\mu_{(K)}\). Assume \(\mu_{(m)}>\mu_{(m+1)}\), and let \(S_m^*\) be the indices of the \(m\) largest means. A stopping rule \(\tau\) and recommendation \(\widehat S_tau\) form a \(\delta\)-correct top-set identification procedure when \(|\widehat S_tau|=m\) and \(\mathbb P_mu(\widehat S_tau=S_m^*)\geq1-delta\) for every instance satisfying the boundary-gap assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Top-set identification returns exactly the prescribed number of highest-mean arms with probability at least one minus delta.
assumptions_latex: The boundary gap satisfies \(\mu_{(m)}>\mu_{(m+1)}\).
The procedure stops almost surely on each admissible instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\widehat S_tau|=m\) and \(\mathbb P_mu(\widehat S_tau=S_m^*)\geq1-delta\).

notation.meaning: true set of the m largest-mean arms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and boundary-gap formulation fit Top-Set Identification, but essential symbols are corrupted throughout: \(\widehat S_tau\), \(\mathbb P_mu\), and \(delta\) do not express the intended indexed notation. No authoritative source is cited.

children.title: Threshold-Based Acceptable-Arm Identification
children.top_down_role: Identification relative to an acceptability threshold.

children.title: Threshold Identification
children.top_down_role: Identification of alternatives according to performance relative to a specified threshold.

knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fixed-confidence classification of all arms relative to a known threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a known threshold \(theta\), define the super-threshold set \(G_theta(mu)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}:\mu_i\geqtheta\}\). A threshold-identification procedure consists of a stopping time \(tau\) and reported set \(\widehat G_tau\). It is \(delta\)-correct on an instance class \(\mathcal M\) when, for every \(\mu\in\mathcal M\), it stops almost surely and satisfies \(\mathbb P_mu(\widehat G_tau=G_theta(mu))\geq1-delta\). Finite expected-sample guarantees are normally stated on instances separated from the threshold, such as \(\min_i|\mu_i-theta|>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Threshold identification classifies every arm as above or below a known threshold with controlled familywise error.
assumptions_latex: The threshold \(theta\) is known.
Arm means are identifiable from their observation distributions.
The target instance class specifies treatment of equality at \(theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P_mu(\widehat G_tau=G_theta(mu))\geq1-delta\).

notation.meaning: true set of arms meeting the threshold

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but the use of \(\mu_i\geq\theta\) makes equality treatment substantive for almost-sure stopping and finite-sample identification. The exact instance class requires a source, and numerous intended commands appear as plain multiletter variables, including \(theta\), \(tau\), \(mu\), and \(delta\).

children.title: Good-Arm Identification
children.top_down_role: Discovery of one or more alternatives meeting an acceptability criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Good-Arm Identification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-confidence discovery of one arm meeting a prescribed quality threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a threshold \(theta\) and let \(G_theta(mu)=\{i:\mu_i\geqtheta\}\). A good-arm identification procedure stops at \(tau\) and returns either an arm \(\widehat i_tau\) or the symbol \(bot\). It is \(delta\)-correct if, whenever \(G_theta(mu)\neq\varnothing\), it returns a member of \(G_theta(mu)\) with probability at least \(1-delta\), and whenever \(G_theta(mu)=\varnothing\), it returns \(bot\) with probability at least \(1-delta\). Exact finite-sample guarantees generally require separation of all relevant means from \(theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Good-arm identification finds one arm above a known threshold, or declares that none exists, with controlled error.
assumptions_latex: The quality threshold \(theta\) is known.
Arm means are identifiable.
The procedure specifies a no-good-arm output \(bot\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P_mu(\widehat i_tau\in G_theta(mu))\geq1-delta\) when \(G_theta(mu)\neq\varnothing\), and \(\mathbb P_mu(\widehat i_tau=bot)\geq1-delta\) otherwise.

notation.meaning: declaration that no good arm exists

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but requiring a correct no-good-arm declaration is a particular objective convention that must be sourced. The record also corrupts intended notation such as \(theta\), \(mu\), \(tau\), \(delta\), and \(bot\).

children.title: Multiple-Good-Arm Discovery
children.top_down_role: Identification settings requiring several acceptable alternatives rather than a single recommendation.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Good-Arm Discovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-confidence discovery of a requested number of distinct threshold-qualified arms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a threshold \(\theta\), a requested count \(m\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\), and the set of qualified arms
\[
G_\theta(\mu)=\{i:\mu_i\ge\theta\}.
\]
A multiple-good-arm discovery procedure stops at \(\tau\) and returns \(\widehat G_\tau\). It is \(\delta\)-correct with completeness certification when
\[
\mathbb P_\mu\!\left(\widehat G_\tau\subseteq G_\theta(\mu),\ |\widehat G_\tau|=\min\{m,|G_\theta(\mu)|\}\right)\ge1-\delta.
\]
Thus it returns \(m\) distinct qualified arms when at least \(m\) exist and otherwise returns every qualified arm, certifying that fewer than \(m\) exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discover the requested number of distinct above-threshold arms, or return all such arms while certifying that fewer exist.
assumptions_latex: The threshold \(theta\) and requested count \(m\) are known.
Arm means are identifiable.
Completeness is required when fewer than \(m\) good arms exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(mathbb P_mubigl(widehat G_tau\subseteq G_theta(mu),\ |widehat G_tau|=min\{m,|G_theta(mu)|\}bigr)geq1-delta\).

notation.meaning: reported set of discovered good arms

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf, but completeness certification when fewer than \(m\) good arms exist is stronger than ordinary discovery and requires precise separation, stopping, and error conventions from a source. The LaTeX is extensively corrupted, including missing commands and an unmatched delimiter in the definition of \(G_\theta(\mu)\).

children.title: Simulation Budget Allocation
children.top_down_role: Allocation principles balancing estimation, screening, and final discrimination.

children.title: Nonadaptive Allocation Family
children.top_down_role: Nonadaptive allocation baselines.

children.title: Equal Allocation
children.top_down_role: Nonadaptive simulation budgets divided uniformly across alternatives.

assumptions_latex: There are \(k\ge 2\) alternatives and an integer simulation budget \(N\ge 0\).
Each replication has the same unit cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n_i\in\{q,q+1\}\) for every \(i\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^k n_i=N\).

notation.meaning: number of alternatives and total replication budget
quotient and remainder in division of N by k

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer equal allocation with unit-cost simulation replications.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Ranking and Selection p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(N=qk+r\), where \(q=\lfloor N/k\rfloor\) and \(0\le r<k\), an equal allocation is any vector \((n_1,\ldots,n_k)\in\mathbb Z_+^k\) having exactly \(r\) components equal to \(q+1\) and the remaining \(k-r\) components equal to \(q\). Thus every replication is assigned and the allocation counts differ pairwise by at most one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal allocation distributes the integer budget as evenly as possible, so every alternative receives either the floor or ceiling of the budget divided by the number of alternatives.

children.title: Static Unequal Allocation
children.top_down_role: Predetermined nonuniform simulation budgets fixed before evidence is observed.

assumptions_latex: There are \(k\ge 2\) alternatives and a fixed integer budget \(N\ge 0\).
The allocation is chosen before observations from the main simulation experiment are revealed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n_i=\lfloor Nw_i\rfloor+\mathbf 1\{i\in R\}\), with \(\sum_i n_i=N\), is a static allocation and is unequal precisely when it is not an equal allocation.

notation.meaning: fixed allocation weight of alternative i

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed weighted allocation, including weights estimated from independent pilot data.

source_refs.locator: 3.1 Ranking and Selection p. 86
source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w=(w_1,\ldots,w_k)\) satisfy \(w_i\ge 0\) and \(\sum_i w_i=1\), and let \(w\) be fixed independently of the main-stage observations. Set \(m_i=\lfloor Nw_i\rfloor\), and choose a set \(R\) of \(N-\sum_i m_i\) indices, conventionally those with largest fractional remainders \(Nw_i-m_i\). The static allocation assigns \(n_i=m_i+\mathbf 1\{i\in R\}\). It is a static unequal allocation when \((n_1,\ldots,n_k)\) is not an equal allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A static unequal rule fixes nonuniform allocation weights before the main experiment, rounds the weighted budget while preserving its total, and produces counts that do not form an equal allocation.
knowledge_statements.title: Static Unequal Allocation

children.title: Nonadaptive Allocation Baselines
children.top_down_role: Fixed allocation policies used as comparison baselines for adaptive procedures.

assumptions_latex: A finite set of alternatives is evaluated under a common total simulation budget.
Every baseline fixes its allocation without using observations generated during the evaluated main stage.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: One-Replication-at-a-Time Sequential OCBA
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-batch sequential OCBA, recommended when simulation replications are relatively costly compared with recalculating the allocation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set $\tau=1$. At iteration $t$, compute tentative continuous OCBA targets satisfying, for nonbest alternatives $(i),(j)$, $\frac{n^{\mathrm{target}}_{(i),t+1}}{n^{\mathrm{target}}_{(j),t+1}}=\left(\frac{\widehat\sigma_{(i)}/d_{(i)(k)}}{\widehat\sigma_{(j)}/d_{(j)(k)}}\right)^2$ and $n^{\mathrm{target}}_{(k),t+1}=\widehat\sigma_{(k)}\sqrt{\sum_{i:(i)\ne(k)}(n^{\mathrm{target}}_{(i),t+1})^2/\widehat\sigma_i^2}$. Choose $(i^*)\in\arg\max_i\{n^{\mathrm{target}}_{(i),t+1}-n_{(i),t}\}$, take one additional sample from $(i^*)$, set $n_{(i^*),t+1}=n_{(i^*),t}+1$ and $n_{(i),t+1}=n_{(i),t}$ for $i\ne i^*$, and continue until $\beta$ is exhausted or the estimated probability of correct selection is sufficiently high.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a unit batch, calculate the continuous OCBA target allocation and identify the alternative with the largest target deficit relative to its current sample count. Give that alternative one additional replication and repeat until the budget is exhausted or the estimated probability of correct selection reaches the chosen stopping level.

d_{(i)(k)}\ne0\quad\text{for every nonbest alternative }(i)
\widehat\sigma_i\ \text{and }d_{(i)(k)}\ \text{are updated from accumulated simulation output}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (i^*)\in\arg\max_i\left(n^{\mathrm{target}}_{(i),t+1}-n_{(i),t}\right),\qquad n_{(i^*),t+1}=n_{(i^*),t}+1,\quad n_{(i),t+1}=n_{(i),t}\ (i\ne i^*).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential OCBA Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential allocation of a finite simulation budget using estimated performance gaps and output variability, including the integer-rounding failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given $k$ alternatives, total budget $\beta$, batch size $\tau$, and initial allocation $n_0\ge 5$, where $\beta-kn_0$ is a nonnegative multiple of $\tau$, initially sample each alternative $n_0$ times. At iteration $t$, update the sample means $\bar x_i$ and standard deviations $\widehat\sigma_i$, and designate an empirically best alternative $(k)\in\arg\max_i\bar x_i$. Compute continuous target allocations whose total budget is increased by $\tau$ and which satisfy, for nonbest alternatives $(i),(j)$, $\frac{n_{(i),t+1}}{n_{(j),t+1}}=\left(\frac{\widehat\sigma_{(i)}/d_{(i)(k)}}{\widehat\sigma_{(j)}/d_{(j)(k)}}\right)^2$ and $n_{(k),t+1}=\widehat\sigma_{(k)}\sqrt{\sum_{i:(i)\ne(k)}n_{(i),t+1}^2/\widehat\sigma_{(i)}^2}$. After integer rounding, simulate alternative $i$ an additional $(n_{(i),t+1}-n_{(i),t})^+$ times and repeat while the accumulated sample count is below $\beta$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initially sample every alternative n0 times. Repeatedly estimate means and standard deviations, identify an empirically best alternative, and calculate OCBA targets: nonbest allocations follow squared standard-deviation-to-gap ratios, and the best allocation satisfies the balancing equation. Round the targets and add the resulting positive sample deficits until the budget is reached. If a newly calculated target is below an alternative's current sample count, monotone sample counts, all OCBA allocation equations, and an exact batch increase of tau may be mutually incompatible; a rounding or allocation constraint must then be relaxed.
assumptions_latex: k\in\mathbb N
n_0\ge 5
\tau\in\mathbb N
\beta-kn_0\in\tau\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}
d_{(i)(k)}\ne0\quad\text{for every nonbest alternative }(i)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The allocation is updated sequentially according to the OCBA ratio and balancing equations until the sampling budget is reached, subject to integer rounding and possible constraint relaxation when a target falls below a current allocation.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential optimal computing budget allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sequential fixed-budget OCBA prescription, not an efficiency or probability-of-correct-selection theorem. The allocation equations require nonzero estimated gaps and usable variance estimates; ties or zero denominators leave the displayed rule undefined. Target allocations are rounded and can decrease, although realized sample counts cannot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M=|\mathcal X|\), take \(n_0\ge2\) pilot observations from every alternative, and divide the remaining budget \(B-Mn_0\) into increments \(\Delta\). At iteration \(n\), compute sample means \(\theta_x^n\), sample variances \(\widehat\sigma_x^{2,n}\), and a current best \(b\in\arg\max_x\theta_x^n\). For distinct nonbest alternatives \(x,x'\), set target allocations in the ratios \[\frac{N_x^{n+1}}{N_{x'}^{n+1}}=\frac{\widehat\sigma_x^{2,n}/(\theta_b^n-\theta_x^n)^2}{\widehat\sigma_{x'}^{2,n}/(\theta_b^n-\theta_{x'}^n)^2},\] and balance the best alternative by \[N_b^{n+1}=\widehat\sigma_b^n\sqrt{\sum_{i\ne b}\left(\frac{N_i^{n+1}}{\widehat\sigma_i^n}\right)^2}.\] Scale and round the targets so that their sum approximates the next cumulative budget. Take \(\max\{N_x^{n+1}-N_x^n,0\}\) additional observations of each \(x\), recompute after every increment, and upon exhausting the budget return an alternative in \(\arg\max_x\theta_x^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential OCBA starts with equal pilot samples and repeatedly estimates the alternatives' means and variances. Each new budget increment is targeted according to estimated output variances and squared gaps from the current best. A target that falls below an already realized sample count produces no new simulations. When the budget is exhausted, the alternative with the largest current sample mean is returned.
assumptions_latex: 2\le M=|\mathcal X|<\infty
n_0\ge2
B\ge Mn_0
\Delta>0
\frac{B-Mn_0}{\Delta}\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}
\theta_b^n-\theta_x^n\ne0\quad\text{for every nonbest }x\text{ used in the ratio rule}
\widehat\sigma_i^n>0\quad\text{for variance terms appearing in denominators}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{After the available budget is exhausted, return }\widehat x\in\arg\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\theta_x^n.

children.title: OCBA Efficiency Results
children.top_down_role: Large-budget allocation and selection-efficiency families.

assumptions_latex: There is a unique best alternative \(b\), and all mean gaps \(\delta_i=\mu_i-\mu_b\) for \(i\ne b\) are nonzero.
Observations are independent normal variables with variances \(0<\sigma_i^2<\infty\).
Allocation fractions converge to strictly positive limits satisfying the classical OCBA equations with true parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected smallest sample mean converges almost surely to \(b\), and the limiting fractions satisfy the OCBA ratio system.

notation.meaning: unique true best alternative for minimization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency and classical large-budget allocation ratios under independent normal sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(n_i(N)/N\to\alpha_i>0\), then every alternative is sampled infinitely often, so the sample means converge almost surely to their true means and selection by the smallest sample mean is consistent. The classical OCBA limiting fractions obey \[\frac{\alpha_i}{\alpha_j}=\frac{(\sigma_i/\delta_i)^2}{(\sigma_j/\delta_j)^2}\quad(i,j\ne b),\qquad \alpha_b=\sigma_b\sqrt{\sum_{i\ne b}\frac{\alpha_i^2}{\sigma_i^2}},\qquad \sum_i\alpha_i=1.\] These equations express the standard large-budget OCBA efficiency prescription.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive limiting sampling fractions ensure consistent selection; classical OCBA further prescribes asymptotic fractions determined by each alternative's variance and mean gap.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: LL multi-alternative allocation with nonnegativity correction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stagewise Bayesian value-of-information allocation under linear opportunity loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an additional budget \(\tau\), current counts \(n_i\), estimated variances \(\widehat\sigma_i^2\), and LL weights \(\gamma_i\), the continuous allocation is
\[
\tau_{(i)}=\frac{\left(\tau+\sum_{j=1}^k n_j\right)(\widehat\sigma_{(i)}^2\gamma_{(i)})^{1/2}}{\sum_{j=1}^k(\widehat\sigma_j^2\gamma_j)^{1/2}}-n_{(i)},
\]
where, for \((i)\ne(k)\),
\[
\gamma_{(i)}=\widehat\lambda_{ik}^{1/2}\frac{v_{(i)(k)}+(d_{ik}^*)^2}{v_{(i)(k)}-1}\phi_{v_{(i)(k)}}(d_{ik}^*),
\qquad
\gamma_{(k)}=\sum_{j:(j)\ne(k)}\gamma_{(j)}.
\]
This rule asymptotically minimizes the LL approximation when \(\tau\) is arbitrarily large and the resulting allocations are nonnegative. For smaller \(\tau\), initialize \(\mathcal S=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), recompute the allocation over \(\mathcal S\), remove alternatives assigned \(\tau_i\le0\), and repeat until all retained allocations are positive; excluded allocations are zero and the retained values are rounded so that \(\sum_i\tau_i=\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The LL rule allocates samples according to estimated variance and information weights after accounting for samples already collected. Its continuous formula is asymptotically optimal for the LL approximation at large stage budgets. At smaller budgets, alternatives with nonpositive tentative allocations are removed and the rule is recomputed, then rounded to the integer budget.
assumptions_latex: \tau>0
\widehat\sigma_i^2\text{ and the LL pairwise statistics are available.}
v_{(i)(k)}>1\text{ wherever the displayed weight is used.}
\text{Asymptotic optimality concerns the large-}\tau\text{ continuous allocation.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \tau_i\ge0\ \forall i,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^k\tau_i=\tau,\qquad \text{and the uncorrected rule asymptotically minimizes the LL approximation as }\tau\to\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At information state \(\mathcal F_n\), define the one-step value of measuring alternative \(x\) by \[\nu_x^n=\mathbb E\!\left[\max_i m_i^{n+1}(x)\mid\mathcal F_n\right]-\max_i m_i^n.\] Choose \(x_n\in\arg\max_x\nu_x^n\), observe its noisy response, and update the joint posterior; correlated posteriors may update unmeasured alternatives as well. Repeat until the sampling budget is exhausted, then recommend any \(i^\star\in\arg\max_i m_i^N\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Single-alternative small-sample EVI rule (LL1/KG1)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-stage lookahead allocation for finite alternatives under posterior expected opportunity cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At each stage, constrain the entire additional batch \(\tau\) to one alternative. For every alternative \(i\), compute \(\operatorname{EVI}_{LL,(i)}\), the expected reward improvement from sampling \(i\) and then selecting the alternative with the greatest updated sample mean. Choose
\[
i^*\in\arg\max_{1\le i\le k}\operatorname{EVI}_{LL,(i)},
\qquad \tau_{i^*}=\tau,
\qquad \tau_\ell=0\quad(\ell\ne i^*).
\]
For a nonbest alternative, its valuation compares it with the best of the other alternatives; for the current best, the relevant comparison is with the second-best alternative. The choice is recomputed at subsequent stages. Because only one alternative is sampled per stage, this rule avoids the LL asymptotic allocation, Bonferroni, and Welch approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: LL1, also called KG or KG1 in this setting, assigns the entire stage budget to the alternative with the largest one-step expected value of information. The choice is recomputed each stage and avoids the approximations used by the multi-alternative LL allocation.
assumptions_latex: \tau>0
\text{Exactly one alternative receives the stage budget.}
\text{Posterior expected opportunity cost, equivalently the stated expected reward improvement, is the criterion.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: i^*\in\arg\max_i\operatorname{EVI}_{LL,(i)},\qquad \tau_{i^*}=\tau,\qquad \tau_\ell=0\ \forall\ell\ne i^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Condition on the search history and its finite output \(C\). Generate a prespecified fresh screening sample for every \(i\in C\), compute statistics \(T_i\), and retain \[C'=\{i\in C:T_i\le c_i\}.\] The direction and thresholds are chosen so that larger \(T_i\) means stronger evidence of inferiority. If \(C'=\varnothing\), apply a prespecified fallback, such as retaining the candidate with smallest \(T_i\). Output only \(C'\) and the fresh screening data required by the subsequent final-selection procedure.

children.title: Independent Final Selection
children.top_down_role: Final selection using simulation evidence separated from candidate generation.

assumptions_latex: A finite candidate set \(C\) is measurable with respect to a search history \(\mathcal H\).
Conditional on \(C\), the final-stage data are independent of \(\mathcal H\) and follow the sampling model assumed by a fixed-set selection procedure.
For every deterministic admissible candidate set, that procedure has conditional erroneous-selection probability at most \(\alpha\), where \(0\le\alpha\le 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(\widehat i\text{ is an erroneous selection}\mid C)\le\alpha\) almost surely and hence \(\Pr(\widehat i\text{ is an erroneous selection})\le\alpha\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generate final-stage observations independently of \(\mathcal H\) conditional on the realized candidate set \(C\), and apply the prespecified fixed-set selection procedure to those observations only. If its erroneous-selection probability is at most \(\alpha\) for every admissible deterministic candidate set, then \[\Pr(\widehat i\text{ is an erroneous selection}\mid C)\le\alpha\quad\text{almost surely},\qquad \Pr(\widehat i\text{ is an erroneous selection})\le\alpha.\] Thus candidate generation does not invalidate the final guarantee, provided the guarantee is interpreted relative to the realized candidate set and the fresh-data assumptions hold.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-stage indifference-zone selection with independent sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent-sampling finite-alternative selection procedure with adaptive alternative-specific sample sizes and a probability-of-correct-selection guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\delta>0\), \(0<\alpha<1\), and a first-stage size \(n_0\). For each of \(K\) alternatives, collect \(n_0\) i.i.d. observations, independently across alternatives, and compute its sample variance \(s_i^2\). Using the prescribed critical constant \(h\), set \(n_i=\max\{n_0,\lceil h^2s_i^2/\delta^2\rceil\}\). Collect \(n_i-n_0\) additional observations independently of the first stage and of all other alternatives, form \(\bar L_i=n_i^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{n_i}y_k(\boldsymbol\theta_i)\), and select an alternative with the smallest \(\bar L_i\). Under the normal-output assumptions of the indifference-zone procedure, if the best alternative \(\boldsymbol\theta^*\) satisfies \(L(\boldsymbol\theta_j)-L(\boldsymbol\theta^*)\ge\delta\) for every \(\boldsymbol\theta_j\ne\boldsymbol\theta^*\), its probability of selection is at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independently sample each alternative, use its first-stage variance to determine its total sample size, independently collect the remaining observations, and select the smallest combined sample mean. Under the procedure's normal-output assumption, the probability of selecting the best alternative is at least 1−alpha when every competitor is worse by at least delta.
assumptions_latex: \(\delta>0\), \(0<\alpha<1\), and \(n_0\) are fixed.
Observations for each alternative are i.i.d., with independence across alternatives and between stages.
The simulation outputs satisfy the normality assumption used by the indifference-zone procedure.
The prescribed critical constant \(h\) corresponds to the chosen \(K\), \(n_0\), and \(\alpha\).
A best alternative \(\boldsymbol\theta^*\) satisfies \(L(\boldsymbol\theta_j)-L(\boldsymbol\theta^*)\ge\delta\) for every \(\boldsymbol\theta_j\ne\boldsymbol\theta^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: n_i=\max\left\{n_0,\left\lceil\frac{h^2s_i^2}{\delta^2}\right\rceil\right\},\qquad \mathbb P\!\left(\boldsymbol\theta^*\text{ is selected}\right)\ge 1-\alpha.

assumptions_latex: The feasible region \(X\) is measurable and each simulation call returns an integrable noisy observation \(Y(x)\) with mean \(f(x)\).
A proposal kernel \(Q_t(\cdot\mid x_t)\), replication rule, and measurable acceptance rule are specified.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(x_0\in X\). At iteration \(t\), draw \(z_t\sim Q_t(\cdot\mid x_t)\), generate the prescribed replications at \(z_t\) and, if required, at \(x_t\), and form an estimate \(\widehat\Delta_t\) of \(f(z_t)-f(x_t)\). With a prespecified measurable acceptance function \(A_t\), set \[x_{t+1}=z_t\quad\text{if }A_t(\widehat\Delta_t,\text{estimated uncertainty})=1,\qquad x_{t+1}=x_t\quad\text{otherwise}.\] Stop when the simulation budget is exhausted and return the terminal incumbent or the best independently validated visited point.

trial point produced by a simplex transformation

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a feasible simplex \(S_0=\{v_{0,0},\ldots,v_{0,d}\}\). At iteration \(t\), allocate replications to obtain \(\widehat f_t(v)\) and uncertainty estimates for vertices requiring comparison. Order the vertices using a prespecified noise-aware comparison rule, generate a feasible trial point \(z_t\) by a fixed simplex transformation such as reflection, expansion, contraction, or shrinkage, and simulate \(z_t\). Accept the transformation only according to the same comparison rule; otherwise increase replication or shrink the simplex. Stop at the budget or declared size-and-precision criterion and return the best validated vertex.

If a point \(z_k\) is accepted, set \(x_{k+1}=z_k\) and \(\Delta_{k+1}=\gamma_+\Delta_k\); otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) and \(\Delta_{k+1}=\gamma_-\Delta_k\). children.title: Noisy Compass Search

assumptions_latex: The objective is \(f(x)=\mathbb{E}[F(x,\xi)]\) on a feasible set \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\).
Simulation estimates at every tested point use a specified finite replication count or sequential sampling rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every iteration tests only coordinatewise neighbors; acceptance moves the incumbent, while failure contracts the common coordinate step.
