knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse-sampling tree search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monte Carlo restriction of outcome branching when actions remain enumerable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When the action space is small enough to enumerate, sparse-sampling tree search replaces exhaustive enumeration of outcomes by Monte Carlo samples of outcomes. With sufficiently many sampled outcomes, approximation-error bounds may be obtained; however, the required sampling can recreate explosive growth of the outcome tree. The procedure is therefore often used heuristically to limit outcome branching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparse-sampling tree search continues to enumerate actions but samples outcomes rather than enumerating all of them. Enough samples may permit error bounds, although the resulting tree can again become prohibitively large, so the method is often used as a branching-limitation heuristic.
assumptions_latex: \text{The action space is small enough for action enumeration.}
\text{Outcomes can be sampled from the applicable conditional distributions.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Monte Carlo sampling limits outcome branching, but accuracy and tree-size requirements remain in tension.}

children.title: Statistical Node Bounds
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty-aware bounds supporting branching and pruning.

assumptions_latex: For each active node \(V\), \(L(V)=\inf_{x\in V}f(x)\) is the node's true minimization bound.
The reported bounds satisfy a simultaneous coverage event with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On the simultaneous coverage event, pruning by comparing a node lower bound with an incumbent upper bound cannot discard a globally optimal node.

notation.meaning: true best objective value attainable in node V
statistical lower confidence bound for node V
upper confidence bound for the incumbent value

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous confidence bounds as a probabilistic safe-pruning certificate.

source_refs.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A\) be the active-node set and let \(x^{\mathrm{inc}}\) be the incumbent. A statistical pruning certificate at level \(1-\alpha\) is the event
\[
\mathcal E=\left\{\underline L(V)\leq L(V)\ \text{for all }V\in\mathcal A,\quad f(x^{\mathrm{inc}})\leq\overline U\right\},
\qquad \mathbb P(\mathcal E)\geq1-\alpha.
\]
On \(\mathcal E\), any node satisfying \(\underline L(V)\geq\overline U\) has \(L(V)\geq f(x^{\mathrm{inc}})\) and may be pruned without removing a strictly better solution. The certificate is verifiable from the reported bounds and their simultaneous coverage calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simultaneously valid node lower bounds and an incumbent upper bound certify pruning whenever a node cannot beat the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Node Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pruning implication is mathematically correct on the displayed simultaneous-coverage event, and certificate is the appropriate content kind. The cited generic branch-and-bound section, however, is not confirmed to support this probabilistic simultaneous-bound certificate.

children.title: Erroneous-Pruning Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of optimal candidates through underresolved simulation bounds.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(S=\{a,b\}\), with true losses \(f(a)=0\) and \(f(b)=\delta>0\).
One simulation observation at each decision is Gaussian with variance \(\sigma^2>0\), independently across decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A one-replication comparison prunes the optimal decision with strictly positive probability \(\Phi(-\delta/(\sqrt2\sigma))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-decision Gaussian example showing positive-probability loss of the optimum.

source_refs.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46
4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y_a\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) and \(Y_b\sim N(\delta,\sigma^2)\) be independent one-replication loss estimates. A rule that retains only the decision with the smaller observed loss prunes the true optimizer \(a\) whenever \(Y_a>Y_b\). Since \(Y_a-Y_b\sim N(-\delta,2\sigma^2)\),
\[
\mathbb P(Y_a>Y_b)=\Phi\left(-\frac{\delta}{\sqrt2\sigma}\right)>0.
\]
Thus pruning from underresolved point estimates can permanently delete the unique optimum. The failure disappears only through a valid error-control mechanism, not merely because the comparison is unbiased.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even unbiased Gaussian estimates can rank two decisions incorrectly, so one-shot pruning discards the unique optimum with positive probability.
knowledge_statements.title: Erroneous-Pruning Failure

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46
4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

children.title: Simulation-Based Branching Policies
children.top_down_role: Node expansion and subdivision choices for simulation-driven search trees.

assumptions_latex: Each active node represents a subset of the discrete feasible set and has a prescribed finite collection of children.
Node statistics are updated from simulation observations, with all sampling and tie-breaking rules specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The policy selects either a node for refinement or a node requiring additional simulation before a reliable branching decision.

notation.meaning: estimated promise score of node V

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Best-bound branching with explicit resampling for statistically unresolved nodes.

source_refs.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(\mathcal A_0\) with the root node and compute simulation-based bounds. At iteration \(k\), remove nodes certified unable to improve the incumbent. For every remaining node, form a measurable priority \(I_k(V)\) from its lower bound, uncertainty, depth, and sampling cost, and select
\[
V_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{V\in\mathcal A_k}I_k(V).
\]
If the uncertainty of \(V_k\) exceeds the declared branching tolerance, allocate additional simulations and recompute its statistics. Otherwise replace \(V_k\) by its children, initialize their bounds, and update the incumbent. Stop when no active node can improve the incumbent at the required confidence level or when the budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prioritize an active node using estimated promise and uncertainty, resample it if unresolved, and otherwise replace it by its children.
knowledge_statements.title: Simulation-Based Branching Policies

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46

children.title: Simulation-Based Bound Construction
children.top_down_role: Construction of node-level bounds from uncertain simulation evidence.

assumptions_latex: A node \(V\) is a finite set of decisions, and decision \(x\in V\) has \(n_x\geq1\) independent simulation observations with mean \(f(x)\).
Each centered observation is sub-Gaussian with known common variance proxy \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed node statistic is a lower confidence bound for \(\min_{x\in V}f(x)\) with coverage at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-node lower bound obtained from simultaneous sub-Gaussian confidence intervals.

source_refs.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46
4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For confidence parameter \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), define decisionwise lower limits and the node bound by
\[
\ell_\alpha(x)=\overline Y_x-\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\log(|V|/\alpha)}{n_x}},
\qquad
\underline L_\alpha(V)=\min_{x\in V}\ell_\alpha(x).
\]
The sub-Gaussian tail inequality and a union bound give simultaneous inequalities \(\ell_\alpha(x)\leq f(x)\) for all \(x\in V\) with probability at least \(1-\alpha\). Hence
\[
\mathbb P\left(\underline L_\alpha(V)\leq\min_{x\in V}f(x)\right)\geq1-\alpha.
\]
Separate error allocation is required when bounds are repeatedly recomputed across many nodes or times.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Take the minimum of simultaneous lower confidence limits for decisions in a finite node to obtain a valid node lower bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Simulation-Based Bound Construction

source_witnesses.locator: 1.5.1 Branch and Bound search p. 46
4 Simulation and sensitivity estimation p. 211

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-node union-bound construction is mathematically valid for a fixed node and time, and representation is a reasonable role for the displayed bound. The cited broad sections do not specifically support the sub-Gaussian formula or its repeated-use qualification, so a direct source is required.

children.title: Population-Based Simulation Search
children.top_down_role: Evolutionary and population search under noisy simulated fitness.

children.title: Genetic-Algorithm Simulation Search
children.top_down_role: Genetic search families with noisy evaluation.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(\mathcal X\), and simulation output satisfies \(Y(x,\xi)=f(x)+\varepsilon(x,\xi)\) with finite mean.
Each fitness estimate uses a finite, explicitly recorded replication count.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is the incumbent with the best final estimated fitness, together with its replication count.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic generational genetic search for minimizing a simulated objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an initial population \(P_0\subset\mathcal X\), evaluate each \(x\in P_t\) by \(\widehat f_m(x)=m^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{m}Y(x,\xi_r)\). Select parents using a rule nonincreasing in estimated fitness, recombine selected parents, and independently mutate offspring according to \(M(\cdot\mid x)\). Form \(P_{t+1}\) from offspring, optionally retaining an elite only after reevaluation with fresh replications. Continue until a prescribed simulation budget or generation limit is reached. Return the point having the smallest final reevaluated sample mean and report the number of replications supporting that comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noisy genetic search repeatedly estimates fitness, selects parents, recombines and mutates them, and returns a reevaluated incumbent when its simulation budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.title: Genetic-Algorithm Simulation Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the selection, recombination, mutation, elitism, reevaluation, and final-incumbent conventions describe no fixed genetic-algorithm variant and have no cited source. An exact authoritative algorithm reference is required.

children.title: Evolution-Strategy Simulation Search
children.top_down_role: Adaptive mutation and population mechanisms for simulated objectives.

assumptions_latex: The objective is observed through \(Y(x,\xi)\) with \(\mathbb E[Y(x,\xi)]=f(x)\).
Candidate points lie in \(\mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), with infeasible proposals repaired or rejected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns the best independently reevaluated search point under the stated budget.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic population evolution strategy with adaptive mutation under simulation noise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(\mu\) parents \(x_{1,0},\ldots,x_{\mu,0}\in\mathcal X\), strategy parameters, and \(\sigma_0>0\). At generation \(t\), generate \(\lambda\) offspring by recombination followed by mutations \(x'=x+\sigma_t A_t z\), where \(z\) has a centered standardized distribution. Estimate each candidate's objective using replicated simulation, select the next \(\mu\) parents from offspring or from parents and offspring according to the chosen \((\mu,\lambda)\) or \((\mu+\lambda)\) rule, and update \(\sigma_t\) and possibly \(A_t\) from successful steps. Stop at the simulation budget and independently reevaluate the incumbent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An evolution strategy samples mutated offspring, ranks replicated simulation estimates, adapts mutation scale or shape, and finally reevaluates its incumbent.
knowledge_statements.title: Evolution-Strategy Simulation Search

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but the record combines alternative evolution-strategy selection schemes and leaves recombination and parameter adaptation unspecified. A source fixing or explicitly supporting this generic family description is required.

children.title: Noise Handling in Population Search
children.top_down_role: Resampling, uncertainty-aware selection, and fitness-ranking failure.

assumptions_latex: For each candidate \(x_i\), independent replications have mean \(f(x_i)\) and finite variance \(\sigma_i^2\).
Selection compares a finite population of candidates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selection should depend on uncertainty as well as point estimates; otherwise noise can dominate the population update.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-population selection for minimization with independently replicated simulation outputs.

source_refs.locator: 3. Simulation-Based Optimization: An Overview p. 29
source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For candidates \(x_i\), use \(\overline Y_i=n_i^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^{n_i}Y_{ir}\) and estimate its standard error by \(s_i/\sqrt{n_i}\). Allocate additional replications when an estimated difference \(|\overline Y_i-\overline Y_j|\) is small relative to \(\sqrt{s_i^2/n_i+s_j^2/n_j}\), and base elimination or parent selection on a stated confidence, posterior, or indifference-zone rule. Ranking once by unequal-precision sample means is not uncertainty-aware: even when \(f(x_i)>f(x_j)\), the event \(\overline Y_i<\overline Y_j\) has positive probability and can propagate an inferior candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Population search should resample close or uncertain candidates and use uncertainty-aware comparisons, because raw noisy rankings can select and propagate inferior points.
knowledge_statements.title: Noise Handling in Population Search

source_witnesses.locator: 3. Simulation-Based Optimization: An Overview p. 29
source_witnesses.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the leaf, but the cited overview locator does not reliably support the specific standard-error comparison and prescribed confidence, posterior, or indifference-zone selection rule. Moreover, finite variance alone does not guarantee that every inferior candidate has positive misranking probability; degenerate or separated-support observations are counterexamples. A direct source and corrected hypotheses or qualified wording are required.

children.title: Global-Search Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Practical boundaries caused by inadequate exploration or unreliable noisy comparisons.

children.title: Premature Convergence
children.top_down_role: Loss of exploration before statistically reliable localization.

assumptions_latex: A population method generates finite populations \(P_t\subset\mathcal X\).
Fitness estimates are noisy, and localization is considered reliable only after a specified statistical validation rule is met.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Premature convergence occurs when diversity is lost before the surviving region is statistically validated.

notation.meaning: population diameter under a chosen metric

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational failure criterion separating diversity loss from statistically supported localization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_t=\max_{x,y\in P_t}d(x,y)\) and \(\tau_\delta=\inf\{t:D_t\leq\delta\}\). Let \(V_t\) denote the event that the region containing \(P_t\) has passed the method's prescribed statistical validation against explored alternatives. Premature convergence is the event \(\{\tau_\delta<\infty\}\cap V_{\tau_\delta}^{c}\), together with an update rule that thereafter assigns zero or negligible probability to candidates outside that region. Thus small population diameter alone is not failure; failure is diversity loss before reliable localization, followed by inability to restore meaningful exploration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Premature convergence is diversity collapse before the surviving region has statistically defeated explored alternatives, coupled with negligible ability to explore elsewhere afterward.
knowledge_statements.title: Premature Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the failure-regime leaf, but the event-based definition using a method-specific validation event, diversity threshold, and negligible future exploration is an operational construction rather than a source-backed standard definition. It needs a direct reference or an explicitly sourced diagnostic framework.

children.title: Extreme-Noise Selection
children.top_down_role: Apparent optima created by searching over many noisy estimates.

assumptions_latex: There are \(M\) candidates with identical true objective value \(\mu\).
Their estimates are \(\widehat f_i=\mu+\varepsilon_i\), where \(\varepsilon_i\) are independent \(N(0,\sigma^2/n)\) variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Searching more candidates can create increasingly optimistic apparent minima even when no candidate is truly better.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian equal-means model illustrating optimizer's curse under minimization.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic optimization procedures and their stochastic counterparts p. 22

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\widehat f_{(1)}=\min_{1\leq i\leq M}\widehat f_i\). Although every candidate has value \(\mu\), \(\mathbb E[\widehat f_{(1)}]=\mu+(\sigma/\sqrt n)\mathbb E[\min_{1\leq i\leq M}Z_i]<\mu\) for \(M>1\), where the \(Z_i\) are independent standard normal variables. Moreover, as \(M\to\infty\), the leading optimism magnitude is \(\mu-\mathbb E[\widehat f_{(1)}]\sim(\sigma/\sqrt n)\sqrt{2\log M}\). Hence fixed replication permits apparent improvement caused solely by searching over more noisy estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed replication, the best among many equally good noisy candidates looks spuriously better; under Gaussian noise the optimism grows like the square root of log population size.
knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Noise Selection

source_witnesses.locator: 1.4 Deterministic optimization procedures and their stochastic counterparts p. 22

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Gaussian calculation is mathematically plausible and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the cited general section is not a sufficiently direct locator for the stated extreme-value asymptotic. A source specifically supporting the expectation formula and the leading sqrt(2 log M) behavior is required.

children.title: Search-Distribution Collapse
children.top_down_role: Degeneration of adaptive proposal distributions before adequate exploration.

assumptions_latex: At iteration \(t\), candidates are sampled from a proposal distribution \(Q_t\) on \(\mathcal X\).
A set \(G\subset\mathcal X\) contains points not yet adequately explored.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Collapse is a failure whenever proposal mass on a relevant unexplored set vanishes before that set is ruled out.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational failure condition for adaptive continuous-space proposal distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Search-distribution collapse relative to \(G\) occurs if \(Q_t(G)\to0\) before available evidence statistically excludes \(G\) from containing a competitive solution. For location-scale proposals on \(\mathbb R^d\), a common sufficient diagnostic is \(\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma_t)\to0\) while the proposal mean converges outside \(G\); then samples concentrate at a single location and the probability of visiting any separated \(G\) vanishes. Covariance degeneration is not itself erroneous after reliable localization. It is a failure when it precedes adequate exploration and the update mechanism lacks a positive exploration component capable of restoring mass to \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A search distribution fails by collapsing when it loses probability mass on a still-plausible unexplored region and cannot restore meaningful exploration there.
knowledge_statements.title: Search-Distribution Collapse

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the definition relative to an arbitrary set G, the statistical-exclusion condition, and the covariance-collapse diagnostic are uncited and proposal-family dependent. A direct source is needed for this named failure regime and its stated sufficient diagnostic.

children.title: Response-Surface Metamodels
children.top_down_role: Low-order polynomial approximations for local or global simulation response.

children.title: First-Order Response Surfaces
children.top_down_role: Local linear approximations supporting directional exploration.

assumptions_latex: Design sites \(x_i\in\mathbb R^d\) have responses \(Y_i\) with finite second moments.
The local mean response is approximated over a specified region by an affine function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The fitted surface is \(\widehat m(x)=\widehat\beta_0+x^{\mathsf T}\widehat\beta\), whose gradient \(\widehat\beta\) supplies a local search direction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local affine response-surface model fitted by least squares.

source_refs.locator: 4. Parametric Optimization: Response Surfaces and Neural Networks p. 37
source_refs.source_title: Simulation-Based Optimization: Parametric Optimization Techniques and Reinforcement Learning

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A first-order response surface represents the local mean simulation response by \(m(x)\approx\beta_0+x^{\mathsf T}\beta\). With rows \((1,x_i^{\mathsf T})\) in \(X\) and observations in \(y\), ordinary least squares chooses \(\widehat\theta\in\arg\min_\theta\|y-X\theta\|_2^2\); if \(X\) has full column rank, \(\widehat\theta=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y\). The fitted value is \(\widehat m(x)=\widehat\beta_0+x^{\mathsf T}\widehat\beta\). For local minimization, \(-\widehat\beta\) is the fitted steepest-descent direction, to be used only within the region where the affine approximation is accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order response surface fits an affine mean model to simulation data; its estimated slope gives a local descent direction.
knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Response Surfaces

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Where the response is believed to have little curvature, a two-variable first-order or main-effects model is η = β₀ + β₁x₁ + β₂x₂.

children.title: Second-Order Response Surfaces
children.top_down_role: Local curvature models supporting stationary-region search.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A second-order response surface represents the local mean by \(m(x)\approx\beta_0+b^{\mathsf T}x+\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Hx\), where \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\). Estimate its coefficients by least squares or generalized least squares on the corresponding linear, squared, and cross-product regressors. The fitted gradient is \(\nabla\widehat m(x)=\widehat b+\widehat Hx\). If \(\widehat H\) is nonsingular, the fitted stationary point is \(x_s=-\widehat H^{-1}\widehat b\). It is a strict fitted minimizer when \(\widehat H\succ0\), a strict fitted maximizer when \(\widehat H\prec0\), and a saddle when \(\widehat H\) is indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order surface fits local slope and curvature; its Hessian classifies the fitted stationary point as a minimum, maximum, or saddle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Response-Surface Model and Necessary Design Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic response-surface regression in m inputs and necessary, but not sufficient, design conditions for estimating all coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A second-order response-surface model has the form
\[
y=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_jx_j+\sum_{j=1}^m\beta_{jj}x_j^2+\sum_{1\le j<k\le m}\beta_{jk}x_jx_k+\varepsilon.
\]
The model has \(1+2m+m(m-1)/2\) regression coefficients. Thus, estimating every coefficient by least squares or likelihood-based methods requires at least this many distinct design locations. Estimating pure quadratic terms also requires at least three levels of each corresponding input variable. These counting and level conditions are necessary rather than sufficient for estimability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order response surface contains an intercept, main effects, pure quadratic terms, pairwise interactions, and an error term. It has 1 + 2m + m(m−1)/2 coefficients, so estimating all coefficients requires at least that many distinct design locations. Each input must also have at least three levels for its pure quadratic coefficient to be estimable. These requirements alone do not guarantee full-rank estimation.
assumptions_latex: m\in\mathbb{N}
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m
\text{All displayed regression coefficients are to be estimated by least squares or likelihood-based methods.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{distinct}}\ge 1+2m+\frac{m(m-1)}2,\qquad \#\{\text{levels of }x_j\}\ge 3\quad(j=1,\ldots,m),\quad\text{as necessary conditions for the stated estimability.}

children.title: Stochastic Kriging
children.top_down_role: Spatial modeling that separates intrinsic simulation noise from response uncertainty.

children.title: Homoskedastic Stochastic Kriging
children.top_down_role: Spatial simulation modeling with uniform noise structure.

assumptions_latex: Observations satisfy \(y_i=\mu+Z(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), with \(Z\) a zero-mean Gaussian process.
The noises are independent of \(Z\), mutually independent, and have common known or estimated variance \(\tau^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed conditional Gaussian mean and variance define the homoskedastic stochastic-kriging predictor.

notation.meaning: process covariance matrix at design sites
covariance vector between design sites and x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process prediction with constant independent simulation-noise variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_{ij}=C(x_i,x_j)\), \(k(x)_i=C(x_i,x)\), and \(V=K+\tau^2I\). Conditional on \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^{\mathsf T}\) and known \(\mu\), the latent mean response \(M(x)=\mu+Z(x)\) has predictor \(\widehat M(x)=\mu+k(x)^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}(y-\mu\mathbf1)\) and conditional variance \(s^2(x)=C(x,x)-k(x)^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}k(x)\). A future noisy observation has predictive variance \(s^2(x)+\tau^2\). The term \(\tau^2I\) distinguishes homoskedastic stochastic kriging from deterministic interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Homoskedastic stochastic kriging uses a Gaussian process plus one common simulation-noise variance, yielding a smoothing predictor rather than exact interpolation.
knowledge_statements.title: Homoskedastic Stochastic Kriging

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and formulas are appropriate for known-mean homoskedastic stochastic kriging, including the distinction between latent-response and noisy-observation variance, but no inspectable source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Heteroskedastic Stochastic Kriging
children.top_down_role: Spatial simulation modeling with input-dependent noise.

assumptions_latex: Observations satisfy \(y_i=\mu+Z(x_i)+\varepsilon_i\), with \(Z\) a zero-mean Gaussian process.
The independent noises satisfy \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i)=\tau_i^2\), allowing input-dependent variances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Replacing a common nugget by \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_1^2,\ldots,\tau_n^2)\) yields the heteroskedastic stochastic-kriging predictor.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gaussian-process prediction with independent, input-dependent simulation-noise variances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(D=\operatorname{diag}(\tau_1^2,\ldots,\tau_n^2)\) and \(V=K+D\), where \(K_{ij}=C(x_i,x_j)\). For known \(\mu\), the conditional predictor of the latent mean response is \(\widehat M(x)=\mu+k(x)^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}(y-\mu\mathbf1)\), with conditional variance \(s^2(x)=C(x,x)-k(x)^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}k(x)\). Thus observations with larger simulation variance receive less effective weight through \(V^{-1}\). If predicting a new simulation output rather than its latent mean, add the new-site noise variance \(\tau^2(x)\) to \(s^2(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heteroskedastic stochastic kriging places input-specific noise variances on the covariance diagonal, reducing the influence of noisier simulation estimates.
knowledge_statements.title: Heteroskedastic Stochastic Kriging

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the leaf and the diagonal input-dependent noise formulation is coherent, but the predictor, variance, weighting interpretation, and new-site variance statement require a specific stochastic-kriging source and locator.

children.title: Replication-Aware Stochastic Kriging
children.top_down_role: Metamodel fitting and prediction exploiting replicated evaluations.

assumptions_latex: At distinct design sites \(x_i\), there are \(r_i\geq2\) independent simulation replications with common site mean \(M(x_i)\).
Within-site simulation variance is finite and replications are independent across sites conditional on the latent response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Site averages are kriged with noise covariance \(D_{ii}=\sigma_i^2/r_i\), so replication directly reduces metamodel observation uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stochastic kriging based on replicated site averages and estimated intrinsic variances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For site \(i\), form \(\overline Y_i=r_i^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}Y_{ij}\) and estimate the intrinsic variance by \(S_i^2=(r_i-1)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{r_i}(Y_{ij}-\overline Y_i)^2\). Under independent replications, \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_i\mid M(x_i))=\sigma_i^2/r_i\). Fit stochastic kriging to \(\overline Y=(\overline Y_1,\ldots,\overline Y_n)^{\mathsf T}\) using \(V=K+D\), where \(D_{ii}=\sigma_i^2/r_i\), commonly estimated by \(S_i^2/r_i\). The latent-response predictor is \(\widehat M(x)=\mu+k(x)^{\mathsf T}V^{-1}(\overline Y-\mu\mathbf1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replication-aware stochastic kriging fits site averages and divides each site's intrinsic variance by its replication count in the observation-noise covariance.
knowledge_statements.title: Replication-Aware Stochastic Kriging

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the replication-aware leaf, and the variance-of-the-site-average formula is standard under the stated independence assumptions. However, the complete stochastic-kriging construction and plug-in intrinsic-variance convention have no cited source or locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Replication-aware stochastic-kriging predictor and its limitations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unique-site stochastic-kriging prediction from replicated observations, including computational savings and inferential failure boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $a_i\ge 2$ observations at each distinct site $ ar x_i$, define $ ar y_i=a_i^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{a_i}y_i^{(j)}$, $\widehat\sigma_i^2=(a_i-1)^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{a_i}(y_i^{(j)}- ar y_i)^2$, and $S_n=\operatorname{Diag}(\widehat\sigma_1^2/a_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_n^2/a_n)$. With $C_n=[K_	heta( ar x_i, ar x_j)]$ and $k_n(x)=[K_	heta(x, ar x_i)]_{i=1}^n$, the stochastic-kriging BLUP is $\mu_n^{\mathrm{SK}}(x)=
u k_n(x)^	op(
u C_n+S_n)^{-1} ar Y_n$ with prediction variance $\sigma_n^{\mathrm{SK}}(x)^2=
u K_	heta(x,x)-
u^2k_n(x)^	op(
u C_n+S_n)^{-1}k_n(x)$. The matrix-decomposition cost is $\mathcal O(n^3)$ instead of $\mathcal O(N^3)$. However, $( ar Y_n,S_n)$ is not sufficient for full likelihood-based hyperparameter inference; independently estimated site variances do not supply a smooth out-of-sample variance model, and their reliability requires substantial replication, with $a_i\ge 10$ cited as a practical recommendation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic kriging can replace all replicated observations at each input by their mean and estimated mean-noise variance, producing a unique-site BLUP and reducing cubic matrix work from N observations to n unique sites. These summaries are not sufficient for full hyperparameter likelihood inference, do not themselves model smoothly varying variance at new inputs, and yield unreliable local variance estimates when replication is sparse.
assumptions_latex: N=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i,\qquad n\ll N
a_i\ge 2\ \text{when }\widehat\sigma_i^2\text{ is estimated}
\nu C_n+S_n\ \text{is invertible}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mu_n^{\mathrm{SK}}(x),\sigma_n^{\mathrm{SK}}(x)^2)\ \text{gives the unique-site BLUP representation with }\mathcal O(n^3)\text{ decomposition cost, subject to the stated sufficiency, variance-modeling, and sparse-replication limitations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact unique-site reduction for replicated Gaussian-process inference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional-on-hyperparameters equivalence of full-data and unique-site prediction, likelihood, and derivative calculations under replicated inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose $N$ observations occur at $n$ unique inputs with replicate counts $a_i\ge 1$, $A_n=\operatorname{Diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$, unique-site means $\bar Y_n$, covariance matrix $C_n$, and diagonal noise matrix $\Lambda_n$. Under the required covariance-matrix invertibility conditions, the Woodbury identities make the full-$N$ Gaussian-process predictive mean and variance identical to their unique-$n$ counterparts based on $C_n+\Lambda_nA_n^{-1}$. Exact concentrated-likelihood inference additionally uses the weighted full-data sum-of-squares statistic $N^{-1}Y_N^\top\Lambda_N^{-1}Y_N$, which is missing from the replicate summaries used by the approximate stochastic-kriging construction. After $\mathcal O(N)$ aggregation, prediction, concentrated-likelihood evaluation, and closed-form likelihood derivatives require $\mathcal O(n^3)$ matrix work. This algebraic equivalence imposes no minimum replicate count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For replicated inputs, Woodbury reduction makes predictions computed from all N observations exactly equal to calculations using the n unique sites, conditional on the hyperparameters. Exact likelihood inference also needs the full-data weighted sum of squares omitted by the simpler replicate summaries. Aggregation is linear in N and subsequent matrix work is cubic in n, with no minimum replication count required for the identity.
assumptions_latex: N\ \text{observations are grouped among }n\ \text{unique inputs with }a_i\ge 1
A_n=\operatorname{Diag}(a_1,\ldots,a_n)
C_n+\Lambda_nA_n^{-1}\ \text{and the corresponding full-data covariance matrices are invertible}
\text{Hyperparameters are fixed when asserting predictive equivalence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\mu_N(x),\sigma_N^2(x))=(\mu_n(x),\sigma_n^2(x)),\qquad \text{and exact replicated-data likelihood calculations use }\mathcal O(N)+\mathcal O(n^3)\text{ work together with }N^{-1}Y_N^\top\Lambda_N^{-1}Y_N.

children.title: Adaptive Response Metamodel Family
children.top_down_role: Data-adaptive representations for nonlinear, discontinuous, or nonstationary response.

children.title: Local-Smoothing Metamodel Family
children.top_down_role: Smooth locally adaptive simulation-response approximations.

children.title: Local-Polynomial Regression
children.top_down_role: Locally fitted polynomial response approximations.

assumptions_latex: Data are \((X_i,Y_i)\) with \(X_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and a nonnegative kernel assigns local weights around a target \(x\).
The weighted polynomial design matrix has sufficient local rank for the chosen degree \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local-polynomial estimate at \(x\) is the fitted intercept \(\widehat m(x)=\widehat\beta_0(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multivariate local-polynomial regression with kernel weighting and fixed degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix degree \(p\geq0\), target \(x\in\mathbb R^d\), kernel \(K\geq0\), and nonsingular bandwidth matrix \(H\). Define \(w_i(x)=K(H^{-1}(X_i-x))\). A local-polynomial fit chooses coefficients \(\widehat\beta_\alpha(x)\), indexed by multi-indices satisfying \(|\alpha|\leq p\), to minimize \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i(x)\left[Y_i-\sum_{|\alpha|\leq p}\beta_\alpha(X_i-x)^\alpha\right]^2\). The estimated conditional mean at the target is \(\widehat m(x)=\widehat\beta_0(x)\). Degrees \(p=0\) and \(p=1\) give local-constant and local-linear regression, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local-polynomial regression fits a kernel-weighted polynomial around each target point and uses its fitted intercept as the local mean estimate.
knowledge_statements.title: Local-Polynomial Regression

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind is suitable for the exact local-polynomial-regression leaf, and the kernel-weighted multi-index formulation is internally coherent. A specific authoritative source and section, theorem, definition, or page locator is nevertheless required.

children.title: Smoothing-Spline Metamodels
children.top_down_role: Penalized spline representations for smooth simulation responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Smoothing-Spline Metamodels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Penalized cubic smoothing spline for a one-dimensional stochastic-simulation response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an integer \(n\ge 2\), distinct design sites \(a\le x_1<\cdots<x_n\le b\), simulation estimates \(y_i\), positive precision weights \(w_i\), and \(\lambda>0\), the smoothing-spline metamodel is the minimizer \(\widehat f_\lambda\in H^2([a,b])\) of
\[\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\bigl(y_i-f(x_i)\bigr)^2+\lambda\int_a^b\bigl(f''(t)\bigr)^2\,dt.\]
The minimizer is the unique natural cubic spline with knots among \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). The parameter \(\lambda\) controls the tradeoff between fidelity to noisy simulation estimates and curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For at least two distinct sampled sites, a smoothing-spline metamodel uniquely balances weighted fit to simulated responses against integrated squared curvature and is a natural cubic spline with knots among those sites.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge2\) and \(a\le x_1<\cdots<x_n\le b\).
\(w_i>0\) and \(y_i\in\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,n\).
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat f_\lambda\) is the unique natural cubic-spline minimizer of the stated penalized criterion.

notation.meaning: Sobolev space of functions with square-integrable weak derivatives through order two.
Precision weight assigned to the estimate at site i.

review_flags: Authoritative support for the penalized natural-cubic-spline characterization is required.

children.title: Adaptive Knot Placement
children.top_down_role: Spline structures whose resolution changes across the decision space.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Knot Placement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential placement of regression-spline knots using residual improvement on a finite candidate set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input observations \(\{(x_i,y_i,w_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), spline degree \(p\), a finite candidate set \(G\subset(a,b)\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\). Initialize the knot set \(K_0=\varnothing\). At iteration \(m\), fit by weighted least squares a degree-\(p\) regression spline \(s_{m,\xi}\) for every \(\xi\in G\setminus K_m\), and choose
\[\xi_m\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\xi\in G\setminus K_m}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\bigl(y_i-s_{m,\xi}(x_i)\bigr)^2.\]
Set \(K_{m+1}=K_m\cup\{\xi_m\}\). Stop when the relative criterion decrease is at most \(\varepsilon\), or a prescribed knot budget is reached, and output the last fitted spline.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Candidate knots are added where they most improve weighted spline fit, stopping when improvement is small or the knot budget is exhausted.
assumptions_latex: \(G\subset(a,b)\) is finite and excludes previously selected knots.
\(w_i>0\), and each candidate spline fit is identifiable.
A maximum number of knots is prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is a regression-spline metamodel whose knot set was selected sequentially by weighted residual reduction.

notation.meaning: Finite set of admissible knot locations.
Polynomial degree of each spline segment.

review_flags: Adaptive knot placement has multiple standard criteria; no supplied source fixes this residual-reduction version.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the leaf, but adaptive knot placement admits many criteria. No source supports this particular greedy residual-reduction rule, and the relative-decrease denominator is not defined.

children.title: Recursive-Partition Metamodel Family
children.top_down_role: Partition-based models for discontinuity and changing response regimes.

children.title: Regression-Tree Metamodels
children.top_down_role: Tree-structured predictors for heterogeneous simulation responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Regression-Tree Metamodels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-constant response metamodel on axis-aligned terminal regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be partitioned by a finite binary axis-aligned tree into disjoint terminal regions \(R_1,\ldots,R_L\) whose union is \(D\). A regression-tree metamodel has the representation
\[\widehat f(x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^L c_\ell\mathbf 1\{x\in R_\ell\},\qquad x\in D.\]
For squared-error fitting to observations \(\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\), each nonempty leaf value is \(c_\ell=|I_\ell|^{-1}\sum_{i\in I_\ell}y_i\), where \(I_\ell=\{i:x_i\in R_\ell\}\). Thus predictions are constant within each terminal simulation-input regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regression tree partitions the input domain by binary coordinate splits and predicts the sample-average response within each terminal region.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1,\ldots,R_L\) form a finite disjoint partition of \(D\).
Every fitted terminal region contains at least one observation.
Squared-error loss is used for leaf fitting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat f\) is piecewise constant, with each leaf value equal to its empirical response mean.

notation.meaning: Terminal region or leaf of the tree.
Indices of observations assigned to leaf l.

review_flags: An authoritative locator for regression-tree representation and squared-error leaf estimation is required.

children.title: Recursive Partition Metamodels
children.top_down_role: Response representations based on recursively subdivided decision regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Recursive Partition Metamodels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greedy binary partitioning by empirical loss reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input observations \(\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) on \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), a leaf-model class, admissible coordinate thresholds, and stopping constraints. Initialize the partition as \(\{D\}\). For each current region \(R\), fit its leaf model and compute empirical loss \(L(R)\). Among admissible splits \(R=R^-_{j,t}\mathbin{\dot\cup}R^+_{j,t}\), choose one maximizing
\[\Delta(R,j,t)=L(R)-L(R^-_{j,t})-L(R^+_{j,t}).\]
Apply a split with positive maximal gain, refit the two child models, and repeat. Stop when no admissible positive-gain split remains or a size/depth budget is reached; output the partition and fitted leaf models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive partitioning repeatedly chooses the admissible binary split with greatest empirical-loss reduction, then returns the fitted terminal-region models.
assumptions_latex: The candidate split set is finite at every iteration.
Leaf-model losses attain finite minima.
Minimum leaf size or depth constraints make termination finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a finite partition whose terminal regions carry separately fitted response models.

notation.meaning: Minimized empirical loss for the leaf model on region R.
Children produced by splitting coordinate j at threshold t.
Empirical loss reduction from a candidate split.

review_flags: No supplied source directly identifies the intended recursive-partition loss and stopping rule.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits recursive partitioning, but no source fixes the proposed loss, greedy global split selection, and stopping rules as the intended variant.

children.title: Regime-Specific Leaf Models
children.top_down_role: Local response models attached to terminal partition regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Regime-Specific Leaf Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise parametric metamodel allowing distinct response laws across terminal regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R_1,\ldots,R_L\) be a finite partition of \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). Assign leaf \(R_\ell\) a feature map \(\phi_\ell:R_\ell\to\mathbb R^{q_\ell}\) and parameter \(\beta_\ell\in\mathbb R^{q_\ell}\). A regime-specific leaf metamodel is
\[\widehat f(x)=\sum_{\ell=1}^L \phi_\ell(x)^\top\widehat\beta_\ell\mathbf 1\{x\in R_\ell\},\]
where each \(\widehat\beta_\ell\) minimizes the empirical loss using only observations in \(R_\ell\). The dimensions and feature maps may differ between leaves, so local constants, linear surfaces, or other prescribed parametric responses can represent distinct simulator regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each terminal region receives its own fitted parametric response law, allowing different local structures in different simulator regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(R_1,\ldots,R_L\) form a finite disjoint partition of \(D\).
Each leaf contains enough observations to identify its chosen model.
Each leaf loss has a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat f\) equals the independently fitted leaf-specific response model on each region.

notation.meaning: Feature map selected for terminal region l.
Parameter vector for terminal region l.

review_flags: An authoritative locator for heterogeneous parametric leaf models is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate linear-regression leaf model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A Bayesian treed linear model using analytically marginalized Gaussian linear regressions in terminal regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a leaf \(\eta\), let \(y^\eta\mid\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2,X^\eta\sim N(X^\eta\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2I)\) and take the reference prior \(p(\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2)\propto\sigma_\eta^{-2}\). When the leaf design supplies an identifiable regression and sufficiently many observations for the marginal integral to be finite, integrating out \((\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2)\) yields an analytic marginal likelihood determined by the leaf design and residual quantities. Thus the linear leaf model can be used in tree-structure inference without sampling its regression parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bayesian treed linear model places a Gaussian linear regression in each leaf and uses a scale-invariant reference prior. With an identifiable leaf design and enough observations, its coefficients and variance integrate out in closed form, producing an analytic leaf marginal likelihood.
assumptions_latex: \(y^\eta\mid\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2,X^\eta\sim N(X^\eta\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2I)\).
\(p(\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2)\propto\sigma_\eta^{-2}\).
The leaf design identifies the regression coefficients.
The leaf contains sufficiently many observations for the marginal integral to be finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p(y^\eta\mid x^\eta)=\int p(y^\eta\mid\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2,x^\eta)p(\beta_\eta,\sigma_\eta^2)\,d\beta_\eta\,d\sigma_\eta^2\quad\text{is available in closed form.}

children.title: Neural Response Surfaces
children.top_down_role: Neural approximations of stochastic simulator response.

knowledge_statements.title: Neural Response Surfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feedforward neural approximation of a stochastic simulator's conditional mean response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For simulator input \(x\in D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let \(Y(x)\) have conditional mean \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x)]\). A feedforward neural response surface with \(H\) hidden units is
\[\widehat f_\theta(x)=\beta_0+\sum_{h=1}^H\beta_h\,\sigma(a_h^\top x+b_h).\]
Given independent simulation outputs \(y_{ir}\) at sites \(x_i\), its fitted parameter \(\widehat\theta\) minimizes a specified regularized empirical loss, for example squared error plus \(\rho\lVert\theta\rVert_2^2\). The resulting deterministic map \(\widehat f_{\widehat\theta}\) approximates the simulator mean and can be optimized over \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A neural response surface fits a deterministic feedforward network to noisy simulation outputs as an approximation of the conditional mean response.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and \(\mathbb E[|Y(x)|]<\infty\) for each sampled input.
Simulation outputs are conditionally independent across replications.
The activation and regularized empirical loss are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat f_{\widehat\theta}:D\to\mathbb R\) is a fitted deterministic surrogate for \(x\mapsto\mathbb E[Y(x)]\).

notation.meaning: Collection of network weights and biases.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Discrete Space-Filling Subset Problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a fixed-cardinality space-filling subset over a finite candidate set and records the exhaustive-search count without asserting a formal complexity class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite set of \(d\) design points and let \(1\le m\le d\). A size-\(m\) space-filling sampling plan is any solution of
\[
\operatorname*{minimize}_{S\subseteq X}\ d_{\max}(X,S)\qquad\text{subject to }|S|=m.
\]
There are \(\binom{d}{m}=\frac{d!}{m!(d-m)!}\) feasible subsets, so exhaustive enumeration tests that many candidates and is described as typically computationally intractable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite candidate set X containing d design points, a size-m space-filling plan minimizes the prescribed d_max metric over all m-element subsets. Exhaustive search tests all d choose m feasible subsets and is typically computationally intractable.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is finite and }|X|=d
1\le m\le d
d_{\max}(X,S)\text{ is the previously defined set-distance metric}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{S\subseteq X,\ |S|=m}d_{\max}(X,S),\qquad \#\{S\subseteq X:|S|=m\}=\binom{d}{m}.

children.title: Latin Hypercube Design
children.top_down_role: Marginally stratified simulator-input design.

knowledge_statements.title: Latin Hypercube Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized marginally stratified design on a unit hypercube.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For integers \(n\ge2\) and \(d\ge1\), a randomized Latin hypercube design in \([0,1]^d\) is constructed by drawing, independently for each coordinate \(j\), a uniform random permutation \(\pi_j\) of \(\{1,ldots,n\}\), drawing independent jitters \(u_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) independently of the permutations, and setting
\[x_{ij}=\frac{\pi_j(i)-u_{ij}}{n},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\]
For every coordinate \(j\) and every stratum \(((k-1)/n,k/n)\), exactly one design point has its \(j\)-th coordinate in that stratum. Coordinatewise transformations extend the design to rectangular domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized Latin hypercube draws random coordinatewise stratum permutations and within-stratum jitters, placing exactly one run in each of n equal strata of every input coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge2\) and \(d\ge1\) are integers.
Each \(\pi_j\) is a uniform random permutation of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), independently across coordinates.
The variables \(u_{ij}\) are independent \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) jitters and are independent of the permutations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every one-dimensional coordinate projection contains exactly one point in each equal-width stratum.

notation.meaning: Number of design points and marginal strata.
Random stratum permutation for coordinate j.
Random within-stratum jitter for run i and coordinate j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal Stratification and Projection Closure of Latin Hypercubes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional stratification and preservation of the Latin-hypercube property under coordinate deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an \(n\)-point Latin hypercube \(X\subset[0,1]^m\), each coordinate \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\) has exactly one point in every interval \([k/n,(k+1)/n)\), \(k=0,\ldots,n-1\). Consequently, for every nonempty retained coordinate set \(J\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), the coordinate projection \(\pi_J(X)\) is an \(n\)-point Latin hypercube in \([0,1]^{|J|}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every coordinate of an n-point Latin hypercube contains exactly one point in each of the n equal unit-interval strata. Dropping any nonempty proper subset of coordinates preserves this condition, so the resulting coordinate projection is also a Latin hypercube.
assumptions_latex: X\text{ is an }n\text{-point Latin hypercube in }[0,1]^m
\varnothing\ne J\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall j,\ \forall k\in\{0,\ldots,n-1\},\ \#\{i:x_{ij}\in[k/n,(k+1)/n)\}=1,\qquad \pi_J(X)\text{ is an LHS in }[0,1]^{|J|}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse-CDF Transformation of a Latin Hypercube
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise quantile transformation of a randomized Latin hypercube to prescribed marginal distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Generate a randomized Latin hypercube \(U=(u_{ij})\) in \([0,1]^m\). For prescribed marginal CDFs \(F_1,\ldots,F_m\) with generalized inverses, set \[x_{ij}=F_j^{-1}(u_{ij}),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,\quad j=1,\ldots,m.\] Over the randomization of the LHS, each \(x_{ij}\) has CDF \(F_j\). The design retains one point associated with each equal-probability stratum of coordinate \(j\), although atoms of \(F_j\) may map distinct probability strata to equal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generate a randomized unit-cube Latin hypercube and apply the desired marginal quantile function coordinatewise. Each transformed coordinate has the prescribed marginal distribution over the LHS randomization and retains probability-scale stratification; discrete marginals may produce tied transformed values.
assumptions_latex: U=(u_{ij})\text{ is a randomized Latin hypercube in }[0,1]^m\text{ with each }u_{ij}\text{ marginally uniform on }[0,1]
F_j\text{ is a prescribed CDF with generalized inverse }F_j^{-1},\quad j=1,\ldots,m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_{ij}=F_j^{-1}(U_{ij})\text{ has CDF }F_j\text{ over the LHS randomization and preserves the coordinate's probability-scale strata, subject to possible ties at atoms.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Latin Hypercube Sample Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a randomized Latin hypercube design on the unit hypercube, including the centered deterministic variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,m\in\mathbb N\). An \(n\)-run, \(m\)-factor Latin hypercube is an \(n\times m\) matrix \(L=(l_{ij})\) such that every column is a permutation of \(\{-(n-1)/2,-(n-3)/2,\ldots,(n-1)/2\}\). Given independent \(u_{ij}\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]\), define \[x_{ij}=\frac{l_{ij}+(n-1)/2+u_{ij}}{n},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,\quad j=1,\ldots,m.\] Then \(X=(x_{ij})\) is a Latin hypercube sample in \([0,1]^m\). Setting every \(u_{ij}=1/2\) places each coordinate at its stratum midpoint and gives a Latin sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each column of a Latin hypercube permutes the same n equally spaced centered levels. Shifting, normalizing, and adding an independent uniform within-stratum displacement produces a sample in the unit hypercube. Using displacement one-half places every coordinate at its stratum midpoint.
assumptions_latex: n,m\in\mathbb N
\text{Each column of }L\text{ is a permutation of }\{-(n-1)/2,-(n-3)/2,\ldots,(n-1)/2\}.
u_{ij}\stackrel{\mathrm{ind}}{\sim}\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{ij}=\frac{l_{ij}+(n-1)/2+u_{ij}}{n}\in[0,1],\quad X\in[0,1]^{n\times m};\qquad u_{ij}=1/2\ \forall i,j\text{ gives the centered Latin sample.}

children.title: Maximin Design
children.top_down_role: Distance-based domain coverage.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximin Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite design maximizing its smallest pairwise separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be compact and contain at least \(n\ge2\) distinct points, and let \(d_D\) be a continuous metric on \(D\). An \(n\)-point maximin design is any set \(X_n^*=\{x_1^*,\ldots,x_n^*\}\subset D\) satisfying
\[X_n^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{\substack{X\subset D\\|X|=n}}\delta(X),\qquad \delta(X)=\min_{\substack{x,x'\in X\\x\ne x'}}d_D(x,x').\]
Thus the criterion maximizes the distance between the closest pair of design sites. Under the stated compactness, continuity, and cardinality assumptions, an optimal configuration exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a compact domain containing at least n distinct points, a maximin design chooses n sites so that the distance between the closest pair is as large as possible.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is compact and contains at least \(n\) distinct points.
\(d_D\) is a continuous metric on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X_n^*\) exists and maximizes the minimum pairwise design-site distance over all \(n\)-point subsets of \(D\).

notation.meaning: An n-point design in the input domain.
Distance metric used to assess separation.
Minimum pairwise distance of design X.

children.title: Sequential Simulation Design

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Surrogate-Based Simulation Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic sequential design loop for a deterministic or noisy simulator using a fitted surrogate and an augmentation criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a simulator producing \(y\sim f(x)\), a design domain \(\mathcal X\), sizes \(n_0\leq N\), a flexible surrogate with possibly unknown hyperparameters, and an augmentation criterion \(J\), construct an initial design \(X_{n_0}\), observe its responses, and set \(D_{n_0}=(X_{n_0},Y_{n_0})\). For each \(n=n_0,\ldots,N-1\), fit the surrogate and its hyperparameters using \(D_n\), choose \(x_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal X}J(x\mid D_n)\), observe \(y_{n+1}\sim f(x_{n+1})\), and update \(D_{n+1}=D_n\cup\{(x_{n+1},y_{n+1})\}\). Finally refit the surrogate using \(D_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Create and evaluate a seed design. Repeatedly fit the surrogate and any unknown hyperparameters, optimize the chosen augmentation criterion, evaluate the simulator at the selected input, and append the observation until the final design size is reached. Return the final data and its fitted surrogate.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ provides deterministic or noisy observations }y\sim f(x)\text{ for }x\in\mathcal X
n_0\leq N
J(\cdot\mid D_n)\text{ is an augmentation criterion that can be optimized over }\mathcal X
\text{The surrogate and any unknown hyperparameters can be fitted from }D_n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_N\text{ and a surrogate fitted using }D_N\text{ are returned after }N-n_0\text{ sequential augmentations.}

children.title: Prediction-Directed Design
children.top_down_role: Design targeting global metamodel uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: Prediction-Directed Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential design minimizing integrated metamodel prediction uncertainty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given current simulation data \(\mathcal D_t\), a fitted probabilistic metamodel with updated predictive variance \(s_{t+1}^2(z;x)\) after sampling candidate \(x\in D\), a finite measure \(\mu\) on \(D\), and candidate set \(C_t\), select
\[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C_t}\int_D s_{t+1}^2(z;x)\,\mu(dz).\]
Run the simulator at \(x_{t+1}\), append the response to \(\mathcal D_t\), refit or update the metamodel, and repeat until the simulation budget is exhausted. Output the final metamodel and accumulated design. The criterion targets global predictive precision rather than objective value alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential samples are chosen to minimize the metamodel's anticipated integrated prediction variance over the input domain.
assumptions_latex: \(C_t\subseteq D\) is nonempty and the displayed minimum is attained.
The metamodel supplies finite look-ahead predictive variances.
\(\mu(D)<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each selected input minimizes the one-step-ahead integrated predictive variance over the current candidate set.

notation.meaning: Simulation data available after t allocations.
Predictive variance at z after a prospective observation at x.
Measure weighting prediction accuracy across the domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrated Mean-Squared Prediction Error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-based global predictive-uncertainty criterion for sequential or batch surrogate design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given existing unique sites \(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_n\) and a candidate \(x_{n+1}\in\mathcal X\), define \[I_{n+1}(x_{n+1})\equiv\operatorname{IMSPE}(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_n,x_{n+1})=\int_{x\in\mathcal X}\breve\sigma_{n+1}^2(x)\,dx.\] IMSPE-based design minimizes this input-space-averaged predictive variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: IMSPE is the predictive variance after design augmentation, integrated over the input space; IMSPE design minimizes this quantity.
assumptions_latex: x_{n+1}\in\mathcal X
\breve\sigma_{n+1}^2(x)\text{ is the predictive variance after augmenting the design}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in\mathcal X}I_{n+1}(z)\quad\text{for an IMSPE-minimizing sequential design}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integrated Mean-Squared Prediction Error Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prediction-directed Gaussian-process design using normalized, optionally weighted integrated predictive variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the Gaussian-process conditional-mean predictor, with model quantities treated as fixed, suppose $\sigma_n^2(x)=\tau^2[1+g-k_n(x)^\top K_n^{-1}k_n(x)]$. Then the conditional mean-squared prediction error satisfies $\operatorname{MSPE}[\widehat y(x)]=\mathbb E[(\widehat y(x)-Y(x))^2\mid D_n]=\sigma_n^2(x)$. Given $w(x)\ge0$ with $\int_{\mathcal X}w(x)\,dx=1$, the IMSPE criterion is $J(X_n)=\int_{\mathcal X}\sigma_n^2(x)\tau^{-2}w(x)\,dx$, and an IMSPE design minimizes $J$. Uniform $w$ assigns equal predictive importance over $\mathcal X$. For rectangular $\mathcal X$ and certain isotropic or separable Gaussian and Matérn kernels, the integral may admit a closed or nearly closed form; otherwise numerical integration may be required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: IMSPE design minimizes normalized predictive variance averaged over the input region with a nonnegative unit-mass weight. For the GP conditional-mean predictor, conditional MSPE equals predictive variance. Closed-form integration is available only for suitable domains and covariance kernels.
assumptions_latex: x\in\mathcal X
\widehat y(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x)\mid D_n]
K_n\text{ is invertible}
w(x)\ge0
\int_{\mathcal X}w(x)\,dx=1
\text{The GP model quantities and hyperparameters are treated as fixed}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_n^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{X_n}\int_{\mathcal X}\frac{\sigma_n^2(x)}{\tau^2}w(x)\,dx

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Directed Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected-improvement sequential design for minimizing a stochastic response surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given data \(\mathcal D_t\), suppose the latent mean response at \(x\in D\) has predictive distribution \(F_t(x)\mid\mathcal D_t\sim N(m_t(x),s_t^2(x))\). Let \(f_t^{\min}\) be the best incumbent mean value. Define improvement \(I_t(x)=(f_t^{\min}-F_t(x))_+\), and choose
\[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C_t}\mathbb E[I_t(x)\mid\mathcal D_t].\]
Simulate at \(x_{t+1}\), update \(\mathcal D_t\) and the metamodel, and repeat until the budget is exhausted. Output the sampled decision having the smallest estimated mean response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The next simulation site maximizes expected improvement over the incumbent, concentrating effort where low response values are plausible.
assumptions_latex: The objective is minimization over a nonempty candidate set \(C_t\subseteq D\).
The metamodel supplies finite Gaussian predictive means and variances for the latent mean response.
The acquisition maximum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each new site maximizes one-step expected improvement over the incumbent among current candidates.

notation.meaning: Predictive mean and variance after t allocations.
Random improvement from sampling candidate x.

knowledge_statements.title: New-Location Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Budget allocation restricted to previously unsampled simulator inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S_t=\{x_1,\ldots,x_{k_t}\}\subset D\) be the set of inputs already simulated, let \(C_t\subseteq D\setminus S_t\) be a nonempty candidate set, and let \(A_t:C_t\to\mathbb R\) be a specified acquisition score combining predicted objective value and uncertainty. Select
\[x_{t+1}\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in C_t}A_t(x).\]
Run one or more replications at \(x_{t+1}\), set \(S_{t+1}=S_t\cup\{x_{t+1}\}\), update the metamodel, and repeat until the location or simulation budget is exhausted. Output the expanded sampled set and updated metamodel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulation budget is spent at an unsampled input maximizing a chosen acquisition score, thereby expanding the explored set.
assumptions_latex: \(C_t\subseteq D\setminus S_t\) is nonempty.
The acquisition score \(A_t\) is finite and attains a maximum on \(C_t\).
A finite allocation budget is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every selected \(x_{t+1}\) is new and maximizes the current acquisition score among unsampled candidates.

notation.meaning: Set of previously sampled input locations.

children.title: Replication Allocation
children.top_down_role: Simulation effort emphasizing local noise estimation and precision.

knowledge_statements.title: Replication Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step allocation among sampled sites to reduce estimation variance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At sampled sites \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\), let \(n_i\ge1\) be the current replication count and let \(\widehat\sigma_i^2\) estimate the variance of one simulation output. Under independent replications, the estimated variance of the sample mean after one additional replication at site \(i\) is \(\widehat\sigma_i^2/(n_i+1)\). Given nonnegative importance weights \(q_i\), allocate the next replication to
\[i^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{1\le i\le k}q_i\widehat\sigma_i^2\left(\frac1{n_i}-\frac1{n_i+1}\right).\]
Update that site's sample statistics and repeat until the replication budget is exhausted; output the updated sitewise mean and variance estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The next replication goes to the sampled site with the largest weighted reduction in estimated sample-mean variance.
assumptions_latex: Replications are independent within and across sampled sites.
Each \(n_i\ge1\), \(q_i\ge0\), and \(\widehat\sigma_i^2<\infty\).
A finite replication budget is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected site maximizes the estimated one-step weighted reduction in sample-mean variance.

notation.meaning: Current number of replications at site i.
Estimated variance of one output at site i.
Importance weight for precision at site i.

review_flags: No supplied locator establishes this specific weighted variance-reduction allocation rule.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits replication allocation, but no source supports this particular weighted one-step rule. Its calculation also treats the current variance estimate as fixed when evaluating the added replication, a convention that must be stated and sourced.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\mathcal D_t\), form the admissible action set \(\mathcal A_t=\{\operatorname{new}(x),\operatorname{rep}(x):x\in\mathcal X\}\), excluding \(\operatorname{new}(x)\) when \(x\) has already been sampled and excluding infeasible actions. Assign each action a cost \(c(a)>0\) and a conditional value score \(A_t(a)\), such as expected reduction in integrated prediction loss or expected decision regret. Select \(a_t\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{a\in\mathcal A_t}A_t(a)/c(a)\), obtain the indicated simulator observation, update \(\mathcal D_{t+1}\) and the noise-aware metamodel, and repeat while the remaining budget admits an action. At termination, output an incumbent minimizing the fitted mean.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequentially choose the new-location or replication action with greatest modeled value per unit cost, update the noise-aware surrogate, and return its final predicted minimizer.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The validated output is \(x^{\mathrm{out}}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in C}\widehat\mu_{\mathrm{val}}(x)\), with uncertainty reported according to the specified validation rule.

children.title: Sequential Local Response-Surface Search
children.top_down_role: Local modeling coupled to directional or trust-region movement.

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally smooth near the current iterate.
Simulator observations are conditionally unbiased with finite variance.
Each local subproblem is solved within its trust region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An accepted step satisfies \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\); otherwise \(x_{k+1}=x_k\) and the region is contracted.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noise-aware local response-surface method with trust-region acceptance and radius updates.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Response surface methodology p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), collect or augment replicated observations in \(B(x_k,\Delta_k)\cap X\) and fit a local linear or quadratic response surface \(q_k\). Compute \(s_k\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}\{q_k(x_k+s):x_k+s\in X,\ \lVert s\rVert\leq\Delta_k\}\). Using sufficiently replicated estimates \(\widehat f_k\), form \(\rho_k=[\widehat f_k(x_k)-\widehat f_k(x_k+s_k)]/[q_k(x_k)-q_k(x_k+s_k)]\) when the denominator is positive. Accept the step when \(\rho_k\geq\eta_1\), expand the region when \(\rho_k\geq\eta_2\), and otherwise reject the step and contract the region, where \(0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1\). Stop under a prescribed radius, precision, or budget rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fit a local response surface, propose a trust-region step, compare observed and predicted improvement, and accept, reject, expand, or contract accordingly.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Local Response-Surface Search

children.top_down_role: Simulation-specific interface to Bayesian sequential-design policies.

children.title: Noisy Improvement Policies
children.top_down_role: Improvement-oriented sampling adjusted for noisy observations.

assumptions_latex: The latent objective \(f\) is minimized over \(X\).
The posterior distribution conditions on observation noise.
The cost \(c(x)\) of another observation is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The next simulation location is \(x_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in X}\operatorname{NEI}_n(x)/c(x)\).

notation.meaning: latent best value among sampled locations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior expected improvement integrates uncertainty in both latent sampled values and a prospective noisy observation.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.1 Optimization and search p. 55
source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_n\subset X\) be the sampled locations and define the random latent incumbent \(f_n^\star=\min_{z\in S_n}f(z)\). For a candidate \(x\), define \(\operatorname{NEI}_n(x)=\mathbb E[(f_n^\star-f(x))_+\mid\mathcal D_n]\), where the expectation is under the joint posterior of latent responses and therefore does not substitute the smallest noisy observation for \(f_n^\star\). Choose a maximizer of \(\operatorname{NEI}_n(x)/c(x)\), simulate at that location, and update the posterior. Replication is permitted by including previously sampled locations in \(X\). Stop when the budget is exhausted or the maximal acquisition value is below a prescribed tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the location with greatest posterior expected latent improvement per cost, integrating over observation noise and allowing previously sampled locations to receive replications.
knowledge_statements.title: Noisy Improvement Policies

children.title: Knowledge-Gradient Simulation Search
children.top_down_role: Value-of-information search over modeled simulator response.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite.
The posterior mean \(m_n(x)\) exists for every \(x\in X\).
A prospective observation has a specified predictive distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The knowledge-gradient decision is \(x_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in X}\operatorname{KG}_n(x)/c(x)\).

notation.meaning: posterior mean after a prospective observation at x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-step value of information for minimizing a posterior mean over finitely many alternatives.

source_refs.locator: 7.4 The Knowledge Gradient Algorithm for Discrete Alternatives p. 262

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each candidate \(x\in X\), let \(m_{n+1}^{x}\) denote the random posterior mean that would result from one additional noisy observation at \(x\). Define \(\operatorname{KG}_n(x)=\min_{z\in X}m_n(z)-\mathbb E[\min_{z\in X}m_{n+1}^{x}(z)\mid\mathcal D_n]\). Select a location maximizing \(\operatorname{KG}_n(x)/c(x)\), observe the simulator there, and update the posterior. After the sampling budget is exhausted, return \(\widehat x_N\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}m_N(x)\). Thus each sampling decision maximizes the expected one-step reduction in the terminal posterior decision value, rather than immediate observed improvement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample the alternative giving the largest expected one-step reduction in the minimum posterior mean per cost, then return the final posterior-mean minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Knowledge-Gradient Simulation Search

children.title: Statistical Upper-Bound Search
children.top_down_role: Optimistic search balancing predicted response and uncertainty.

assumptions_latex: The simulator reward \(g(x)\) is maximized over \(X\).
The posterior provides mean \(m_n(x)\) and standard deviation \(s_n(x)\).
The exploration coefficient satisfies \(\beta_n>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimistic sampling decision is \(x_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{x\in X}\{m_n(x)+\beta_n s_n(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-confidence search stated for reward maximization; minimization uses the corresponding lower confidence bound.

source_refs.locator: 2.4.1 Optimization and search p. 55
source_refs.source_title: Surrogates: Gaussian Process Modeling, Design, and Optimization for the Applied Sciences

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(n\), construct the statistical upper score \(U_n(x)=m_n(x)+\beta_n s_n(x)\) and simulate at a maximizer of \(U_n\). The mean term favors locations predicted to have high reward, while the uncertainty term favors locations whose reward remains poorly determined. Incorporate the new noisy observation into the posterior and repeat until the budget or stopping rule is met. For minimizing a cost \(f=-g\), the equivalent rule minimizes the lower score \(L_n(x)=m_n^f(x)-\beta_n s_n^f(x)\). The sequence \((\beta_n)\) must be fixed by the selected confidence or exploration schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For reward maximization, sample where posterior mean plus an uncertainty bonus is largest; for cost minimization, use posterior mean minus that bonus.
knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Upper-Bound Search

children.title: Predictive Validation
children.top_down_role: Assessment of response prediction away from sampled decisions.

assumptions_latex: Validation observations are excluded from surrogate fitting.
Validation responses have finite second moments.
The predictive distribution supplies a mean and positive predictive variance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Predictive adequacy is accepted only when the predeclared statistics computed from \(\{e_i\}_{i=1}^M\) satisfy their calibration and loss tolerances.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Out-of-sample validation of response prediction, distinct from validation of the optimizer's recommendation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For held-out observations \((x_i,y_i)\), define \(e_i=(y_i-m(x_i))/\sqrt{v(x_i)}\). A predictive-validation certificate consists of the held-out data, fitted predictions, and predeclared tolerances showing simultaneously that a proper predictive loss, such as \(M^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^M[-\log p(y_i\mid x_i)]\), is below its tolerance and that empirical coverage of specified predictive intervals is within its calibration tolerance. If validation uses replicated sample means, \(v(x_i)\) must include both latent predictive uncertainty and the sampling variance of that mean. Passing only an in-sample residual check is not a predictive-validation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Held-out predictions pass validation only when predeclared predictive-loss and interval-calibration criteria are met with observation noise included in predictive variance.
