children.title: Optimization-Aware Validation
children.top_down_role: Assessment focused on ranking, local geometry, and recommended decisions.

assumptions_latex: A finite validation set \(V\subset X\) contains decision-relevant alternatives.
Independent validation estimates \(\widehat f_V(x)\) are available on \(V\).
Ranking and recommendation tolerances are declared before validation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The surrogate is optimization-adequate on \(V\) only if \(R_V\leq\varepsilon_R\), \(E_{\mathrm{rank}}\leq\varepsilon_{ho}\), and the local-geometry criterion passes.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: optimization validation should test recommendation regret, ranking, and local geometry rather than global prediction alone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-focused validation on recommendation quality, ranking accuracy, and local geometry near competitive solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat x\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in V}m(x)\) and define \(R_V=\widehat f_V(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in V}\widehat f_V(x)\). For declared nonnegative weights \(w_{ij}\), define \(E_{\mathrm{rank}}=\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}\mathbf 1\{[m(x_i)-m(x_j)][\widehat f_V(x_i)-\widehat f_V(x_j)]<0\}/\sum_{i<j}w_{ij}\). An optimization-aware certificate reports uncertainty for \(R_V\), verifies \(E_{\mathrm{rank}}\leq\varepsilon_{\rho}\), and checks a declared local-geometry statistic, such as directional-slope agreement around \(\widehat x\). It is valid only when the upper confidence bound for \(R_V\) is at most \(\varepsilon_R\) and all declared criteria pass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validate a surrogate by bounding recommendation regret, weighted ranking errors among competitive decisions, and disagreement in local geometry near the recommended solution.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Aware Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this particular three-part certificate. In addition, allowing all ranking weights to be zero leaves the displayed ranking error undefined, and the local-geometry requirement is not specified sufficiently to yield the asserted conclusion. An authoritative source and a precise criterion are required.

children.title: Surrogate Support Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Spurious recommendations outside well-supported simulation regions.

children.title: Surrogate False Optima
children.top_down_role: Spurious recommended solutions created by metamodel error.

assumptions_latex: The decision domain is \(X=[0,1]\).
The true objective and surrogate are minimized.
No validation observation is taken at the surrogate recommendation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The surrogate minimizer \(0\) has true regret \(f(0)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)=1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct evaluation of the displayed functions establishes the counterexample
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete false optimum created by a surrogate whose minimizer reverses the true objective's minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=(x-1)^2\) be the true objective on \(X=[0,1]\), and let the fitted surrogate be \(m(x)=x^2\). Then \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}m(x)=\{0\}\), whereas \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}f(x)=\{1\}\). Consequently, optimizing the surrogate recommends \(\widehat x=0\), whose true regret equals \(f(0)-f(1)=1\). Thus numerical accuracy in solving the surrogate optimization problem does not certify quality for the simulator objective; independent simulation at the recommendation or a support-expanding design is required to detect this false optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A surrogate can be optimized exactly yet recommend the worst true decision: the displayed surrogate selects zero while the true objective is minimized at one.
knowledge_statements.title: Surrogate False Optima

children.title: Unsupported Extrapolation
children.top_down_role: Predictions or recommendations outside simulation-supported regions.

assumptions_latex: Simulator data are available only on \(S=[0,1/2]\).
The decision domain is \(X=[0,1]\).
The fitting rule uses only observations from \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Observations confined to \(S\) cannot distinguish whether the minimizer set is \(S\) or the singleton \(\{1\}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed objectives agree on sampled support but have different global minimizer sets
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonidentifiability of an optimizer outside sampled support without structural assumptions controlling extrapolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f_0(x)=0\) for \(x\in S\) and \(f_0(x)=x-1/2\) for \(x>1/2\). Define \(f_1(x)=0\) for \(x\in S\) and \(f_1(x)=-2(x-1/2)\) for \(x>1/2\). The two objectives generate identical noiseless responses, and identical noisy-response distributions under a common additive noise law, at every sampled location in \(S\). Nevertheless, \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}f_0(x)=S\), whereas \(\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}f_1(x)=\{1\}\). Hence observations confined to \(S\) cannot support an optimization claim in \(X\setminus S\) unless additional shape, smoothness, or prior assumptions link sampled and unsampled regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two objectives can agree at every sampled location yet have different global minimizer sets, so extrapolated optimization requires additional structural assumptions.
knowledge_statements.title: Unsupported Extrapolation

children.title: Design-Hull Boundary Risk
children.top_down_role: Reliability loss near or beyond the boundary of sampled designs.

assumptions_latex: The sampled design has convex hull \(H\subsetneq X\).
A surrogate recommendation \(\widehat x\) lies on \(\partial H\).
There exist \(d\in N_H(\widehat x)\setminus\{0\}\) and \(t>0\) such that \(\widehat x+td\in X\setminus H\), with no observations beyond the supporting face in that direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A boundary recommendation alone cannot certify descent beyond \(H\) or local optimality for the true objective on \(X\).

notation.meaning: surrogate recommendation on the hull boundary

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: one-sided design support leaves outward behavior unidentified
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided support at a design-hull face prevents validation of outward behavior and boundary optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\in N_H(\widehat x)\setminus\{0\}\) and suppose \(\widehat x+td\in X\setminus H\) for some \(t>0\). Observations confined to \(H\) provide no comparison with responses beyond the supporting face in direction \(d\). In particular, two response functions may agree at every sampled design point yet be extended outside \(H\) so that one increases and the other decreases along \(\widehat x+sd\) for sufficiently small admissible \(s>0\). Therefore a surrogate minimum on \(\partial H\) is a support warning: its predicted outward gradient and curvature are extrapolations. Certification requires sampling beyond the face, restricting optimization to a supported interior region, or imposing validated structural assumptions on the extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a design-hull boundary, data support only one side of the recommendation; outward gradients and curvature remain extrapolations unless new data or validated structure are supplied.
knowledge_statements.title: Design-Hull Boundary Risk

children.title: Noise-Model Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Failure caused by incorrect replication, dependence, or heteroskedasticity models.

assumptions_latex: Replications obey \(Y_r=\mu+Z+\varepsilon_r\).
The common effect satisfies \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=\tau^2>0\).
The errors \(\varepsilon_r\) are mutually independent, independent of \(Z\), and satisfy \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_r)=\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Treating replications as independent makes the reported variance vanish, although \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_R)\to\tau^2>0\).

notation.meaning: common random effect shared by replications

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: variance decomposition directly establishes the misspecification failure
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete dependence misspecification showing that nominal replication precision can be arbitrarily overconfident.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because the same random effect \(Z\) enters every replication and is independent of the errors, \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_r,Y_s)=\tau^2\) for \(r\neq s\), and \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_R)=\tau^2+\sigma^2/R\). A model that incorrectly treats the \(Y_r\) as independent assigns variance \((\tau^2+\sigma^2)/R\) to their mean. The reported variance converges to \(0\), while the true variance converges to \(\tau^2\). Consequently, increasing the nominal replicate count cannot remove the shared uncertainty, and acquisition scores, confidence intervals, or stopping rules based on the independence model become increasingly overconfident.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shared dependence among nominal replications leaves irreducible variance, while an independence model reports variance approaching zero and produces increasingly overconfident optimization decisions.
knowledge_statements.title: Noise-Model Misspecification

children.title: Irregular-Response Metamodel Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of smooth stationary metamodels on irregular responses.

children.title: Response-Drift Failure
children.top_down_role: Predictive degradation caused by gradual response evolution.

assumptions_latex: For each design point \(x\in\mathcal X\), observations satisfy \(Y_t(x)=m_t(x)+\varepsilon_t(x)\) with \(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_t(x)\mid x,t]=0\).
The metamodel is fitted as time-homogeneous using observations through time \(n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Consistency for the historical average response does not imply consistency for the current response when drift persists.

notation.meaning: Mean simulation response at design x and time t.
Time-homogeneous metamodel fitted through time n.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this formal response-drift failure criterion.
Authoritative source for nonstationary metamodel-assisted simulation optimization is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent temporal drift invalidates a metamodel trained to represent a stationary simulation response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\bar m_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n m_t(x)\). A response-drift failure occurs when \(\widehat m_n\) consistently estimates \(\bar m_n\), but the optimization target is the current response \(m_n\), and
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|\bar m_n(x)-m_n(x)|>0.
\]
Then even if \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|\widehat m_n(x)-\bar m_n(x)|\to0\) in probability, it need not follow that \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal X}|\widehat m_n(x)-m_n(x)|\to0\). Consequently, a design minimizing \(\widehat m_n\) may remain separated from the minimizers of the current response.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary surrogate can learn the historical average accurately yet remain persistently inaccurate for the current objective when the simulator response drifts over time.
knowledge_statements.title: Response-Drift Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role and mathematics are plausible, but no cited source supports this particular uniform response-drift criterion or its optimization consequence.

children.title: Change-Point Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Failure to represent abrupt changes between response regimes.

assumptions_latex: The true one-dimensional response has a single jump at \(\tau\): \(m(x)=a\) for \(x<\tau\) and \(m(x)=b\) for \(x\ge\tau\), where \(a\ne b\).
The fitted metamodel places the jump at \(\widehat\tau\ne\tau\) while using the correct regime levels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonvanishing change-point location error produces a nonvanishing integrated squared approximation error.

notation.meaning: Change point imposed by the metamodel.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports this formal change-point misspecification boundary.
A source on discontinuous or change-point surrogate models is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional single-jump model illustrating irreducible error from a misplaced change point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the fitted response by \(\widetilde m(x)=a\) for \(x<\widehat\tau\) and \(\widetilde m(x)=b\) for \(x\ge\widehat\tau\). On any interval containing both \(\tau\) and \(\widehat\tau\), the two responses disagree exactly between those locations, so
\[
\int |m(x)-\widetilde m(x)|^2\,dx=(b-a)^2|\widehat\tau-\tau|.
\]
Hence, if a sequence of fitted change points satisfies \(\liminf_{n\to\infty}|\widehat\tau_n-\tau|>0\), its integrated squared response error is bounded away from zero. Optimization decisions near the regime boundary can therefore remain incorrect despite accurate estimation of both regime levels.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Misplacing a response change point creates an error region whose integrated squared bias equals the squared jump size times the location error.
knowledge_statements.title: Change-Point Misspecification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The single-jump calculation is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable source for the formal misspecification boundary or its optimization interpretation.

children.title: Discontinuity Smoothing Bias
children.top_down_role: Optimization distortion caused by smoothing across response jumps.

assumptions_latex: The response has finite one-sided limits \(m(x_0-)\ne m(x_0+)\) at a discontinuity \(x_0\).
The surrogate locally applies kernel smoothing with \(K_h(u)=h^{-1}K(u/h)\), where \(K\ge0\) and \(\int_{\mathbb R}K(u)\,du=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Kernel smoothing converges to a mixture of the one-sided limits and therefore retains nonzero one-sided bias at a jump.

notation.meaning: Response function with a jump at x_0.
Kernel mass on the positive half-line.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the displayed discontinuity-smoothing limit.
A nonparametric smoothing or surrogate-model source with boundary limits is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel-smoothing limit at an interior jump discontinuity of a one-dimensional simulation response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the population smoother \(m_h(x_0)=\int_{\mathbb R}K(u)m(x_0-hu)\,du\), dominated convergence gives the limiting value
\[
\lim_{h\downarrow0}m_h(x_0)=p_+m(x_0-)+(1-p_+)m(x_0+).
\]
Thus the limit generally equals neither one-sided response. For a symmetric kernel, \(p_+=1/2\), so the limiting value is \(\{m(x_0-)+m(x_0+)\}/2\). Its bias relative to either regime has magnitude \(|m(x_0+)-m(x_0-)|/2\), showing that vanishing bandwidth alone does not remove pointwise bias at the discontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth surrogate averages the two sides of a jump, leaving persistent pointwise bias at the discontinuity even as its bandwidth vanishes.
knowledge_statements.title: Discontinuity Smoothing Bias

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source is supplied, and finite one-sided limits alone do not justify dominated convergence for an arbitrary unbounded-support kernel; additional boundedness or domination assumptions are required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Alternative Simulation Optimization and Run-Length Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the finite-alternative simulation-optimization problem and its frequentist allocation of a simulation budget across noisily evaluated designs or policies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a finite set of designs or policies with noisy performance \(F(x,W)\), typically evaluated through discrete-event simulation. The design-selection problem is \(\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\mathbb E[F(x,W)]\). Under a global simulation budget \(N\), assign run lengths \(n_x\) satisfying \(\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}n_x=N\); increasing \(n_x\) improves the accuracy of the estimate for design \(x\). A standard frequentist two-stage strategy initially samples every design and then allocates the remaining budget preferentially to promising designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-alternative simulation optimization selects the design or policy with the greatest expected simulated performance. A global simulation budget is divided into design-specific run lengths. In a standard frequentist two-stage strategy, every design is sampled initially and the remaining effort is concentrated on promising alternatives.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a finite set of designs or policies.
Performance observations \(F(x,W)\) are noisy and are typically produced by discrete-event simulation.
A global simulation budget \(N\) is divided into run lengths \(n_x\).
The two-stage strategy requires enough budget to obtain an initial sample from every \(x\in\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{x\in\mathcal X}\mathbb E[F(x,W)]\), with simulation-effort allocation satisfying \(\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}n_x=N\); initial estimates may be used to concentrate subsequent effort on promising designs.

children.top_down_role: Optimization of continuous or discrete parameters affecting event dynamics.

assumptions_latex: The feasible parameter set \(\Theta\) may contain continuous, integer, or mixed-valued event parameters.
For each \(\theta\in\Theta\), the terminating or integrable simulation output \(Y(\theta,\xi)\) has finite expectation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An event-parameter optimization problem is
\[
\theta^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\theta\in\Theta}J(\theta),\qquad J(\theta)=\mathbb E[Y(\theta,\xi)].
\]
The parameter \(\theta\) modifies event dynamics, such as arrival or service rates, event-time distributions, thresholds, or transition probabilities, while the event-system structure and decision rule remain fixed. When constraints are simulated, feasibility is additionally specified by \(G_j(\theta)=\mathbb E[C_j(\theta,\xi)]\le0\) for each \(j\). The simulator supplies noisy observations rather than a closed-form expression for \(J\) or \(G_j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose continuous, discrete, or mixed event parameters to minimize expected simulated performance, optionally subject to expected simulation constraints.
knowledge_statements.title: Event-Parameter Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An event-policy optimization problem over the policy class \(\Pi\) is
\[
\eta^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\eta\in H}\mathbb E[C(\pi_\eta,\xi)].
\]
At each decision event, \(\pi_\eta\) maps the available event history or current state to a feasible routing, scheduling, admission, or control action. The system transition law is induced jointly by the event mechanism, the chosen action, and \(\xi\). Optimization is restricted to admissible parameters for which actions satisfy the system constraints and the displayed expectation exists; the simulator estimates the objective by policy replications.

children.title: Event-System Design Optimization
children.top_down_role: Configuration, capacity, and resource decisions in event-driven systems.

assumptions_latex: The feasible design set \(D\subseteq\mathbb Z^p\times\mathbb R^q\) encodes configuration, capacity, and resource restrictions.
For every \(d\in D\), the simulated operating measure \(Y(d,\xi)\) is integrable and the deterministic design cost \(c(d)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Event-system design optimization balances deterministic design cost against expected simulated operating performance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mixed discrete-continuous configuration, capacity, and resource design for event-driven systems.

source_refs.locator: 3. Simulation-Based Optimization: An Overview p. 29

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An event-system design optimization problem has the form
\[
d^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{d\in D}\{c(d)+\mathbb E[Y(d,\xi)]\}.
\]
The design vector \(d\) fixes structural attributes before simulation, including resource counts, capacities, network configuration, or equipment choices. Conditional on \(d\), the discrete-event simulator generates operating outcomes under randomness \(\xi\). Feasibility may also require \(\mathbb E[C_j(d,\xi)]\le b_j\) or sample-path constraints. Unlike event-parameter optimization, changing \(d\) may change the simulated system's structure or available resources, not merely a transition parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose system configuration, capacities, or resources to minimize design cost plus expected operating performance estimated by discrete-event simulation.
knowledge_statements.title: Event-System Design Optimization

children.title: Next-Event Representation
children.top_down_role: Simulation advanced by the next scheduled event.

assumptions_latex: At event time \(T_n\), the state \(X_n\) and a finite event calendar \(\mathcal C_n\) are available.
Each calendar entry contains a scheduled time, event type, and event data, and ties are resolved by a fixed rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Repeatedly removing and executing the earliest scheduled event defines the next-event representation of the simulation path.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the next-event recurrence.
A discrete-event simulation text covering event-calendar representations is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-calendar state recurrence with deterministic tie-breaking among simultaneously scheduled events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The next-event representation advances the simulation by selecting
\[
e_{n+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{e\in\mathcal C_n}t(e),\qquad T_{n+1}=t(e_{n+1}).
\]
After removing \(e_{n+1}\) from the calendar, an event routine updates the state and calendar according to
\[
(X_{n+1},\mathcal C_{n+1})=\Phi(X_n,\mathcal C_n\setminus\{e_{n+1}\},e_{n+1},\xi_{n+1}).
\]
Between \(T_n\) and \(T_{n+1}\), no scheduled event changes the state. Iteration stops at a prescribed terminal event or horizon, and the resulting ordered event times and post-event states represent the simulated sample path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain an event calendar, execute its earliest event, update the state and calendar, and repeat until the stopping condition is reached.
knowledge_statements.title: Next-Event Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The event-calendar recurrence is a suitable next-event representation, but no inspectable citation supports its formalization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Future-event-list next-event simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chronological processing algorithm for a discrete-event simulation calendar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain one future-event-list record for each event type whose clock is not halted. Each record contains its event type and scheduled event time and may additionally contain the clock's last reset time and lifetime distribution. Keep the records ordered by scheduled time. Repeatedly: (1) set the simulation time to the scheduled time of the first record; (2) execute that event, update the system state, and cancel, insert, or reschedule records while preserving their ordering; and (3) remove or reschedule the record of the event just executed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Store active events in a future event list ordered by scheduled time. Advance the simulation clock to the earliest record, execute its state and scheduling effects while maintaining list order, and then remove or reschedule the event that fired.
assumptions_latex: Each nonhalted event clock has a future-event-list record containing a scheduled event time.
The future event list is maintained in chronological order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration advances to and processes the next scheduled event while preserving the chronologically ordered future event list.

children.title: Process-Interaction Representation
children.top_down_role: Entity- and process-oriented organization of event dynamics.

assumptions_latex: Each simulated entity has a process state consisting of a program location and local attributes.
Process primitives suspend an entity until an event condition, delay expiration, or resource availability is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A process-interaction model represents event dynamics through resumable entity processes whose suspensions induce an event calendar.
review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the process-interaction formalization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entity-oriented representation implemented by resumable processes and scheduled activation events.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A process-interaction representation specifies one resumable process \(P_i\) for each entity \(i\). The complete simulation state is \((R,(Z_i)_i,\mathcal C)\), where \(R\) records shared resources and queues. When active, \(P_i\) applies state changes until it executes a suspension primitive such as a delay, wait, seize, or request. A delay of duration \(D_i\ge0\) schedules a resumption at \(T+D_i\); a conditional wait resumes when an event makes its predicate true. Executing resumptions in increasing scheduled-time order yields the same event-time state trajectory as the event calendar generated by these process primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model each entity as a resumable process; delays and resource waits schedule activations whose chronological execution generates the event trajectory.
knowledge_statements.title: Process-Interaction Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf, but the asserted equivalence with the generated event-calendar trajectory requires a source and precise process-primitive semantics.

children.title: Markov Jump-Process Simulation
children.top_down_role: Event simulation with Markovian state transitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Markov Jump-Process Simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct event-by-event simulation of a nonexplosive time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(T_0=0\) and \(X_0=i_0\). Given \(X_n=i\), if \(\lambda_i=0\), treat \(i\) as absorbing and schedule no departure. If \(\lambda_i>0\), independently sample a holding time \(H_n\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda_i)\) and a destination \(X_{n+1}=j\ne i\) with
\[
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j\mid X_n=i)=\frac{q_{ij}}{\lambda_i}.
\]
Set \(T_{n+1}=T_n+H_n\) and keep the continuous-time state equal to \(i\) on \([T_n,T_{n+1})\). Repeating these steps until the terminal time or event condition generates the nonexplosive Markov jump process with generator \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nonabsorbing state, sample an exponential holding time and choose the next state in proportion to its transition rate; a zero-rate state is absorbing.
assumptions_latex: The state space \(S\) is finite or countable, with transition rates \(q_{ij}\ge0\) for \(j\ne i\).
For each \(i\in S\), \(\lambda_i=\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}<\infty\), and the generator diagonal is \(q_{ii}=-\lambda_i\).
The resulting minimal jump process is nonexplosive on the simulated time horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exponential holding times and rate-normalized destination probabilities simulate the nonexplosive Markov jump process with generator \(Q\), with zero-rate states treated as absorbing.

notation.meaning: Total departure rate from state i.

children.title: Semi-Markov Simulation
children.top_down_role: Event simulation with general state sojourn times.

assumptions_latex: The embedded state space \(S\) is finite or countable.
For every current state \(i\), \(Q_{ij}(t)=\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j,H_n\le t\mid X_n=i)\) is a proper semi-Markov kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sampling each next-state and holding-time pair from the semi-Markov kernel generates the associated semi-Markov process.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-by-event simulation from a semi-Markov kernel with generally nonexponential sojourns.

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Semi-Markov processes p. 112

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Initialize \(T_0=0\) and \(X_0=i_0\). At jump \(n\), conditional on \(X_n=i\), sample the pair \((X_{n+1},H_n)\) according to the kernel \(Q_{ij}\), so that
\[
\mathbb P(X_{n+1}=j,H_n\le t\mid X_n=i)=Q_{ij}(t).
\]
Set \(T_{n+1}=T_n+H_n\) and hold the continuous-time state at \(i\) on \([T_n,T_{n+1})\). Repeat until the stopping rule holds. Unlike a Markov jump process, the conditional distribution of \(H_n\) need not be exponential and may depend on both \(i\) and \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each jump, sample the next state and a generally nonexponential sojourn time from the semi-Markov kernel, then advance the clock.
knowledge_statements.title: Semi-Markov Simulation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semi-Markov process representation and stationary performance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a semi-Markov process through an embedded Markov chain of sojourn-state pairs and states its stationary performance formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((R,r)\) be a metric space and let \(M(k)=[T(k),Z(k)]\), \(k\ge 1\), be a Markov chain on \(\mathbb{R}_+\times R\), where \(T(k)\) is the sojourn time at state \(Z(k)\), and set \(T(0)=0\). The associated semi-Markov process satisfies \[S(t)=Z(n)\quad\text{if}\quad \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}T(i)\le t<\sum_{i=0}^{n}T(i).\] If \(M\) is ergodic and \([T,Z]\) is distributed according to its stationary distribution, then for a real performance function \(H:R\to\mathbb{R}\), provided the expectations are finite and \(\mathbb{E}[T]>0\), \[\mathbb{E}[H(S(\cdot))]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[T H(Z)]}{\mathbb{E}[T]}.\] In general, this is not equal to \(\mathbb{E}[H(Z)]\); it is a quotient of expectations and is not linear in the stationary law of \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A semi-Markov process occupies state Z(k) for the generally distributed sojourn time T(k). Under ergodicity, its stationary performance for H is the sojourn-time-weighted expectation of H(Z), divided by the mean sojourn time. This generally differs from the stationary expectation over the embedded states.
assumptions_latex: (R,r)\text{ is a metric space}
M(k)=[T(k),Z(k)]\text{ is a Markov chain on }\mathbb{R}_+\times R
M\text{ is ergodic for the stationary-performance formula}
H:R\to\mathbb{R}\text{ has finite required expectations and }\mathbb{E}[T]>0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(t)=Z(n)\text{ if }\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}T(i)\le t<\sum_{i=0}^{n}T(i),\qquad \mathbb{E}[H(S(\cdot))]=\frac{\mathbb{E}[T H(Z)]}{\mathbb{E}[T]}.

children.top_down_role: Event simulation using competing clocks with general lifetime laws.

assumptions_latex: At state \(x\), a finite enabled-event set \(E(x)\) is maintained.
Each newly enabled event \(e\) receives a nonnegative lifetime with its specified distribution, and simultaneous expirations use a fixed tie rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Selecting the smallest residual lifetime and updating competing clocks simulates the generalized semi-Markov process.

notation.meaning: Residual lifetime of enabled event e.

source_refs.locator: 2.5.3 Simulation of Generalized Semi-Markov processes p. 122

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize state \(X_0\), time \(T_0=0\), and one sampled residual lifetime \(r_e\) for every \(e\in E(X_0)\). At step \(n\), choose \(e^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{e\in E(X_n)}r_e\), set \(\delta_n=r_{e^*}\), and update \(T_{n+1}=T_n+\delta_n\) and \(X_{n+1}=\Phi(X_n,e^*,\xi_{n+1})\). Subtract \(\delta_n\) from clocks that remain enabled, discard disabled clocks, and sample lifetimes for newly enabled events. Repeat until the prescribed stopping condition holds. The general lifetime laws permit nonexponential competing clocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain general residual event clocks, execute the earliest expiration, update the state and enabled events, and resample newly enabled clocks.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized semi-Markov process
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-oriented definition and augmented Markov representation of a GSMP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Z\) be finite or countably infinite and let \(E_1,\ldots,E_q\) be finitely many event types. A generalized semi-Markov process is a piecewise-constant discrete-event process that has the Markov property after its discrete state is augmented by finitely many clock-time variables. At jump epochs its augmented state can be represented as \(M(n)=[T(n),Z(n),V^{(1)}(n),\ldots,V^{(q)}(n)]\in\mathbb R_+\times\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R_+^q\). If an event of type \(E_i\) occurs, the state changes according to \(N^{(i)}\); event types in the associated canceling set are canceled, those in the scheduling set are reset with delays having distributions \(G^{(j)}\), and all other event clocks remain unchanged. Simultaneous events are handled in increasing event-type order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized semi-Markov process is a piecewise-constant discrete-event process whose state becomes Markov after adding finitely many event-clock times. An event changes the discrete state and may cancel, reset, or leave other clocks unchanged; simultaneous events are processed by event-type order.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal Z\) is finite or countably infinite.
There are finitely many event types with transition maps \(N^{(i)}:\mathcal Z\to\mathcal Z\), disjoint canceling and scheduling sets, and lifetime distributions \(G^{(j)}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented sequence \((M(n))_{n\ge1}\) is Markov on \(\mathbb R_+\times\mathcal Z\times\mathbb R_+^q\), although the unaugmented discrete-state process need not be Markov.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual lifetimes and competing-clock hazards
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-lifetime and competing-clock identities used in GSMP simulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a nonnegative lifetime \(V\) have distribution function \(G\) and integrated hazard \(\Lambda\). For \(s\ge0\) with \(G(s)<1\), the residual lifetime \(V-s\mid V>s\) has distribution function \(G_s(u)=\frac{G(s+u)-G(s)}{1-G(s)}\) and integrated hazard \(\Lambda_s(u)=\Lambda(s+u)-\Lambda(s)\) for \(u\ge0\). If \(V^{(1)},\ldots,V^{(q)}\) are independent nonnegative lifetimes with distribution functions \(G^{(i)}\) and integrated hazards \(\Lambda^{(i)}\), then \(W=\min_iV^{(i)}\) satisfies \(\mathbb P(W\le u)=1-\prod_{i=1}^q(1-G^{(i)}(u))\) and \(\Lambda_W(u)=\sum_{i=1}^q\Lambda^{(i)}(u)\). If hazard functions \(\lambda^{(i)}\) exist, then wherever \(\sum_j\lambda^{(j)}(v)>0\), \(\mathbb P(V^{(i)}=W\mid W=v)=\frac{\lambda^{(i)}(v)}{\sum_{j=1}^q\lambda^{(j)}(v)}\), and \(\mathbb P(V^{(i)}=W)=\int_0^\infty\lambda^{(i)}(u)\exp\{-\sum_{j=1}^q\Lambda^{(j)}(u)\}\,du\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditioning a lifetime on survival through time s subtracts the integrated hazard accumulated through s. For independent competing lifetimes, the minimum has product survival and summed integrated hazard. When hazard functions exist, each clock's instantaneous share of the total hazard determines its probability of being the next clock to ring.
assumptions_latex: \(s\ge0\) and \(G(s)<1\) for the residual-lifetime formula.
\(V^{(1)},\ldots,V^{(q)}\) are independent nonnegative lifetimes.
The clock-selection identities require the hazard functions \(\lambda^{(i)}\) to exist; the conditional ratio is asserted where \(\sum_j\lambda^{(j)}(v)>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Lambda_s(u)=\Lambda(s+u)-\Lambda(s),\qquad \Lambda_{\min_iV^{(i)}}(u)=\sum_{i=1}^q\Lambda^{(i)}(u),\qquad \mathbb P(V^{(i)}=W\mid W=v)=\frac{\lambda^{(i)}(v)}{\sum_j\lambda^{(j)}(v)}.

children.title: Terminating Event Simulation
children.top_down_role: Event-system replications with natural terminal conditions.

assumptions_latex: For each decision \(x\), the event system has a terminal stopping time \(\tau_x\) satisfying \(\mathbb P(\tau_x<\infty)=1\).
The replication performance \(H_x=h((X_x(t))_{0\le t\le\tau_x})\) is integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Independent complete paths through the natural terminal event provide unbiased replication observations of the terminating-system objective.

notation.meaning: Natural terminal stopping time under decision x.

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports the terminating-replication definition.
A discrete-event output-analysis source distinguishing terminating and steady-state regimes is required.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon or naturally terminating discrete-event replications with complete-path performance measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A terminating event simulation under decision \(x\) starts from a specified initial distribution and runs until the natural terminal time \(\tau_x\), such as completion of all jobs or occurrence of a designated event. One replication returns
\[
H_x=h((X_x(t))_{0\le t\le\tau_x}),
\]
and the optimization objective is \(J(x)=\mathbb E[H_x]\). With independent simulation inputs, complete replications \(H_x^{(1)},\ldots,H_x^{(n)}\) are identically distributed and their average \(\widehat J_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^nH_x^{(r)}\) is unbiased for \(J(x)\). No artificial warm-up deletion or steady-state horizon is part of this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A terminating simulation runs each independent replication from its specified initial state to a natural terminal event and evaluates the complete path.
knowledge_statements.title: Terminating Event Simulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and unbiased-replication statement are standard and fit the terminating-run leaf, but no output-analysis source is supplied to support the distinction from steady-state simulation.

children.title: Steady-State Event Simulation
children.top_down_role: Persistent event systems evaluated through long-run behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Steady-State Event Simulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Long-run performance estimation for a persistent discrete-event system at a fixed design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For design \(x\), let \(Z_x(t)\) be a positive Harris recurrent event-system state process with invariant distribution \(\pi_x\), and let \(r_x\) be integrable under \(\pi_x\). Its steady-state response and time-average estimator are
\[J(x)=\int r_x(z)\,\pi_x(dz),\qquad \widehat J_T(x)=\frac{1}{T}\int_0^T r_x(Z_x(t))\,dt.\]
A simulation is steady-state when its target is \(J(x)\), rather than a finite-horizon response. Under the ergodic theorem, \(\widehat J_T(x)\to J(x)\) almost surely as \(T\to\infty\), for every admissible initial distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A steady-state simulation estimates invariant long-run performance by a time average from a persistent recurrent event system.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_x\) is positive Harris recurrent with invariant law \(\pi_x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat J_T(x)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}J(x)\) as \(T\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: event-system state at time t under design x

children.title: Discrete-Event Estimation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Event-system specializations of output and sensitivity estimation.

children.title: Discrete-Event Regenerative Estimation
children.top_down_role: Cycle-based output estimation in recurrent event systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Event Regenerative Estimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ratio estimation from independent regeneration cycles of a recurrent event system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a design \(x\) and regeneration times \(0=T_0<T_1<\cdots\). For cycle \(k\), define its length and accumulated reward by
\[\tau_k=T_k-T_{k-1},\qquad R_k=\int_{T_{k-1}}^{T_k}r_x(Z_x(t))\,dt.\]
If \((R_k,\tau_k)\) are identically distributed independent cycles with \(0<\mathbb E[\tau_1]<\infty\) and \(\mathbb E[|R_1|]<\infty\), then the steady-state response and its regenerative estimator are
\[J(x)=\frac{\mathbb E[R_1]}{\mathbb E[\tau_1]},\qquad \widehat J_n(x)=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^nR_k}{\sum_{k=1}^n\tau_k},\]
and \(\widehat J_n(x)\to J(x)\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Long-run performance equals expected reward per regenerative cycle divided by expected cycle length and is estimated by the corresponding sample ratio.
assumptions_latex: \((R_k,\tau_k)_{k\ge1}\) are identically distributed independent regenerative cycles.
\(0<\mathbb E[\tau_1]<\infty\) and \(\mathbb E[|R_1|]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J(x)=\mathbb E[R_1]/\mathbb E[\tau_1]\) and \(\widehat J_n(x)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{a.s.}}J(x)\).

children.title: Discrete-Event Infinitesimal Perturbation Analysis
children.top_down_role: Pathwise sensitivity estimation specialized to event dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Event Infinitesimal Perturbation Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pathwise derivative propagation through differentiable event-state recursions with almost-surely stable event ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(X_0(\theta)\), primitive inputs \((U_k)\), event recursions \(X_{k+1}(\theta)=F_k(X_k(\theta),\theta,U_k)\), and sample cost \(L(\theta)=G(X_0(\theta),\ldots,X_K(\theta),\theta)\), initialize \(D_0=dX_0/d\theta\) and update
\[D_{k+1}=\partial_xF_k(X_k,	heta,U_k)D_k+\partial_\theta F_k(X_k,	heta,U_k).\]
Return
\[\widehat g=\partial_\theta G+\sum_{k=0}^K\partial_{x_k}G\,D_k.\]
If event ties and ordering changes occur with probability zero and differentiation may pass through expectation, then \(\mathbb E[\widehat g]=d\mathbb E[L(\theta)]/d\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: IPA differentiates each event update along one simulated path and combines the propagated state derivatives into a gradient estimate.
assumptions_latex: The realized event recursion and cost are differentiable in a neighborhood of \(\theta\) almost surely.
Event ties or parameter-induced event-order changes have probability zero.
A dominating integrable derivative permits interchange of derivative and expectation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat g]=\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E[L(\theta)]\).

notation.meaning: pathwise derivative of the state after event k

children.title: Discrete-Event Weak Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Distributional sensitivity estimators for discrete-event simulation outputs.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Event Weak Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Signed-measure differentiation of parameterized event-transition laws without pathwise differentiability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q_\theta(z,\cdot)\) be a parameterized event-transition probability kernel. A weak-derivative representation at \(\theta\) is a scalar \(c_\theta(z)\ge0\) and probability kernels \(Q_\theta^+(z,\cdot)\), \(Q_\theta^-(z,\cdot)\) such that
\[\partial_\theta Q_\theta(z,\cdot)=c_\theta(z)\bigl(Q_\theta^+(z,\cdot)-Q_\theta^-(z,\cdot)\bigr)\]
as finite signed measures. Consequently, for every bounded measurable \(h\),
\[\partial_\theta\int h(y)Q_\theta(z,dy)=c_\theta(z)\left(\mathbb E[h(Y^+)]-\mathbb E[h(Y^-)]\right),\]
where \(Y^+\sim Q_\theta^+(z,\cdot)\) and \(Y^-\sim Q_\theta^-(z,\cdot)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transition-law derivative is represented as a scaled difference of two probability laws, enabling derivative estimation from positive and negative event transitions.
assumptions_latex: \(Q_\theta(z,\cdot)\) is differentiable as a finite signed measure.
\(h\) is bounded and measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_\theta Q_\theta=c_\theta(Q_\theta^+-Q_\theta^-)\) yields the displayed expectation derivative.

children.title: Discrete-Event Process Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Process-level sensitivity representations for event-system trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Discrete-Event Process Derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak differentiation of the complete event-process law on path space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_\theta\) be the law on a measurable path space \(\mathcal D\) of a discrete-event process over a fixed horizon. A process-derivative representation at \(\theta\) is
\[\dot P_\theta=c_\theta(P_\theta^+-P_\theta^-),\]
where \(\dot P_\theta\) is the signed-measure derivative of \(P_\theta\), \(c_\theta\ge0\), and \(P_\theta^+,P_\theta^-\) are probability laws on \(\mathcal D\). Hence, for every bounded measurable path functional \(H\),
\[\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[H]=c_\theta\left(\mathbb E_{P_\theta^+}[H]-\mathbb E_{P_\theta^-}[H]\right).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The derivative of an entire event-process law is a scaled difference of two path laws, so path-functional sensitivities become expectation differences.
assumptions_latex: \(P_\theta\) is differentiable as a finite signed measure on \(\mathcal D\).
\(H:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R\) is bounded and measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[H]=c_\theta(\mathbb E_{P_\theta^+}[H]-\mathbb E_{P_\theta^-}[H])\).

notation.meaning: law of the discrete-event process path
signed-measure derivative of the path law
measurable performance functional of a path

children.title: Coupled-Path Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity information obtained through coupled event-system sample paths.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled-Path Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity estimation by coupling nearby designs on a shared probability space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L(\theta,U)\) and \(L(\theta+h,U_h)\) be event-system outputs coupled on one probability space, and define
\[D_h=\frac{L(\theta+h,U_h)-L(\theta,U)}{h}.\]
If the coupling preserves the intended primitive randomness, \(D_h\to D\) in \(L^1\), and differentiation may pass through expectation, then
\[\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E[L(\theta,U)]=\mathbb E[D].\]
If convergence holds in \(L^2\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(D_h)\to\operatorname{Var}(D)\); effective coupling avoids the variance growth that can occur when the two outputs are generated independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearby event-system designs are simulated on coupled paths; convergence of their difference quotient supplies a valid sensitivity and can control variance.
assumptions_latex: Both outputs are defined on a common probability space with correctly coupled primitive inputs.
\(D_h\to D\) in \(L^1\) as \(h\to0\).
Differentiation and expectation are interchangeable at \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac{d}{d\theta}\mathbb E[L(\theta,U)]=\mathbb E[D]\).

children.title: Common-Random-Stream Event Coupling
children.top_down_role: Cross-design event coupling preserving intended random-input alignment.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Random-Stream Event Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stream-aligned paired simulation for comparing two event-system designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given designs \(x,y\), replication count \(m\), and a semantic stream assignment for primitive input classes, generate for each replication \(i\) one collection \(U_i=(U_{i,s,k})\). Run both event systems using the same \(U_{i,s,k}\) whenever they request the \(k\)-th variate from class \(s\), irrespective of differences in event ordering. Record outputs \(L(x,U_i)\) and \(L(y,U_i)\), and return
\[\widehat\Delta_m=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(L(x,U_i)-L(y,U_i)\bigr).\]
With independent replications and integrable outputs, \(\widehat\Delta_m\) is unbiased for \(\mathbb E[L(x,U)-L(y,U)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two designs use identically indexed random-input streams by input class, producing a paired unbiased estimator of their performance difference.
assumptions_latex: Stream assignment is based on primitive input class and within-class index.
Replications \(U_1,\ldots,U_m\) are independent.
\(L(x,U)\) and \(L(y,U)\) are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat\Delta_m]=\mathbb E[L(x,U)]-\mathbb E[L(y,U)]\).

notation.meaning: k-th random variate from semantic stream s in replication i
paired estimator of the response difference

children.title: Metamodels for Discrete-Event Systems
children.top_down_role: Surrogate representations specialized to event-driven system response.

children.title: Local Discrete-Event Response Surfaces
children.top_down_role: Local approximations supporting directional or region-based search.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Discrete-Event Response Surfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted polynomial approximation of a simulated mean response near a current design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_c\in\mathbb R^d\) be a center, \(u=x-x_c\), and let \((x_i,Y_i,w_i)\) be simulation observations with \(w_i>0\) concentrated near \(x_c\). A local quadratic response surface is
\[m_c(x)=\beta_0+\beta^\top u+\tfrac12u^\top Bu,\]
where \(B=B^\top\) and
\[(\widehat\beta_0,\widehat\beta,\widehat B)\in\arg\min\sum_iw_i\bigl(Y_i-m_c(x_i)\bigr)^2.\]
The fitted surface supplies the local direction \(-\widehat\beta\) or a trial point minimizing \(m_c\) over a prescribed neighborhood of \(x_c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted quadratic model is fitted near the current design and used to select a local search direction or a trial point within the prescribed neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(x_i\) lie in a prescribed neighborhood of \(x_c\).
The weighted polynomial design matrix has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_c\) is the weighted least-squares local quadratic approximation used for neighborhood search.

notation.meaning: local fitting weight for observation i

children.title: Global Discrete-Event Metamodels
children.top_down_role: Global approximations spanning broad event-system design spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Discrete-Event Metamodels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single fitted predictor covering the full prescribed design domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be a prescribed event-system design domain, let \(f(x)=\mathbb E[Y(x)]\), and let
\[\mathcal S=\{(x_i,Y_{ij}):i=1,\ldots,n,\ j=1,\ldots,m_i\}\]
be simulation data with design sites spanning \(D\). Given a model class \(\mathcal M\), a loss \(\ell:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)\), a regularizer \(\mathcal R:\mathcal M\to[0,\infty]\), and \(\lambda\ge0\), a global metamodel is a fitted predictor \(\widehat f_D:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfying
\[\widehat f_D\in\arg\min_{g\in\mathcal M}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^{m_i}\ell(Y_{ij},g(x_i))+\lambda\mathcal R(g)\right\}.\]
It induces the surrogate decision
\[\widehat x\in\arg\min_{x\in D}\widehat f_D(x).\]
Unlike a local response surface, its declared prediction and optimization domain is all of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global metamodel fits one possibly regularized predictor to simulation observations across the declared design domain and optimizes that predictor over the entire domain.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is the declared design and prediction domain.
The design sites \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) span the portion of \(D\) where global prediction is required.
The displayed fitting problem has at least one minimizer in \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat x\in\arg\min_{x\in D}\widehat f_D(x)\) is the metamodel-based decision over the global domain.

children.title: Heteroskedastic Event-System Metamodels
children.top_down_role: Metamodels representing decision-dependent simulation variability.

knowledge_statements.title: Heteroskedastic Event-System Metamodels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mean-response modeling with simulation noise whose variance depends on the design.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For design sites \(x_i\) and replications \(j=1,\ldots,m_i\), a heteroskedastic event-system metamodel uses
\[Y_{ij}=f(x_i)+\varepsilon_{ij},\qquad \mathbb E[\varepsilon_{ij}\mid x_i]=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_{ij}\mid x_i)=\tau^2(x_i).\]
Thus the replication mean satisfies
\[\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_i\mid x_i)=\frac{\tau^2(x_i)}{m_i}.\]
The fitted model estimates or otherwise represents both the mean surface \(f\) and the nonconstant variance surface \(\tau^2\); prediction uncertainty and replication allocation must use the site-specific noise variance rather than a common nugget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metamodel represents both mean performance and design-dependent simulation variance, accounting for replication-specific precision at each design site.
assumptions_latex: Replications are conditionally independent at each design site.
\(0<\tau^2(x_i)<\infty\) for every sampled site.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Var}(\overline Y_i\mid x_i)=\tau^2(x_i)/m_i\), so observation precision is design dependent.

notation.meaning: replication count at design site i

children.title: Single-Period Staffing
children.top_down_role: Static staffing for a fixed operating interval.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Period Staffing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer staffing optimization with one fixed capacity level over an operating interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb Z_+^q\) be staffing levels held fixed throughout one operating interval, let \(C(n)\) be staffing cost, and let \(G_r(n,U)\) be simulated service measures under random input \(U\). A constrained single-period staffing model is
\[\min_{n\in\mathcal N} C(n)\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \mathbb E[G_r(n,U)]\le b_r,\quad r=1,\ldots,R,\]
where \(\mathcal N\subseteq\mathbb Z_+^q\) contains operationally admissible staffing vectors. Simulation supplies estimators of the expectations because the queueing dynamics need not yield closed-form service measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One integer staffing vector is used throughout the interval and optimized against simulated expected service constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal N\subseteq\mathbb Z_+^q\) is the admissible set of fixed staffing vectors.
Each \(G_r(n,U)\) is integrable for \(n\in\mathcal N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n^*\in\arg\min\{C(n):n\in\mathcal N,\ \mathbb E[G_r(n,U)]\le b_r\ \forall r\}\).

notation.meaning: staffing vector fixed over the operating interval

children.title: Time-Varying Staffing
children.top_down_role: Staff schedules for nonstationary demand.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Varying Staffing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Period-indexed integer staffing schedules for nonstationary arrivals and service demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Partition the planning horizon into periods \(p=1,
\ldots,P\), and let \(n_p\in\mathbb Z_+^q\) be staffing during period \(p\). For admissible schedules \(n=(n_1,\ldots,n_P)\in\mathcal N\), switching costs \(K_p\), and simulated time-dependent service measures \(G_r(n,U)\), a time-varying staffing model is
\[\min_{n\in\mathcal N}\left\{\sum_{p=1}^P C_p(n_p)+\sum_{p=2}^P K_p(n_{p-1},n_p)\right\}\]
subject to
\[\mathbb E[G_r(n,U)]\le b_r,
\qquad r=1,\ldots,R.\]
The simulation propagates congestion across period boundaries, so each constraint may depend on the entire schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A period-indexed integer staff schedule is optimized under nonstationary simulated demand, including service constraints and optional costs for changing staffing levels.
assumptions_latex: Demand and service primitives may vary by period and are represented by \(U\).
\(\mathcal N\) encodes feasible schedules and interperiod staffing rules.
Each \(G_r(n,U)\) is integrable for \(n\in\mathcal N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n^*\) minimizes total staffing and switching cost subject to all simulated expected-service constraints.

notation.meaning: cost of changing staffing between adjacent periods
simulated service measure depending on the full schedule

children.title: Skill-Based Staffing

knowledge_statements.title: Skill-Based Staffing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon staffing with heterogeneous server skills and simulation-evaluated service performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let customer classes be \(i\in I\), skill groups be \(k\in K\), and \(A_{ik}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether group \(k\) can serve class \(i\). A skill-based staffing design is represented by
\[\min_{y\in\mathbb Z_+^{K},\,\theta\in\Theta(y)} c^\top y+\mathbb E[L(y,\theta;\xi)]\]
subject to \(g_j(y,\theta)=\mathbb E[G_j(y,\theta;\xi)]\le b_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). Here \(y_k\) is the number of group-\(k\) servers, \(\theta\) specifies admissible routing among compatible class-group pairs, and a discrete-event simulation driven by \(\xi\) estimates congestion loss and service constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose integer numbers of differently skilled servers and compatible routing parameters to minimize staffing plus expected congestion cost while satisfying simulation-estimated service requirements.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(K\) are finite.
\(\Theta(y)\) permits service only when \(A_{ik}=1\).
The simulated losses and constraint responses are integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((y,\theta)\) jointly determines heterogeneous staffing, compatible routing, and simulated service performance.

notation.meaning: number of servers in skill group k

knowledge_statements.title: Server-Capacity Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer selection of pooled parallel-server capacity using simulation-based congestion measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For candidate capacities \(s\in S\subseteq\mathbb Z_+\), let \(C(s)\) be capacity cost and let \(H(s;\xi)\) be an integrable performance response from a finite-horizon or steady-state queue simulation. One server-capacity design formulation is
\[\min_{s\in S} C(s)+\mathbb E[H(s;\xi)].\]
Alternatively, given integrable simulated service measures \(H_j(s;\xi)\), thresholds \(b_j\), and an index set \(J\), a constrained formulation is
\[\min_{s\in S}C(s)\quad\text{subject to}\quad \mathbb E[H_j(s;\xi)]\le b_j\quad\text{for every }j\in J.\]
The simulation must implement the arrival, service, pooling, abandonment, and queue-discipline assumptions associated with each evaluated capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Select an integer number of parallel or pooled servers using either a capacity-plus-congestion objective or capacity-cost minimization subject to simulation-evaluated service constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a nonempty finite set of admissible capacities.
Each simulated performance response used in the objective or constraints is integrable.
All compared designs use the same stated queueing conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimizer of the selected formulation is a least-objective admissible server capacity under that formulation's simulated performance criterion and constraints.

simulated service measure indexed by j
finite index set of service constraints

children.title: Queueing-Network Capacity Design
children.top_down_role: Allocation of capacity across interconnected service stations.

knowledge_statements.title: Queueing-Network Capacity Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer capacity allocation across stations of an interconnected queueing network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be the stations of a queueing network and \(s_v\in S_v\subseteq\mathbb Z_+\) its capacity at station \(v\). With routing and service rules fixed, a simulation-based network design is
\[\min_{s\in\prod_{v\in V}S_v}\sum_{v\in V}c_v(s_v)+\mathbb E[H(s;\xi)]\]
subject, when required, to \(\mathbb E[G_j(s;\xi)]\le b_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). The discrete-event simulator propagates jobs between stations and measures networkwide delay, throughput, loss, or station congestion, thereby retaining interactions that cannot be assessed station by station.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate integer capacity among connected service stations to minimize total capacity and simulated network congestion costs while meeting networkwide requirements.

children.title: Capacity-Reliability Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Service reliability and congestion risk in capacity selection.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Reliability Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-risk frontier for simulation-based queueing capacity selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a feasible capacity design \(s\in S\), let \(C(s)\) be capacity cost and let \(R(s)=\mathbb P\{Z(s;\xi)>z_{\max}\}\) be the probability of violating a congestion threshold. The capacity-reliability tradeoff is represented by the attainable set
\[\mathcal A=\{(C(s),R(s)):s\in S\}\]
and its nondominated frontier. An equivalent reliability-constrained scalarization is
\[\min_{s\in S}C(s)\quad\text{subject to}\quad R(s)\le\varepsilon.\]
Discrete-event replications estimate \(R(s)\); the probability convention, horizon, initial condition, and congestion statistic must remain fixed across designs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare capacity designs by cost and simulated probability of unacceptable congestion; efficient designs form the nondominated cost-risk frontier.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a nonempty set of feasible capacity designs.
\(Z(s;\xi)\) and the violation threshold \(z_{\max}\) are consistently defined for all \(s\).
\(0<\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A reliability-constrained solution has minimum capacity cost among designs whose congestion-violation probability does not exceed \(\varepsilon\).

The policy \(\pi_\theta\) is nonanticipative for each \(\theta\in\Theta\).
The simulated objective and constraint responses are integrable.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Horizon Lost-Sales Inventory Model Assumptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Application-model conditions for simulating or optimizing a capacitated finite-horizon inventory system with discrete stochastic demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an inventory system over a deterministic known horizon of $T$ stages with known initial inventory $x_1$. An order placed at the beginning of a stage arrives at the end of that stage, when demand is also realized. The unit holding cost $h$, fixed ordering cost $A$, and unit lost-sales cost $p$ are known with certainty.

children.title: Event-Order Instability
children.top_down_role: Abrupt response changes caused by reordered events.

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Order Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-path discontinuity caused by a parameter-dependent reversal of competing event times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two pending event times \(\tau_1(\theta)\) and \(\tau_2(\theta)\) depend continuously on a scalar parameter \(\theta\), and suppose \(\tau_1(\theta_0)=\tau_2(\theta_0)\) while their order reverses across \(\theta_0\). If processing the first event changes the feasibility, state transition, or scheduled time of the second, then the simulated response \(L(\theta;\xi)\) need not be continuous at \(\theta_0\). Thus pathwise finite-difference or infinitesimal-perturbation estimates that assume a locally unchanged event sequence can fail at, or across, the event-order boundary \(\tau_1(\theta)=\tau_2(\theta)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When parameter changes reverse two interacting events, the simulated state trajectory and response may jump, invalidating derivatives that assume a fixed local event order.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_1\) and \(\tau_2\) are continuous near \(\theta_0\).
The ordering of the two events differs on opposite sides of \(\theta_0\).
The first processed event affects the transition associated with the other.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Continuity or pathwise differentiability of \(L(\theta;\xi)\) at \(\theta_0\) is not guaranteed.

notation.meaning: scheduled time of competing event r

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and cautious 'need not be continuous' conclusion fit the node, but no citation supports the event-order discontinuity mechanism or the stated limitation of pathwise sensitivity estimators. children.title: Rare-Event Congestion Resolution Boundary
children.top_down_role: Failure to resolve infrequent but operationally dominant congestion.

children.title: Rare-Congestion Episodes
children.top_down_role: Infrequent congestion events with large operational impact.

knowledge_statements.title: Rare-Congestion Episodes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-replication resolution boundary for a rare congestion event.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the indicator of a congestion episode in one independent replication be Bernoulli with probability \(p\in(0,1)\), and let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). For an integer \(N\geq1\), the episode count \(K\) over \(N\) independent replications satisfies \(K\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(N,p)\), and
\[\Pr(K=0)=(1-p)^N.\]
Consequently, the probability of observing at least one episode is at least \(1-\alpha\) if and only if
\[N\geq\frac{\log\alpha}{\log(1-p)},\]
equivalently, if and only if \(N\geq\left\lceil\log(\alpha)/\log(1-p)\right\rceil\). When \(Np\ll1\), \(\Pr(K=0)\approx e^{-Np}\), so ordinary replication is unlikely to resolve congestion behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an event with per-replication probability p, the probability of no observations in N independent replications is (1-p)^N. Detection with probability at least 1-alpha requires N to be at least the ceiling of log(alpha)/log(1-p), and detection is unlikely when Np is small.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\{1,2,\ldots\}\) simulation replications are independent.
Each replication has the same congestion-event probability \(p\in(0,1)\).
The missed-event tolerance satisfies \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(K=0)=(1-p)^N\), and detection probability at least \(1-\alpha\) holds exactly when \(N\geq\left\lceil\log(\alpha)/\log(1-p)\right\rceil\).

notation.meaning: Probability of a congestion episode in one replication.
Maximum probability of observing no congestion episode.

children.title: Tail-Probability Underresolution
children.top_down_role: Insufficient simulation evidence for low-probability adverse events.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Probability Underresolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-precision boundary for crude Monte Carlo estimation of a rare tail probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I_1,\ldots,I_N\) be independent Bernoulli indicators with \(\Pr(I_i=1)=p\in(0,1)\), where \(N\in\{1,2,\ldots\}\), and define \(\widehat p_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N I_i\). Then
\[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat p_N)=\frac{p(1-p)}{N},\qquad \frac{\sqrt{\mathbb E[(\widehat p_N-p)^2]}}{p}=\sqrt{\frac{1-p}{Np}}.\]
For any target \(\varepsilon>0\), relative root-mean-square error at most \(\varepsilon\) holds if and only if
\[N\geq\frac{1-p}{p\varepsilon^2}.\]
Thus crude Monte Carlo underresolves the tail when \(Np\) is small.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Bernoulli tail event of probability p, crude Monte Carlo has relative root-mean-square error sqrt((1-p)/(Np)). Achieving a target epsilon therefore requires N at least (1-p)/(p epsilon squared).
assumptions_latex: \(I_1,\ldots,I_N\) are independent and identically distributed Bernoulli variables.
\(p\in(0,1)\), \(N\in\{1,2,\ldots\}\), and \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{RRMSE}(\widehat p_N)=\sqrt{(1-p)/(Np)}\), so the target \(\operatorname{RRMSE}(\widehat p_N)\leq\varepsilon\) holds exactly when \(N\geq(1-p)/(p\varepsilon^2)\).

notation.meaning: Indicator of the tail event in replication i.
Crude Monte Carlo estimator of the tail probability.

children.title: Extreme-Delay Underestimation

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Delay Underestimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-point delay distribution exposing missed-tail bias in finite simulation runs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(p\in(0,1)\) and \(M>0\), and let a simulated delay satisfy \(D=M\) with probability \(p\) and \(D=0\) otherwise. Although \(\mathbb E[D]=pM\), the sample mean \(\overline D_N\) from \(N\) independent replications equals zero whenever every replication misses the extreme delay. Hence
\[\Pr(\overline D_N=0)=(1-p)^N.\]
On this event, the estimated mean underestimates the true mean by \(pM\). For fixed \(N\), choosing small \(p\) and large \(M\) with \(pM\) fixed makes this failure highly probable while preserving a nonzero mean contribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rare but large delay can contribute materially to the true mean while every finite-run observation remains zero with high probability.
assumptions_latex: \(D_1,\ldots,D_N\) are independent copies of the stated two-point delay.
The estimator is the ordinary sample mean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(\overline D_N=0)=(1-p)^N\) despite \(\mathbb E[D]=pM>0\).

children.title: Unstable Queueing Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Unstable Queueing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability boundary for a continuous-time single-server Markovian queue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an \(M/M/1\) queue with Poisson arrival rate \(\lambda>0\), exponential service rate \(\mu>0\), and traffic intensity \(\rho=\lambda/\mu\). A stationary probability distribution exists exactly when \(\rho<1\). If \(\rho=1\), the queue-length chain is null recurrent; if \(\rho>1\), it is transient and \(Q(t)/t\to\lambda-\mu\) almost surely. Thus steady-state simulation estimators are not well-defined for \(\rho\geq1\), and increasing warm-up or run length cannot create a stationary regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An M/M/1 queue has no stationary probability distribution when arrivals meet or exceed service capacity, invalidating steady-state simulation.
assumptions_latex: Arrivals form a Poisson process of rate \(\lambda\).
Service times are independent exponential variables of rate \(\mu\).
The service discipline is non-idling and work conserving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stationary distribution exists if and only if \(\rho<1\); no steady-state queue-length target exists for \(\rho\geq1\).

notation.meaning: Number of customers in the system at time t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The M/M/1 stability classification and fluid-rate assertion are nontrivial claims requiring an authoritative queueing source with a specific locator.

children.title: Near-Critical Queueing Regimes
children.top_down_role: Queueing systems operating close to their stability boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Critical Queueing Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary congestion blow-up as an M/M/1 queue approaches its stability boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a stationary \(M/M/1\) queue with traffic intensity \(0<\rho<1\), the queue length has distribution
\[\Pr(Q=k)=(1-\rho)\rho^k,\qquad k\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}.\]
Consequently,
\[\mathbb E[Q]=\frac{\rho}{1-\rho},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Q)=\frac{\rho}{(1-\rho)^2}.\]
Both moments diverge as \(\rho\uparrow1\). Therefore, even within the stable region, near-critical designs exhibit growing congestion and variability, making fixed-horizon steady-state comparisons increasingly difficult to resolve.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Queue length and its variance diverge as utilization approaches one from below, producing difficult but formally stable simulation regimes.
assumptions_latex: The queue is an \(M/M/1\) system in stationarity.
The traffic intensity satisfies \(0<\rho<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Q]=\rho/(1-\rho)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Q)=\rho/(1-\rho)^2\), both diverging as \(\rho\uparrow1\).

notation.meaning: Stationary number of customers in the system.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stationary geometric distribution and moment formulas are standard and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied.

children.title: Long-Transient Contamination
children.top_down_role: Bias or variability caused by exceptionally persistent initialization effects.

knowledge_statements.title: Long-Transient Contamination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon bias caused by an initially large queue that cannot drain rapidly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider an \(M/M/1\) queue initialized at \(Q(0)=q_0\), and let \(D(t)\) count potential service completions by time \(t\). Pathwise, arrivals cannot reduce the queue and
\[Q(t)\geq q_0-D(t).\]
Since \(\mathbb E[D(t)]=\mu t\), the finite-horizon time average satisfies
\[\mathbb E\!\left[\frac1T\int_0^T Q(t)\,dt\right]\geq q_0-\frac{\mu T}{2}.\]
Thus, whenever \(q_0-\mu T/2\) substantially exceeds the stationary mean \(\rho/(1-\rho)\), the run remains contaminated by initialization; replication alone does not remove this finite-horizon bias.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A queue initialized far above stationarity retains a quantifiable finite-horizon bias when the run is too short to drain its initial backlog.
assumptions_latex: The queue has exponential service rate \(\mu\) and starts with \(q_0\) customers.
Potential service completions are counted by a rate-\(\mu\) Poisson process.
For the stationary comparison, \(0<\rho<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[T^{-1}\int_0^T Q(t)\,dt]\geq q_0-\mu T/2\), giving an explicit long-transient contamination boundary.

notation.meaning: Potential service-completion count by time t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pathwise and integrated transient bounds are plausible, but the record supplies no source for the potential-completion coupling or the stated contamination boundary.

children.title: Event-Calendar Scalability
children.top_down_role: Computational bottlenecks from large event populations or synchronization.

knowledge_statements.title: Event-Calendar Scalability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time and memory cost of a comparison-based future-event calendar.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a discrete-event simulation processes \(N\) events while maintaining at most \(M\) pending events in a binary-heap calendar. Each insertion or deletion of the earliest event costs \(O(\log M)\) comparisons, and accessing the earliest event costs \(O(1)\). Hence sequential processing costs \(O(N\log M)\) time and \(O(M)\) memory. If each processed event schedules at most \(b\) new events for a constant \(b\), these bounds remain unchanged up to constants. Large pending-event populations therefore create a logarithmic per-event calendar bottleneck and linear storage demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A binary-heap event calendar processes N events in O(N log M) time and stores O(M) pending events.
assumptions_latex: The event calendar is implemented as a binary min-heap.
At most \(M\) events are pending at once.
Each processed event schedules at most a constant number of new events.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The calendar requires \(O(N\log M)\) processing time and \(O(M)\) memory.

notation.meaning: Maximum number of simultaneously pending events.
Maximum number of events scheduled by one processed event.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The binary-heap time and memory bounds are standard and the complexity-bound kind fits the container, but the record has no cited source.

children.title: Statistical Optimality Certificates

children.title: Confidence-Interval Stopping
children.top_down_role: Termination based on uncertainty around performance comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence-Interval Stopping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential termination using simultaneous, optional-stopping-valid confidence bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite set, let \(\widehat x\in X\) be the incumbent, and define \(\Delta_x=f(\widehat x)-f(x)\). Initialize \(n=0\). At each stage, obtain additional paired simulation outputs, increment \(n\), and construct simultaneous upper confidence-sequence bounds \(U_{x,n}\) satisfying
\[\Pr\!\left(\forall n\geq1,\ \forall x\in X:\Delta_x\leq U_{x,n}\right)\geq1-\alpha.\]
Stop at \(\tau=\inf\{n:\max_{x\in X}U_{x,n}\leq\varepsilon\}\) and return \(\widehat x\). On the simultaneous-coverage event, stopping certifies \(f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stop when optional-stopping-valid simultaneous upper bounds show that no competitor can improve the incumbent by more than the tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite and the objective is minimized.
The bounds are simultaneous over alternatives and all inspected stages.
The tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At the stopping time \(\tau\), the returned incumbent is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Upper confidence-sequence bound for the incumbent-versus-alternative difference.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.1 Variational inequalities and confidence bounds p. 21

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.1 Variational inequalities and confidence bounds p. 21
