The objective function and alpha domain also require explicit introduction once sourced.

children.title: Optimality-Gap Estimation
children.top_down_role: Statistical assessment of recommendation suboptimality.

children.title: Fixed-Candidate Gap Validation
children.top_down_role: Validation of a prespecified recommendation.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Candidate Gap Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent simultaneous gap certificate for a recommendation fixed before validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a nonempty finite set, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be an objective to be minimized, let \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), and let \(\bar x\in X\) be fixed independently of the validation data. For each \(x\in X\), set \(\Delta_x=f(\bar x)-f(x)\). Suppose validation produces simultaneous upper bounds \(U_x\) satisfying
\[\Pr\!\left(\forall x\in X:\Delta_x\leq U_x\right)\geq1-\alpha.\]
Define \(G^+=\max\{0,\max_{x\in X}U_x\}\). Since
\[f(\bar x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)=\max_{x\in X}\Delta_x,\]
the pair \((\bar x,G^+)\) certifies with confidence at least \(1-\alpha\) that the fixed recommendation has optimality gap at most \(G^+\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a prespecified candidate in a finite minimization problem, simultaneous upper confidence bounds on all candidate-versus-alternative differences yield an upper confidence bound on the candidate's optimality gap.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty finite set and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is minimized.
The candidate \(\bar x\in X\) is fixed independently of validation observations.
The bounds \(U_x\) have joint coverage at least \(1-\alpha\), where \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(f(\bar x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\leq G^+)\geq1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Upper confidence bound for the candidate-versus-alternative difference.
Certified upper bound on the candidate's optimality gap.
Objective function to be minimized over X.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Bounds p. 19

children.title: Adaptive-Candidate Gap Validation
children.top_down_role: Gap assessment after adaptive candidate generation.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Candidate Gap Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sample-split gap certificate for a candidate selected adaptively from training simulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let training data select a random candidate \(\widehat x\in X\), where \(X\) is finite. Generate independent validation data and, conditional on the training data, construct simultaneous bounds \(U_x\) satisfying
\[\Pr\!\left(\forall x\in X:\ f(\widehat x)-f(x)\leq U_x\mid\text{training data}\right)\geq1-\alpha.\]
Then \(G^+=\max\{0,\max_{x\in X}U_x\}\) obeys
\[\Pr\!\left(f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in X}f(x)\leq G^+\right)\geq1-\alpha.\]
Independence of validation from selection is the condition that converts fixed-candidate conditional coverage into a valid unconditional adaptive-candidate certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent post-selection validation preserves optimality-gap coverage for an adaptively generated candidate; ordinary bounds from reused selection data need not do so.
assumptions_latex: The candidate is measurable with respect to the training data.
Validation data are independent of training data.
Conditional simultaneous coverage is at least \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sample-split bound \(G^+\) covers the adaptive candidate's optimality gap with probability at least \(1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Conditional validation upper bound against alternative x.

source_refs.locator: 1.3 Bounds p. 19

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3 Bounds p. 19

A source addressing independent validation after adaptive selection is required; f and the alpha domain should also be introduced.

children.title: Variational Optimality Bounds
children.top_down_role: Optimization-structure bounds used to assess candidate solution quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Variational Optimality Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order variational gap certificate for differentiable convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subset\mathbb R^d\) be nonempty, compact, and convex, and let \(f\) be a real-valued convex function on an open convex neighborhood of \(X\) that is differentiable there. For \(x\in X\), define
\[g(x)=\max_{y\in X}\langle\nabla f(x),x-y\rangle.\]
Then
\[0\leq f(x)-\min_{y\in X}f(y)\leq g(x).\]
Moreover, \(g(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\) minimizes \(f\) over \(X\). Thus \(g(x)\leq\varepsilon\), for \(\varepsilon\geq0\), certifies that \(x\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For differentiable convex minimization over a compact convex set, the maximum first-order linearization improvement upper-bounds the true optimality gap and vanishes exactly at minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subset\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
\(f\) is real-valued, convex, and differentiable on an open convex neighborhood of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\leq f(x)-\min_{y\in X}f(y)\leq g(x)\), and \(g(x)=0\) exactly when \(x\) minimizes \(f\) over \(X\).

notation.meaning: Gradient of the convex objective at x.

children.title: Sampling-Based Confidence Bounds
children.top_down_role: Uncertainty bounds derived from simulation sampling.

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling-Based Confidence Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Student confidence bound for a simulation-estimated optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_N\) be independent normal simulation outputs with unknown mean \(g\) and variance \(\sigma^2>0\), where a candidate's deterministic optimality gap \(G\) satisfies \(G\leq g\). Let \(N\geq2\) be an integer and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). If \(\overline Y_N\) and \(S_N\) are the sample mean and sample standard deviation, then
\[U_{1-\alpha}=\overline Y_N+t_{N-1,1-\alpha}\frac{S_N}{\sqrt N}\]
satisfies \(\Pr(g\leq U_{1-\alpha})=1-\alpha\). Consequently,
\[\Pr(G\leq U_{1-\alpha})\geq1-\alpha,\]
so \(U_{1-\alpha}\) is a valid upper confidence certificate for the candidate's optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent normal simulation outputs, the exact one-sided Student upper confidence bound for their unknown mean also covers any deterministic optimality gap bounded above by that mean.
assumptions_latex: \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_N\) are independent normal variables with common mean \(g\) and variance \(\sigma^2>0\).
The deterministic optimality gap satisfies \(G\leq g\).
\(N\in\{2,3,\ldots\}\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Pr(G\leq U_{1-\alpha})\geq1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: Sample standard deviation of the simulation outputs.
One-minus-alpha quantile of Student's t distribution with N−1 degrees of freedom.

children.title: Hybrid Bound Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates combining optimization structure with sampling uncertainty.

knowledge_statements.title: Hybrid Bound Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate combining a deterministic lower bound with a statistical upper bound for a minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the optimal value be \(f^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)\), and let \(\widehat x\in X\) be the recommended solution. Suppose \(L\le f^*\) is a deterministic valid lower bound and the simulation-derived random variable \(U\) satisfies \(\mathbb P\{f(\widehat x)\le U\}\ge 1-\alpha\). Then \([L,U]\) is a hybrid bound certificate: with probability at least \(1-\alpha\), \[L\le f^*\le f(\widehat x)\le U,\qquad 0\le f(\widehat x)-f^*\le U-L.\] Thus the certificate verifies an optimality gap of at most \(\varepsilon\) whenever the observed width satisfies \(U-L\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A deterministic lower bound and a valid statistical upper bound jointly certify that the recommended solution’s optimality gap does not exceed their difference.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\) and \(f^*>-\infty\).
\(L\le f^*\) holds without statistical error.
\(U\) has simultaneous coverage for the selected recommendation at level \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb P\{0\le f(\widehat x)-f^*\le U-L\}\ge 1-\alpha\).

notation.meaning: deterministic lower bound on the optimal value
statistical upper confidence bound on the recommendation's value

review_flags: Exact hybrid-certificate formulation lacks a directly supporting supplied locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate is mathematically coherent, but no citation supports the hybrid construction or the required coverage after selecting the recommendation.

children.title: Out-of-Sample Simulation Validation
children.top_down_role: Independent simulation assessment of the final recommendation.

knowledge_statements.title: Out-of-Sample Simulation Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent fixed-recommendation validation using simulation randomness excluded from optimization and selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a recommendation \(\widehat x\), generate validation outputs \(Y_1(\widehat x),\ldots,Y_m(\widehat x)\) using random streams independent of all optimization data. Compute \(\overline Y_m=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mY_i(\widehat x)\) and \(S_m^2=(m-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m(Y_i(\widehat x)-\overline Y_m)^2\). Under independent normal outputs, or an applicable asymptotic approximation, report \[\overline Y_m\mathbin{\pm}t_{m-1,1-\alpha/2}\frac{S_m}{\sqrt m}.\] Accept the stated validation tolerance \(h>0\) only if the confidence interval lies inside the prespecified acceptable performance region and its half-width is at most \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Re-simulate the frozen recommendation with independent randomness, report a confidence interval, and accept it only under prespecified performance and precision criteria.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge2\) validation replications are independent of the optimization and selection data.
\(Y_i(\widehat x)\) are independent with finite, positive variance.
The acceptance region, \(\alpha\), and \(h\) are fixed before examining validation outputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is an independent performance estimate and confidence interval for the fixed recommendation \(\widehat x\).

children.title: Simulation-Optimization Complexity

children.title: Simulation-Call Complexity
children.top_down_role: Simulator evaluations required for target decision quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Simulation-Call Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-call complexity for producing a probably approximately optimal simulation-optimization decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a minimization problem with nonempty decision set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), objective \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), and optimal value \(f^*=\inf_{x\in X}f(x)>-\infty\). For an algorithm \(A\), accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\), and failure probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), define its simulation-call complexity by \[N_{\mathrm{call}}(A,\varepsilon,\delta)=\inf\left\{n\in\mathbb N: A\text{ using at most }n\text{ simulator calls returns }\widehat x^{(n)}\in X\text{ with }\mathbb P\!\left(f(\widehat x^{(n)})-f^*\le\varepsilon\right)\ge1-\delta\right\}.\] A bound \(N_{\mathrm{call}}(A,\varepsilon,delta)=O(g(\varepsilon,\delta,d))\) means that, for the specified problem class and oracle model, a constant independent of \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\), and \(d\) bounds the required number of calls by that multiple of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulation-call complexity is the minimum simulator-call budget sufficient for the algorithm to return an epsilon-optimal decision with probability at least one minus delta under a specified problem class and oracle model.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty and \(f^*>-\infty\).
Each invocation of the specified simulator counts as one call, regardless of its internal runtime.
The algorithm returns a measurable recommendation, and the problem class and stochastic-oracle information supplied per call are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{call}}(A,\varepsilon,\delta)\) measures the simulator-call budget required for \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-quality.

children.title: Statistical Sample Complexity
children.top_down_role: Observation requirements for estimation or identification reliability.

knowledge_statements.title: Statistical Sample Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observation complexity for a prescribed estimation or correct-identification guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) denote scalar observations extracted from simulator calls, and let \(E_n\) be the required statistical success event, such as estimation error at most \(\varepsilon\) or correct selection. The statistical sample complexity is \[N_{\mathrm{stat}}(\varepsilon,\delta)=\inf\left\{n\in\mathbb N:\mathbb P(E_n)\ge1-\delta\right\}.\] In the basic mean-estimation model with independent \(\sigma^2\)-sub-Gaussian observations, the sample mean satisfies the sufficient bound \[n\ge \frac{2\sigma^2}{\varepsilon^2}\log\frac{2}{\delta},\] which ensures \(\mathbb P\{\lvert\overline Z_n-\mathbb EZ_1\rvert\le\varepsilon\}\ge1-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample complexity counts observations needed for a specified reliability event; sub-Gaussian mean estimation requires order sigma-squared epsilon-to-minus-two log one-over-delta samples.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\) are independent and identically distributed.
\(Z_i-\mathbb EZ_i\) is \(\sigma^2\)-sub-Gaussian.
\(\varepsilon>0\) and \(\delta\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{stat}}(\varepsilon,\delta)\le\left\lceil2\sigma^2\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2/\delta)\right\rceil\) for sub-Gaussian mean estimation.
review_flags: Supplied locators do not specifically support the stated concentration bound.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sub-Gaussian bound is standard and correctly scoped, but the record supplies no source for either the sample-complexity definition or the stated constant.

children.title: Execution-Time Complexity Family

children.title: Wall-Clock Cost
children.top_down_role: Elapsed-time cost of simulation-optimization execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Wall-Clock Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elapsed-time accounting for simulation, coordination, and finalization in a concurrent run.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a run beginning at time \(s_0\) and returning its final recommendation at time \(F\), define wall-clock cost as \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}=F-s_0\). If simulation jobs \(j=1,\ldots,n\) start at \(s_j\), have realized runtimes \(R_j\), and all completed jobs are required before finalization of duration \(H\), then \[T_{\mathrm{wall}}=\max_{1\le j\le n}(s_j+R_j)-s_0+H.\] This cost includes queuing, synchronization, communication, and idle delays through the realized start and finish times; it is generally not equal to either the number of simulator calls or the sum of their runtimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wall-clock cost is elapsed time from launch to recommendation, including simulation, queuing, communication, synchronization, idle time, and finalization.
assumptions_latex: All required jobs have finite start and completion times.
\(H\ge0\) measures finalization after the last required completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{wall}}=\max_j(s_j+R_j)-s_0+H\).

notation.meaning: realized runtime of simulation job j

children.title: Simulation Runtime Variability
children.top_down_role: Effects of heterogeneous or stochastic replication durations.

knowledge_statements.title: Simulation Runtime Variability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Runtime is modeled as a random computational output distinct from the simulated performance response.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(x,\xi)\ge0\) be the runtime of one simulation at decision \(x\) under random input \(\xi\). Runtime variability is characterized by its conditional distribution \(F_{R\mid x}\), not solely by \(r(x)=\mathbb E[R(x,\xi)]\). For independent concurrent jobs with runtimes \(R_1,\ldots,R_p\), \[\mathbb E\!\left[\max_{1\le j\le p}R_j\right]\ge\max_{1\le j\le p}\mathbb E[R_j].\] Hence replacing random runtimes by their means can underestimate synchronization time. Quantiles or tail probabilities such as \(\mathbb P\{R(x,\xi)>t\}\) are required when deadline or straggler risk is relevant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random simulation runtimes create stragglers; mean runtime alone can understate synchronization delay, so runtime tails or quantiles may be necessary.
assumptions_latex: Each \(R_j\) is nonnegative and integrable.
Concurrent completion requires all listed jobs to finish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\max_jR_j]\ge\max_j\mathbb E[R_j]\), so mean-runtime substitution can understate expected batch completion time.

notation.meaning: runtime at decision x under simulator randomness

review_flags: Supplied locators do not specifically address stochastic runtime distributions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expectation inequality is correct and independence is unnecessary, but no source supports the runtime-distribution and synchronization interpretation.

children.title: Parallel Makespan Effects
children.top_down_role: Completion-time behavior under concurrent simulation workloads.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Makespan Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic list-scheduling bound exposing workload, worker-count, and longest-job effects.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(n\in\mathbb N\) nonpreemptive simulation jobs, all available at time zero, with realized processing times \(r_1,\ldots,r_n\ge0\). Schedule them by greedy list scheduling on \(p\in\mathbb N\) identical workers. Let \(W=\sum_{j=1}^n r_j\), \(r_{\max}=\max_{1\le j\le n}r_j\), and let \(C_{\max}\) be the completion time of the last job. Then \[\max\left\{\frac{W}{p},r_{\max}\right\}\le C_{\max}\le\frac{W}{p}+\left(1-\frac1p\right)r_{\max}.\] Thus parallel speedup is limited by both average workload per worker and the longest realized simulation job.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For jobs all available initially, greedy scheduling finishes no earlier than the larger of average workload and the longest job, and no later than the stated workload-plus-longest-job bound.
assumptions_latex: All \(n\) jobs are available at time zero.
Workers are identical and execute at most one nonpreemptive job at a time.
Communication and scheduling overhead are excluded from \(r_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{W/p,r_{\max}\}\le C_{\max}\le W/p+(1-1/p)r_{\max}\).

children.title: Problem-Scale Complexity Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Scaling with decision dimension, alternative count, or simulated system size.

children.title: Decision-Dimension Scaling
children.top_down_role: Computational or statistical dependence on continuous or mixed decision dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Dimension Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity scaling obtained by varying decision-space dimension while holding other problem parameters explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P_d\) be a family of simulation-optimization problems whose decisions lie in subsets \(X_d\subseteq\mathbb R^d\). For a fixed algorithm \(A\), accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\), failure probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\), and stated regularity parameters \(\theta\), define decision-dimension scaling by the function \[C_d(A;\varepsilon,\delta,\theta)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_d}C(A,P;\varepsilon,\delta),\] where \(C\) is a declared resource such as simulator calls, observations, or elapsed time. A polynomial, exponential, or dimension-free scaling claim refers to the asymptotic growth of \(C_d\) as \(d\to\infty\), with \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\), and \(\theta\) controlled as stated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decision-dimension scaling tracks worst-case resource growth as the number of decision coordinates increases, with accuracy and regularity parameters explicitly controlled.
assumptions_latex: \(X_d\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) defines the decision dimension consistently across the problem family.
The resource \(C\), success criterion, and controlled parameters \(\theta\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The asymptotic behavior of \(C_d\) as \(d\to\infty\) is the decision-dimension scaling.

notation.meaning: worst-case resource complexity at dimension d

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative-Count Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity scaling for finite decision sets as the number of alternatives grows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_K=\{x_1,\ldots,x_K\}\) be a finite set of simulated alternatives, and let \(\mathcal P_K\) be a specified class of corresponding selection problems. For algorithm \(A\), define \[C_K(A;\varepsilon,\delta,\theta)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_K}C(A,P;\varepsilon,\delta),\] where success means returning \(\widehat x\in X_K\) with \(f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in X_K}f(x)\le\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Alternative-count scaling is the asymptotic growth of \(C_K\) as \(K\to\infty\), with the gap structure, noise parameters, accuracy, and confidence convention recorded in \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternative-count scaling measures resource growth as a finite choice set expands under a fixed approximate-selection guarantee and declared noise or gap conditions.
assumptions_latex: \(X_K\) contains exactly \(K\) alternatives.
The resource \(C\) and success criterion are fixed across \(K\).
Noise and indifference-zone or gap assumptions are included in \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The growth of \(C_K\) as \(K\to\infty\) is the alternative-count scaling.

notation.meaning: worst-case resource complexity for K alternatives

children.title: Simulated-System-Size Scaling
children.top_down_role: Dependence on the scale of the modeled operational system.

knowledge_statements.title: Simulated-System-Size Scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity scaling with the size of the simulated model underlying each objective evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s\in\mathbb N\) index simulated-system size, such as the number of agents, network nodes, state variables, or events processed per replication, and let \(\mathcal P_s\) be a specified problem family. For algorithm \(A\), define \[C_s(A;\varepsilon,\delta,\theta)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_s}C(A,P;\varepsilon,\delta).\] Simulated-system-size scaling is the asymptotic growth of \(C_s\) as \(s\to\infty\). The resource \(C\) must be stated: call complexity may remain unchanged while per-call runtime, memory, and consequently wall-clock complexity increase with \(s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Simulated-system-size scaling tracks resource growth as the model simulated per evaluation becomes larger, distinguishing call counts from per-call time and memory.
assumptions_latex: The size index \(s\) has one consistent interpretation across \(\mathcal P_s\).
Accuracy, confidence, and controlled structural parameters \(\theta\) are stated.
The measured resource \(C\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The growth of \(C_s\) as \(s\to\infty\) is the simulated-system-size scaling.

notation.meaning: problem family at system size s
worst-case resource complexity at system size s

children.title: Concurrent Simulation-Optimization Architecture
children.top_down_role: Computational organizations for concurrent simulation and asynchronous search.

children.title: Parallel Replication
children.top_down_role: Concurrent simulation runs at a common decision.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Replication
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concurrent independent replications at one fixed decision, followed by statistically valid aggregation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a decision \(x\), replication count \(m\), and \(p\) workers, assign replication indices \(1,\ldots,m\) to workers. Generate each output as \(Y_i(x)=G(x,\xi_i)\) using mutually independent random streams \(\xi_i\). Workers return indexed outputs asynchronously or in batches; after all required indices arrive, compute \[\widehat f_m(x)=\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^mY_i(x),\qquad \widehat v_m(x)=\frac1{m-1}\sum_{i=1}^m\bigl(Y_i(x)-\widehat f_m(x)\bigr)^2.\] Stop when the prescribed replication count or a valid sequential precision rule is met, and output the estimate with its uncertainty summary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distribute independent replications of one decision across workers, then aggregate indexed outputs into a performance estimate and uncertainty measure.
assumptions_latex: \(m\ge2\) and \(p\ge1\).
Random streams \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\) are mutually independent and correctly indexed.
Aggregation waits for every replication required by the stopping rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm outputs \(\widehat f_m(x)\) and \(\widehat v_m(x)\) from \(m\) independent replications.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Simulation techniques p. 211

children.title: Parallel Candidate Evaluation
children.top_down_role: Concurrent simulation of multiple alternatives or search points.

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Candidate Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concurrent evaluation of distinct search points with explicit allocation and aggregation rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given candidates \(x_1,\ldots,x_K\), a total replication budget \(B\in\mathbb N\), and \(p\in\mathbb N\) workers, choose allocations \(m_1,\ldots,m_K\in\mathbb N_0\) satisfying \(\sum_{k=1}^K m_k\le B\). Dispatch tasks \((k,i)\) that generate \(Y_{k,i}=G(x_k,\xi_{k,i})\), using independent streams unless a declared common-random-number design is employed. For every candidate with \(m_k>0\), compute \(\widehat f_k=m_k^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{m_k}Y_{k,i}\). After the prescribed tasks complete, update the allocation or search state; stop at the budget or a declared statistically valid rule and return the candidate selected by the stated comparison criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allocate an integer number of simulation replications among several candidates, evaluate them concurrently, aggregate results by candidate, and select or reallocate using a prespecified rule.
assumptions_latex: \(K\ge1\), \(B\in\mathbb N\), and \(p\in\mathbb N\).
Every result carries its candidate and replication indices.
Dependence induced by variance-reduction designs is retained in statistical comparisons.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a candidate chosen from concurrently estimated performances under replication budget \(B\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative integer number of replications allocated to candidate k

children.title: Asynchronous Simulation Search
children.top_down_role: Search with pending evaluations and variable completion times.

children.title: Asynchronous Stochastic Approximation
children.top_down_role: Recursive updates using delayed or partially available information.

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous Stochastic Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected coordinate stochastic approximation with bounded information delays.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, and initialize \(x_0\in X\). At accepted completion event \(k\), worker \(i_k\) returns \(G_k\in\mathbb{R}^d\), a stochastic gradient estimate computed at \(x_{k-\tau_k}\), and \(D_k\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) is a diagonal coordinate-selection matrix. Set \[x_{k+1}=\Pi_X\!\left(x_k-a_kD_kG_k\right).\] Advance the logical counter on accepted completions, rather than synchronized worker rounds. Stop at a prescribed event budget or stopping test and return the latest iterate or a specified weighted average.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each accepted worker completion, the method applies a projected stochastic-gradient update using the delayed iterate and the worker's selected coordinates; the logical counter advances by completions rather than synchronized rounds.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable.
Relative to a filtration \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\geq0}\), \(\mathbb{E}[G_k\mid\mathcal F_{k-\tau_k}]=\nabla f(x_{k-\tau_k})\), and the conditional second moments of \(G_k\) are bounded.
\(0\leq\tau_k\leq B\), every coordinate is selected infinitely often, \(a_k>0\), \(\sum_k a_k=\infty\), and \(\sum_k a_k^2<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=\Pi_X(x_k-a_kD_kG_k)\) defines the asynchronous recursive update.

notation.meaning: age of the iterate used by the completed estimate
Euclidean projection onto the feasible set
information filtration for the stochastic updates

children.title: Asynchronous Model-Based Search
children.top_down_role: Metamodel-guided sampling with pending evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous Model-Based Search
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Surrogate-guided sequential design with evaluations already in flight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the admissible design set. At completion event \(t\), let \(C_t\) and \(Q_t\) be the sets of completed and pending evaluation indices, respectively, with \(D_t=\{(x_j,y_j):j\in C_t\}\) and \(P_t=\{x_j:j\in Q_t\}\). Fit a probabilistic surrogate to \(D_t\). If \(Y_{P_t}=(Y_p)_{p\in P_t}\) has the surrogate's joint predictive distribution at the pending sites, define \[\widetilde a_t(x)=\mathbb E\!\left[a\!\left(x;D_t\cup\{(p,Y_p):p\in P_t\}\right)\mid D_t\right].\] Whenever a worker becomes free, dispatch any \(x_{t+1}\in\arg\max_{x\in X\setminus P_t}\widetilde a_t(x)\). On completion, move the corresponding observation from the pending set to \(D_t\), refit as prescribed, and continue until the evaluation budget is exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each worker availability event, the method integrates the acquisition function over the joint predictive outcomes of pending evaluations and dispatches a maximizing nonpending design.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is the admissible design set, and duplicate pending evaluations are excluded unless replication is requested.
The surrogate supplies a joint predictive distribution for \(Y_{P_t}=(Y_p)_{p\in P_t}\).
The acquisition expectation exists, and its maximization over \(X\setminus P_t\) is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{t+1}\in\arg\max_{x\in X\setminus P_t}\widetilde a_t(x)\) is the next asynchronously dispatched design.

notation.meaning: indices of completed evaluations at event t
indices of pending evaluations at event t

children.title: Asynchronous Information-Timing Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Search degradation from obsolete information or duration-dependent completion.

children.title: Stale-Information Failure
children.top_down_role: Search degradation caused by decisions based on obsolete evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale-Information Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A delayed-gradient example where a synchronously stable step becomes unstable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f(x)=x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb R\) with constant step \(a=3/2\). The synchronous iteration is \(x_{k+1}=(1-a)x_k=-x_k/2\) and therefore converges to zero. If every gradient is delayed by one iteration, the update becomes \[x_{k+1}=x_k-a x_{k-1}.\] Its characteristic polynomial is \(r^2-r+a\). Because the product of its two roots is \(a=3/2\), at least one root has modulus greater than one. Except for initial states lying in the stable invariant subspace, the delayed iterates fail to converge and grow in magnitude.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a quadratic objective, step size 3/2 is stable without delay but a one-iteration gradient delay produces a root outside the unit disk.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=x^2/2\) and exact gradients are used.
The step size is constant with \(a=3/2\).
Every update uses the one-step-stale gradient \(\nabla f(x_{k-1})\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-(3/2)x_{k-1}\) is generically unstable although the synchronous iteration converges.

notation.meaning: characteristic root of the delayed recurrence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically consistent and the failure-boundary kind fits, but no inspectable source supports the delayed-instability claim.

children.title: Completion-Time Selection Bias
children.top_down_role: Preferential use of results associated with shorter simulation durations.

knowledge_statements.title: Completion-Time Selection Bias
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias caused by observing simulation outputs in completion-time order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two independent evaluations have \(Y_i=\mu+\varepsilon_i\), where \(\mathbb P(\varepsilon_i=-1)=\mathbb P(\varepsilon_i=1)=1/2\). Assign completion time \(T_i=1\) when \(\varepsilon_i=-1\) and \(T_i=2\) when \(\varepsilon_i=1\), and select the first completed response, breaking ties symmetrically. The selected error equals \(-1\) unless both errors equal \(1\). Consequently, \[\mathbb E[Y_{I}]=\mu-\tfrac12,\qquad I\in\arg\min_{i\in\{1,2\}}T_i.\] Thus an unbiased response becomes biased when selection is based on an outcome-dependent completion time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When low responses finish sooner, the first completed result has expectation μ−1/2 even though every individual simulation response is unbiased for μ.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(\varepsilon_2\) are independent Rademacher variables.
Completion time is the specified deterministic function of each response error.
Ties are resolved independently and symmetrically.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[Y_I]=\mu-1/2\neq\mu\).

notation.meaning: index of the first completed evaluation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite probability calculation is correct and matches the failure leaf, but the record supplies no inspectable citation for completion-time selection bias.

children.title: Duration-Dependent Search Distortion
children.top_down_role: Systematic search effects arising when runtime depends on candidate behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Duration-Dependent Search Distortion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Wall-clock allocation distortion when candidate evaluation durations differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose alternatives \(i=1,\ldots,m\) are evaluated continuously on dedicated identical workers, with independent positive durations \(T_{i,r}\) having finite means \(d_i\). Let \(N_i(t)\) be the number of completed evaluations of alternative \(i\) by wall time \(t\). Renewal limits give \(N_i(t)/t\to 1/d_i\) almost surely. Hence the empirical fraction of all completed results satisfies \[\frac{N_i(t)}{\sum_{j=1}^m N_j(t)}\longrightarrow\frac{d_i^{-1}}{\sum_{j=1}^m d_j^{-1}}.\] Treating completions as if they arose from equal allocation therefore overrepresents fast alternatives and changes the search measure unless durations are equal or explicitly corrected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Completion-count-driven search samples alternatives in inverse proportion to mean duration, so faster simulations are overrepresented unless the allocation corrects for time.
assumptions_latex: For each alternative, evaluation durations are independent and identically distributed, positive, and have finite mean.
Workers remain continuously assigned to their respective alternatives.
Search statistics are indexed by wall-clock completions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_i(t)/\sum_jN_j(t)\to d_i^{-1}/\sum_jd_j^{-1}\) almost surely.

notation.meaning: mean evaluation duration for alternative i
number of evaluations completed by time t

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Under the dedicated-worker assumptions the renewal limit and inverse-duration allocation formula are sound, but neither the renewal result nor its simulation-search interpretation has an inspectable source.

children.title: Distributed Search Coordination
children.top_down_role: Coordination of search state, candidate work, and simulation evidence across distributed workers.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Search Coordination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ledger-based coordination of concurrent simulation-search tasks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a coordinator state \((D_0,Q_0)\), where \(D_0\) contains accepted observations and \(Q_0\) is an empty task ledger. At decision event \(t\), the search policy proposes a finite batch \(B_t=\pi(D_t,Q_t)\). Assign every proposed evaluation a unique logical identifier, record it atomically in \(Q_t\), and dispatch it to an available worker. When a result arrives, accept it only if its identifier is outstanding; atomically move it from \(Q_t\) to \(D_t\), making duplicate reports idempotent. Recompute proposals after each accepted completion. Stop at the declared accepted-evaluation budget and return the incumbent selected from \(D_t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A coordinator atomically tracks unique tasks, dispatches policy proposals, accepts each result once, and updates the search after every accepted completion.
assumptions_latex: The task ledger supports atomic insertion and completion transitions.
Every simulation request has a globally unique logical identifier.
The search policy \(\pi\) is defined for completed and outstanding task states.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each logical task contributes at most one accepted observation to \(D_t\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: atomic ledger and idempotent completion semantics

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ledger algorithm fits distributed search coordination, but its atomic and idempotent coordination guarantees are unsupported by an inspectable source.

children.title: Distributed Worker Fault Recovery
children.top_down_role: Execution resilience under worker loss, retries, or partial task completion.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributed Worker Fault Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lease-based retry with reproducible tasks and idempotent result commitment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent each simulation task by \(q=(u,x,s)\), containing a unique identifier, design, and random-stream key. The coordinator grants a worker a lease expiring at \(e(q)\). If no valid completion is committed before expiry, return \(q\) to the dispatch queue without changing \(x\) or \(s\). A worker computes \(y=H(x,s)\) and submits \((u,y)\). Commit the first valid submission for \(u\) atomically and reject subsequent duplicates. Continue retrying expired tasks until they are committed or a declared retry limit is reached; report unresolved tasks explicitly rather than treating them as observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expired tasks are retried with the same design and stream key, while an atomic first-result commit prevents duplicate observations after worker failures.
assumptions_latex: For fixed \((x,s)\), the simulator output \(H(x,s)\) is reproducible.
Lease expiry can be detected by the coordinator.
Result commitment is atomic and keyed by the unique task identifier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every resolved logical task \(u\) produces exactly one committed value \(H(x,s)\), despite duplicate execution.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: leases, deterministic retry, and idempotent commit

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lease, retry, reproducible-stream, and idempotent-commit construction fits the algorithm leaf, but no inspectable source supports the stated recovery guarantee.

children.title: Random-Stream Architecture
children.top_down_role: Organization of random inputs for reproducible, coupled, and parallel simulation experiments.

children.title: Hierarchical Random-Stream Architecture
children.top_down_role: Partitioned random-number streams for replications and alternatives.

children.title: Independent Random Streams
children.top_down_role: Top-level random-number streams assigned to replications, methods, or alternatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Independent Random Streams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mutual independence of streams assigned to distinct logical simulation units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U_i=(U_{i,1},U_{i,2},\ldots)\) be the random-number sequence assigned to logical unit \(i\) in an index set \(I\). The streams are independent if the generated sigma-fields \(\mathcal G_i=\sigma(U_{i,1},U_{i,2},\ldots)\) are mutually independent: for every finite \(J\subseteq I\) and events \(A_i\in\mathcal G_i\), \[\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{i\in J}A_i\right)=\prod_{i\in J}\mathbb P(A_i).\] Distinct initialization labels alone do not establish this property; the stream construction or generator allocation must justify the stipulated joint law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Random streams are independent when events determined by any finite collection of distinct streams factor into the product of their probabilities.
assumptions_latex: Each \(U_i\) is a random sequence on a common probability space.
The logical-unit index set \(I\) is fixed independently of realized stream values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The family \(\{\mathcal G_i:i\in I\}\) is mutually independent.

notation.meaning: random-number stream assigned to logical unit i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: mutual independence of generated sigma-fields

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generated-sigma-field definition correctly states mutual independence and fits the definition leaf, but it lacks an inspectable random-stream reference.

children.title: Nested Random Substreams
children.top_down_role: Reproducible subdivisions within a parent random-number stream.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Random Substreams
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hierarchical nonoverlapping index blocks of a master random-number sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((Z_n)_{n\geq0}\) be a master generator sequence. Fix positive integers \(L_0>L_1\) with \(L_1\mid L_0\). For each parent-stream index \(r\geq0\) and substream index \(s\in\{0,\ldots,L_0/L_1-1\}\), define the index block \[I_{r,s}=\{rL_0+sL_1+j:0\leq j<L_1\}\] and the corresponding substream \[U_{r,s}=\bigl(Z_n\bigr)_{nin I_{r,s}}.\] The blocks \(I_{r,s}\) partition the parent block \(\{rL_0,ldots,(r+1)L_0-1\}\), and blocks for distinct pairs \((r,s)\) are disjoint. A task must consume at most \(L_1\) generated values from its assigned block to avoid index overlap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each parent block of the master generator is partitioned into disjoint child index blocks, and each child block defines one nested substream.
assumptions_latex: The master sequence \((Z_n)_{n\geq0}\) supports deterministic indexed access or equivalent jump-ahead operations.
\(L_0\) and \(L_1\) are positive integers satisfying \(L_1\mid L_0\).
A task does not consume values outside its assigned index block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I_{r,s}\cap I_{r',s'}=\varnothing\) whenever \((r,s)\neq(r',s')\).

notation.meaning: length of each parent stream block
length of each nested substream block
master-sequence indices assigned to substream s of parent r
generated-value sequence indexed by the block I_{r,s}

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: deterministic partition of generator indices

children.title: Random-Stream Allocation Schemes
children.top_down_role: Mappings of streams or substreams to concurrent simulation tasks.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Stream Allocation Schemes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schedule-invariant assignment of disjoint streams to logical simulation tasks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a logical task-key set \(K\), a stream-label set \(S\), and an injective allocation map \(h:K\to S\). Before dispatch, form each task key from stable attributes such as alternative, replication, and stochastic component, then assign stream label \(h(k)\). Initialize or jump the generator to that label and record \((k,h(k))\) with the result. Retries reuse the same label, while newly created logical tasks receive unused labels. Stop allocating before the reserved label space or any substream length is exhausted. Because allocation depends on logical keys rather than worker identity or completion order, changing the execution schedule does not change assigned random inputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An injective map assigns stream labels from stable task keys, so retries reproduce inputs and worker scheduling cannot change random-number assignments.
assumptions_latex: Task keys are unique and stable across retries.
Distinct stream labels identify nonoverlapping generator segments.
The reserved stream and substream capacities are not exceeded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k\neq k'\Rightarrow h(k)\neq h(k')\), and retries of \(k\) reuse \(h(k)\).

notation.meaning: set of logical simulation task keys

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The schedule-invariant injective allocation is a suitable algorithm for the leaf, but its generator-segment and reproducibility claims lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Coupling-Preserving Parallelism
children.top_down_role: Parallel execution retaining intended cross-alternative dependence.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupling-Preserving Parallelism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schedule-invariant parallel execution preserving a prescribed joint input law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For alternatives \(x,x'\), let \((U_x,U_{x'})\sim\pi_{x,x'}\) be the intended coupled random inputs, and let responses be \(Y_x=H(x,U_x)\) and \(Y_{x'}=H(x',U_{x'})\). A parallel implementation preserves coupling when its logical-key allocation produces \((\widetilde U_x,\widetilde U_{x'})\sim\pi_{x,x'}\) for every admissible worker schedule. Then \[(H(x,\widetilde U_x),H(x',\widetilde U_{x'}))\overset{d}{=}(Y_x,Y_{x'}),\] so the distribution and variance of paired differences are unchanged by parallel execution. Preservation concerns the joint law, not merely the marginal law of each stream.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel execution preserves coupling when every schedule retains the intended joint input distribution, thereby leaving paired-response and difference distributions unchanged.
assumptions_latex: The intended coupling \(\pi_{x,x'}\) is specified for each compared pair.
Random inputs are assigned by logical keys rather than completion order.
The simulator is a measurable function of its design and random input.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H(x,\widetilde U_x)-H(x',\widetilde U_{x'})\overset{d}{=}Y_x-Y_{x'}\) for every admissible schedule.

notation.meaning: intended joint law of inputs for two alternatives

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: preservation of a prescribed joint distribution

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle correctly requires preservation of the joint input law rather than only its marginals, but no inspectable source supports its use in parallel simulation.

children.title: Random-Stream Contamination
children.top_down_role: Unintended dependence, stream overlap, or loss of reproducibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Random-Stream Contamination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stream overlap or schedule-dependent consumption invalidating intended dependence and reproducibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) be independent and identically distributed random inputs, let \(H(U_j)\) have variance \(\sigma^2>0\), and suppose two replication means intended to use independent streams instead reuse the same indexed inputs: \[\bar Y_1=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n H(U_j),\qquad \bar Y_2=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n H(U_j).\] Then \[\operatorname{Cov}(\bar Y_1,\bar Y_2)=\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_1)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n},\] rather than zero, so uncertainty formulas assuming independent replications are invalid. Separately, if logical tasks draw sequentially from one mutable global stream and draw assignment depends on worker interleaving, different admissible interleavings can assign different indexed inputs to the same task and thereby destroy task-level reproducibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identical input reuse creates covariance between replication means, while interleaving-dependent draws from a shared mutable stream can destroy task-level reproducibility.
assumptions_latex: \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) are independent and identically distributed.
\(H(U_j)\) has finite positive variance \(\sigma^2\).
The contaminated replication means reuse the same indexed inputs.
For the schedule-dependent mechanism, draw assignment to logical tasks depends on worker interleaving.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Cov}(\bar Y_1,\bar Y_2)=\sigma^2/n\neq0\), contradicting intended independence.

notation.meaning: sample mean attributed to replication stream i
j-th random input reused by both contaminated replications

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: covariance induced by identical independent inputs

children.title: Computational Experiment Assurance System
children.top_down_role: Experimental architecture for comparing simulation-optimization methods.

children.title: Benchmark Problem Design
children.top_down_role: Problem families spanning geometry, noise, dimension, and simulation cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark Problem Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage condition for a finite simulation-optimization benchmark suite and its declared target population.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal B=\{(P_j,\nu_j,c_j):j=1,\ldots,m\}\), where \(P_j\) is a simulation-optimization problem, \(\nu_j\) its noise law, and \(c_j\) its evaluation-cost model. Given declared strata \(\mathcal G_1,\ldots,\mathcal G_K\) describing geometry, noise, dimension, and cost, the suite is coverage-valid for a target distribution \(\pi\) only if every stratum with \(\pi(\mathcal G_k)>0\) is represented and the reported aggregate is prespecified as \(R(A)=\sum_{j=1}^m w_jL(A,P_j)\), with \(w_j\geq0\), \(\sum_jw_j=1\), and weights justified as an approximation to \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A benchmark suite must represent every declared positive-mass problem stratum and aggregate algorithm loss using prespecified weights tied to its target population.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal B\) is finite and every benchmark has a defined loss and evaluation-cost model.
The target population and its strata are declared before algorithms are compared.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(A)=\sum_{j=1}^m w_jL(A,P_j)\) is interpretable only relative to the declared coverage and weighting scheme.

notation.meaning: Prespecified loss of algorithm A on problem P.

children.title: Budget-Normalized Comparison
children.top_down_role: Comparison under aligned simulation, runtime, or information budgets.

knowledge_statements.title: Budget-Normalized Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fair-comparison condition using a common resource accounting rule and matched stopping budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each algorithm \(A\), let \(C_A(t)\) be cumulative resource consumption after step \(t\) under one prespecified accounting rule, and define \(\tau_A(B)=\sup\{t:C_A(t)\leq B\}\). Algorithms \(A_1,\ldots,A_q\) are budget-normalized at budget \(B\) when every reported outcome is \(L(A_i,P;B)=L(X_{A_i}(\tau_{A_i}(B)),P)\), using the same \(B\), cost functional, initialization policy, and treatment of preprocessing. Comparisons may be indexed by simulation calls, wall-clock time, or information units, but distinct budget types must not be pooled as if interchangeable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare algorithms at the last output affordable under the same declared budget, accounting rule, initialization, and preprocessing convention.
assumptions_latex: \(C_A(t)\) is nondecreasing and measurable for every algorithm.
All charged operations and the budget unit are fixed before execution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The comparison \(L(A_i,P;B)-L(A_k,P;B)\) attributes differences to algorithms conditional on the common resource convention.

notation.meaning: Cumulative charged resource used by algorithm A.
Last algorithm step affordable within budget B.

review_flags: authoritative source needed for resource-accounting and stopping conventions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resource-normalization condition fits the container, but no source supports its accounting conventions. Moreover, the domain of step t is unspecified, and a supremum need not be an attained 'last output' unless discrete steps and attainment are assumed.

children.title: Paired Algorithm Comparison
children.top_down_role: Comparative experiments using controlled random-stream coupling.

knowledge_statements.title: Paired Algorithm Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matched-replication comparison based on common random streams within each independent pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each replication \(r=1,\ldots,n\), run algorithms \(A\) and \(B\) on the same problem and normalized budget using a coupled random stream \(\omega_r\), and define \(D_r=L(A;\omega_r)-L(B;\omega_r)\). If the pairs are independent across \(r\), then the estimated mean difference and its estimated standard error are \(\widehat\Delta=n^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^n D_r\) and \(\widehat{\operatorname{se}}(\widehat\Delta)=s_D/\sqrt n\), where \(s_D^2=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^n(D_r-\widehat\Delta)^2\). Pairing is valid only when the coupling preserves each algorithm's required marginal input law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run both algorithms with matched random streams, analyze within-pair loss differences, and retain independence across pairs without altering either algorithm's marginal simulation law.
assumptions_latex: The paired streams \(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_n\) are independent and identically distributed across replications.
Both algorithms use the same problem instance and normalized budget within each pair.
\(\mathbb E[D_r^2]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\Delta\) estimates \(\Delta=\mathbb E[D_r]\) with variance \(\operatorname{Var}(D_r)/n\).

notation.meaning: Sample standard deviation of paired differences.
Coupled random stream used by both algorithms in replication r.

review_flags: authoritative source needed for paired common-random-number comparison

children.title: Benchmark Generalization Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Misleading performance caused by repeated tuning on narrow test collections.

children.title: Benchmark-Suite Overfitting
children.top_down_role: Method specialization to a narrow or repeatedly reused problem collection.

knowledge_statements.title: Benchmark-Suite Overfitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure caused by selecting an algorithm on the same finite suite used for reporting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the target population be uniform on instance types \(z\in\{1,\ldots,M\}\), with \(M\geq3\). For each \(k\), define algorithm loss \(L(A_k,z)=\mathbf 1\{z\neq k\}\), and let a baseline satisfy \(L(A_0,z)=1/2\). On a one-instance benchmark \(\mathcal B=\{z_0\}\), adaptive selection chooses \(A_{z_0}\), whose reported suite loss is \(0<1/2\), while its population loss is \(1-1/M>1/2\). Thus suite superiority need not generalize when the reporting suite is reused for algorithm selection; an independent evaluation suite removes this particular adaptive reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selecting on the reporting suite can produce perfect benchmark performance while yielding worse population loss than a fixed baseline.
assumptions_latex: The benchmark instance is sampled from the stated target population.
The selected algorithm may depend on the observed benchmark suite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_{\mathcal B}(A_{z_0})<L_{\mathcal B}(A_0)\) but \(\mathbb E_zL(A_{z_0},z)>\mathbb E_zL(A_0,z)\).

notation.meaning: Instance type drawn from the target population.
Algorithm specialized to instance type k.

review_flags: constructed counterexample is self-contained but requires an external methodological source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constructed example correctly illustrates benchmark-suite overfitting and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf. No source is supplied, and the population-loss comparison should explicitly distinguish the benchmark draw z_0 from an independent target-population draw z.

children.title: Hyperparameter-Tuning Overfitting
children.top_down_role: Overoptimistic performance caused by repeated tuning on evaluation instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Hyperparameter-Tuning Overfitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection-induced optimism from tuning many configurations on one noisy validation sample.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(K\geq2\) hyperparameter configurations have equal population loss \(R_k=0\), while their validation estimates are \(\widehat R_k=\sigma Z_k/\sqrt n\), where \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_K\) are independent standard normal variables. Selecting \(\widehat k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{1\leq k\leq K}\widehat R_k\) and reporting the same validation score gives \(\mathbb E[\widehat R_{\widehat k}]=-(\sigma/\sqrt n)\mathbb E[\max_{1\leq k\leq K}Z_k]<0\), although \(R_{\widehat k}=0\). Hence validation performance is optimistically biased after adaptive tuning; evaluation on fresh data independent of \(\widehat k\) has conditional mean \(R_{\widehat k}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choosing the best of many noisy validation scores makes the reused validation score optimistically biased, even when every configuration has identical true performance.
assumptions_latex: Validation errors \(Z_1,ldots,Z_K\) are independent standard normal variables in this counterexample.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\widehat R_{\widehat k}]<\mathbb E[R_{\widehat k}]=0\).

notation.meaning: Population loss of hyperparameter configuration k.
Noisy validation loss of configuration k.
Configuration selected by minimum validation loss.
Independent standard normal validation error for configuration k.

review_flags: constructed Gaussian selection example requires an external selection-bias source

children.title: Cross-Benchmark Generalization Failure
children.top_down_role: Performance degradation on problem families outside the tuning collection.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Benchmark Generalization Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance rankings can reverse when the deployment benchmark distribution differs from the evaluation distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let instances be \(z\in\{0,1\}\), and define losses \(L(A,z)=z\) and \(L(B,z)=1-z\). Under benchmark distribution \(Q\) concentrated at \(z=0\), \(R_Q(A)=0<1=R_Q(B)\). Under distribution \(R\) concentrated at \(z=1\), \(R_R(A)=1>0=R_R(B)\). Therefore an algorithm ranking established on one benchmark distribution does not imply the same ranking on another without assumptions linking their supports, density ratios, or conditional loss structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two algorithms can reverse rankings across benchmark distributions, so performance transfers only under explicit assumptions connecting evaluation and deployment populations.
assumptions_latex: Benchmark risk is \(R_D(C)=\mathbb E_{z\sim D}[L(C,z)]\).
No structural relation between distributions \(Q\) and \(R\) is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_Q(A)<R_Q(B)\) does not imply \(R_R(A)<R_R(B)\).

notation.meaning: Expected loss of algorithm C under distribution D.
Loss of algorithm C on instance z.

review_flags: constructed distribution-shift counterexample requires an external generalization source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ranking-reversal counterexample is mathematically coherent and the failure-boundary kind matches the leaf, but no external source supports the broader cross-benchmark generalization claim.

children.title: Reproducible Experiment Records
children.top_down_role: Persistent records of configurations, seeds, budgets, outputs, and comparison settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Reproducible Experiment Records
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A machine-checkable record supporting replay and audit of a simulation-optimization experiment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An experiment record is a tuple \(\mathcal R=(I,V,A,H,B,S,O,M)\) containing immutable problem inputs \(I\), version identifiers \(V\), algorithm specification \(A\), hyperparameters \(H\), resource budget and accounting rule \(B\), random seeds or stream states \(S\), raw outputs \(O\), and metric definitions \(M\). It is a replay certificate when an independent executor can reconstruct the prescribed run from \((I,V,A,H,B,S)\), recompute \(M(O)\), and verify declared cryptographic digests and numerical tolerances. Summary statistics alone do not constitute such a certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reproducible record preserves inputs, versions, algorithms, tuning, budgets, randomness, raw outputs, and metrics so an independent executor can replay and verify results.
assumptions_latex: All referenced artifacts are immutable or content-addressed.
Numerical equality and any permitted tolerance are declared before replay.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful replay and digest checks certify consistency of the reported results with \(\mathcal R\), not correctness of the scientific claim.
review_flags: reproducibility-record requirements need an authoritative computational-science source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role is appropriate because the statement requires replay and verification, but no authoritative reproducibility source supports the asserted record fields or the sufficiency of the replay criterion.

children.title: Computational Environment Capture
children.top_down_role: Preservation of software, hardware, simulator, and dependency context for repeated experiments.

knowledge_statements.title: Computational Environment Capture
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Environment manifest sufficient to audit or reproduce the executable computational context.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A computational-environment manifest is \(\mathcal E=(O,H,R,L,C,F)\), recording operating system and architecture \(O\), hardware \(H\), language runtimes and compilers \(R\), dependency versions and hashes \(L\), container or build description \(C\), and numerical or concurrency flags \(F\). The manifest is a reproduction certificate for an experiment only if it resolves every execution-affecting dependency and permits reconstruction of an environment in which the recorded program and inputs reproduce prescribed output digests or declared numerical tolerances. Capturing package names without versions, hashes, and relevant hardware settings is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capture all execution-affecting software, hardware, build, dependency, and numerical settings; verify the reconstruction against output hashes or declared tolerances.
assumptions_latex: The experiment's code and input artifacts are content-addressed.
The replay criterion specifies exact hashes or explicit numerical tolerances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A successful reconstruction from \(\mathcal E\) certifies environment-level reproducibility under the stated replay criterion.
review_flags: environment-capture sufficiency criteria need an authoritative reproducibility standard

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The environment-certificate role fits the leaf, but the claim that every execution-affecting dependency must be resolved and that the listed manifest is sufficient requires an authoritative reproducibility standard or computational-science source.
